docs.title: easyMeasure
docs.text:
A generic Python framework for controlling test instrumentation and running automatic, arbitrary-dimensional measurements, with a crash-proof backend and a PySide6 GUI that can be closed, killed or restarted at any time without disturbing a running measurement.

Install it Quick start Tutorials Supported instruments

docs.title: New here?
docs.text:
easyMeasure is made for the measurements of a physics lab: sweep a gate, step a magnetic field, record a lock-in, a source-measure unit or a network analyzer, and watch the result appear as a curve or a colour map. You do all of that from the window above; no programming is needed.

  1. Install it: a few minutes.
  2. Quick start: your first measurement, on a simulated graphene sample that comes with easyMeasure. You add the instruments, give the channels names and safe limits, and sweep a gate voltage to find the Dirac peak. No hardware needed.
  3. Tutorials: a Landau fan (a 2-D map), rotated gate sweeps in density and displacement field, stopping a sweep when the leakage current gets too high, and the power dependence of a microwave resonator measured with a network analyzer.

Key ideas explains the few words easyMeasure uses (instrument, alias, sweep, dimension, …) on one page.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
You describe your instruments once (a setup): which driver, which port, which channels you care about and how far and how fast each may be driven. You then describe a measurement as a sweep: which channels step through which values, in how many nested dimensions, and what is recorded at each point. easyMeasure checks every setpoint against the limits before the first one is set. It then runs the sweep, streams the data into a crash-safe file, plots it live in as many windows as you like, and appends a summary slide to your PowerPoint file when it ends.

When clicking is no longer enough, the same can be done from Python: loops over conditions, measurements that decide where to measure next, control from a Jupyter notebook.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Backend / frontend split. The backend is its own process. The GUI talks to it only over non-blocking sockets. Killing a frozen GUI never touches the backend, and a reopened GUI picks up the running sweep where it is.
  • Hardened against buggy hardware.
    • Every driver call runs on a guarded worker thread with a hard deadline.
    • Hung drivers are abandoned and the instrument reconnected.
    • Any exception is contained, even SystemExit.
    • Replies are validated against the channel type and shape.
    • Transient errors are retried.
    • A channel that keeps hanging is quarantined by a circuit breaker, so it cannot block the rest of its instrument.
  • Crash-safe data. Sweeps stream into an append-only, CRC-checked journal that is fsync-ed continuously. After a crash or power cut, everything up to the last fraction of a second loads as a partial dataset; missing points are NaN.
  • Arbitrary N-D sweeps. Each dimension can have any number of swept and recorded channels. Also supported:
    • mapping functions for non-uniform or vector / tensor setpoints;
    • per-dimension delays and snake scans;
    • pre / post constants, recordings and hooks;
    • per-point actions with continue / break / exit flow control.
  • Protection. Limits and ramp rates live on aliases. Every setpoint of a sweep is limit-checked before it starts, and composite channels respect the ramp rate of every target.
  • Composite channels. These are software channels built on the hardware ones:
    • multivariate writes, where several variables drive several gates;
    • computed reads;
    • one-to-one mappings, checked to be invertible.
  • Live N-D plotting. Plots can be curves, stacked curves or heat maps with draggable levels and colormaps, with sliders for the extra dimensions. There is also a monitor panel, and automatic PowerPoint slides at the end of every run.
  • Ready-made hardware drivers, each tested against an emulator built from the instrument's programming manual:
    • SMUs: Keithley 2400, Keysight B2901 / B2902;
    • SR830 / SR850 lock-in amplifiers;
    • HP 34401A multimeter;
    • Yokogawa 7651 source;
    • HP 4145 / 4155 parameter analyzers;
    • NI USB-6211 and USB-63xx DAQs;
    • Cygnus 16430 supply.

A Driver Wizard builds drivers for other command-based instruments from a form. See Supported instruments. * Remote access over the internet. A TLS gateway, running in its own process, serves a browser version of the GUI and a Python RemoteClient. It has accounts, roles, brute-force lock-out, rate limits and an audit log.

docs.title: Key ideas
docs.text:
Eight words cover almost everything in easyMeasure.

Instrument One device in your rack, connected through a driver (which kind of instrument it is) at an address (where it is connected: GPIB0::24::INSTR, COM3, …). You give it a short name: bg, lockin, vna. Channel

Anything with a name that you read or write. Every channel is read and written the same way (the Manual panel, a sweep, a script: get(name), set(name, value)) and has an access: readable (r), writable (w) or both (rw), which is always respected. There are a few kinds:

kind name access a quantity of an instrument bg.voltage, lockin.X, vna.S11 what the instrument allows a setting of an instrument (⚙) lockin.sensitivity, dmm.function what the instrument allows an action of an instrument dmm.reset, lockin.auto_gain w: writing it runs it an alias Vbg the instrument channel's a composite channel Rxx, nD.n r (a formula), rw (variables, mappings) a parameter Cb rw (a value), r (a formula) a user action gates_to_zero w: writing it runs it the clock @time r

A channel holds a number, an array (a spectrum, a VNA trace, a camera image) or a text; an action holds nothing. Names are unique: no alias, composite, parameter, user action and instrument share a name. The channels of an instrument sit under its name (bg.…) and are written as they are, without limits or ramps.

Alias Your name for a channel of an instrument, for example Vbg for bg.voltage. It carries the protection: minimum, maximum and ramp rate, and an optional scale (V → Ω, an amplifier gain). Measurements use aliases. Composite channel

A channel computed from others. Examples:

  • carrier density and displacement field, driving two gates (nD.n, nD.D; tutorial 2);
  • a resistance computed from a voltage and a current measured by two lock-ins (tutorial 2);
  • a temperature in °C on a controller that works in K.
Parameter A named constant of your setup: a capacitance, a bias resistor, a gain. Formulas of composite channels and actions use it by name (Cb), so a new calibration is one change. It can be a formula of other parameters (Ct/Cb). See Parameters. Sweep A measurement. Some channels step through values in one or more nested dimensions, and others are recorded at every step. Dimension 1 is the innermost (fastest) loop. Every value is checked against the limits before the first one is set. Queue Sweeps wait in the queue and run one after another, so you can line up a night's worth of measurements. The queue also runs scripts: Python programs for what a single sweep can't do, such as a sweep at each of a list of temperatures (an advanced topic: Scripting and Python). Setup Everything above that describes your experiment: instruments, aliases, composite channels, the monitor list and your actions. It is saved automatically, and you can keep copies as files.

And two programs:

  • the backend owns the instruments and runs the measurements;
  • the GUI is a window onto it.

Close, crash or restart the GUI as you like; the measurement is not affected. Several windows can be open at once, also from other computers through the web app.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: easyMeasure needs Python 3.9 or newer and runs on Windows, Linux and macOS. Measurements with real instruments are usually done on Windows, where the vendors' VISA and DAQ runtimes are best supported.

docs.title: From the repository
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/caoyuan96421/easyMeasure.git
cd easyMeasure
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate          # Windows;  source .venv/bin/activate on Linux / macOS
pip install -e .

pip install -e . installs easyMeasure with everything it needs:

package for numpy, h5py data, HDF5 export PySide6, pyqtgraph, matplotlib desktop GUI, plots, slide figures python-pptx (+ pywin32 on Windows) PowerPoint slides, also into an open presentation pyvisa, pyserial GPIB / USB / LAN / serial instruments nidaqmx NI DAQ cards (ni6211, ni63xx) aiohttp, cryptography remote access (HTTPS / WSS gateway, certificates)

Optional extras:

pip install -e ".[hardware]"     # + pyvisa-py: VISA without NI-VISA (LAN, USB-TMC, serial)
pip install -e ".[test]"         # + pytest, pytest-timeout
pip install -e ".[webtest]"      # + playwright (browser test of the web app)
python -m playwright install chromium   # after [webtest]

docs.title: Windows shortcuts
docs.text:
The repository has three batch files:

file does setup_venv.bat creates .venv and installs everything run_demo_backend.bat starts a backend with the simulated demo instruments run_gui.bat starts the GUI

docs.title: Vendor runtimes for real instruments
docs.text:
pip cannot install the vendors' driver runtimes. Install the ones your instruments need:

instruments install GPIB, USB-TMC, VISA LAN (GPIB0::…, USB0::…, TCPIP0::…) a VISA library: NI-VISA or Keysight IO Libraries Suite, plus the GPIB card's driver (NI-488.2 for NI cards). Without a vendor VISA, pip install pyvisa-py covers LAN, USB-TMC and serial. NI DAQ (DAQ::Dev1) NI-DAQmx (the Python package nidaqmx already comes with easyMeasure) Serial / USB-serial (COM3, /dev/ttyUSB0) nothing beyond the adapter's driver (FTDI, CH340 …) Raw TCP sockets, Prologix GPIB-Ethernet (TCP::host::port) nothing

You can check what the backend computer sees from the GUI: Instruments → Add… lists the ports and devices found per interface, and Refresh scans again. The backend command discover_resources does the same.

If pyvisa, a VISA library or the NI-DAQmx runtime is missing, the scan says so. Nothing else is affected, and the simulated instruments always work.

docs.title: Check the installation
docs.text:
python -m easymeasure.backend --help
python -m easymeasure.frontend --start-backend     # GUI + a backend in the background

The GUI opens and asks for a data folder and a PowerPoint file the first time. Continue with the Quick start.

docs.title: Run the tests (optional)
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[test]"
python -m pytest -q tests            # a few minutes; GUI tests run offscreen

See Testing for the stress tests.

docs.title: Build this documentation
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[docs]"
mkdocs serve                          # http://127.0.0.1:8000

The reference pages for drivers, commands and modules are generated from the code at every build. The site on GitHub Pages is rebuilt by a GitHub Actions workflow on every push to main.

docs.title: Emulated hardware
docs.text: Give a hardware driver the address SIM::<anything> (NI DAQs: DAQ::SIM) and it talks to a built-in emulator of the instrument instead of a port - useful to rehearse a measurement before the instrument is connected.

docs.title: Quick start: your first measurement
docs.text:
This page takes you from an empty program to a finished measurement, clicking through the GUI. It takes about fifteen minutes. You need no hardware: easyMeasure comes with simulated instruments that behave like real ones, connected to a simulated graphene device.

The story. You have a graphene Hall bar with a back gate. You want the classic first measurement: the four-probe resistance \(R_{xx}\) as a function of the back-gate voltage. It shows a peak, the Dirac peak, where the carrier density crosses zero. In the lab you would wire it up like this:

role real instrument simulated stand-in (this page) back-gate voltage, and measure the gate leakage current a source-measure unit, e.g. Keithley 2400 (keithley2400, GPIB) sim_smu four-probe voltage; its 10 mV sine output drives about 10 nA through a 1 MΩ series resistor and the sample a lock-in amplifier, e.g. SR830 (sr830, GPIB) sim_lockin with sample = graphene

The steps are the same with the real instruments. Only the driver and the address differ.

docs.title: 1. Start easyMeasure
docs.text:
After installing, start the GUI. It starts the backend too:

python -m easymeasure.frontend --start-backend

On Windows you can also double-click run_gui.bat.

easyMeasure runs as two programs:

  • the backend, which talks to the instruments and runs the measurements;
  • the GUI (the window), which is only a view of the backend.

You can close the window at any time; a running measurement goes on. A small tray icon shows what the backend is doing.

The first time, the GUI asks where to save your data and which PowerPoint file to append a summary slide to after every measurement. Leave the PowerPoint file empty if you don't want slides. Both can be changed later in File → Settings.

  1. Data folder: every measurement is saved here, in one sub-folder per day.
  2. PowerPoint file: optional; a slide with plots is added after each measurement.
  3. Use these.

docs.title: 2. The window
docs.text:
• Left: three tabs.
    • Instruments & channels: which instruments you have, and what you call their channels.
    • Sweep editor: where you describe a measurement.
    • Queue: what is running, and what ran before.
  • Middle: the data, with Live data for the running measurement and one tab for each file you open.
  • Right: the Monitor, which shows values that are read continuously, and the Manual panel, which sets values by hand.
  • Bottom: the log.

docs.title: 3. Add the instruments
docs.text:
On the Instruments & channels tab, click Add… under Instruments:

The gate source. Fill in the dialog:

  • Name: a short name you choose. bg for back gate.
  • Driver: the kind of instrument. sim_smu is a simulated source-measure unit. For a real Keithley 2400 you would pick keithley2400. See the full list of supported instruments.
  • Address: where the instrument is connected. Simulated instruments need no port: NONE. For real instruments the list offers every port and device found on the computer, for example GPIB0::24::INSTR, with the ones that answer as this kind of instrument marked ✓.

Click OK. The instrument appears in the list as connected.

The lock-in. Click Add… again. Name lockin, driver sim_lockin, address NONE. In Options, change "sample": "dot" to "sample": "graphene", so the simulated lock-in measures the graphene device:

Options are settings of the instrument that you set once. Every driver has its own options, listed in the driver's reference page. Real instruments mostly need none.

docs.title: 4. Name the channels you care about
docs.text:
Select an instrument on the left. Its channels appear in the middle list. bg has voltage (what it sources), current (what it measures), and two settings marked ⚙: output and compliance.

You won't use bg.voltage directly. Instead you give it a name, an alias, which also carries its protection: how far and how fast it may ever be driven. A gate dielectric breaks if the voltage is too high, and a fast jump can damage the sample. easyMeasure checks these limits for every value it sets, including every point of a measurement before the measurement starts.

  1. Select bg.
  2. Select voltage.
  3. Click Make alias….

  • Name Vbg.
  • Minimum −10 and Maximum 10 (V): nothing will ever set the gate beyond ±10 V.
  • Ramp rate 5 (V/s): every change of the gate is a smooth ramp at most this fast, never a jump.
  • Unit V, and a Description if you like.

Do the same for bg.current, naming it Ileak with unit A. It is the gate leakage current, worth watching.

The resistance. The lock-in measures a voltage, \(V_{xx}\). With 10 nA flowing, \(R_{xx} = V_{xx} / 10\,\text{nA} = V_{xx} \times 10^8\). An alias can do this conversion for you. Select lockin, then its channel X, then Make alias…:

  • Name Rxx.
  • Scale 1e8, since the alias value is the raw value × scale.
  • Unit Ω.

This assumes the current stays at 10 nA, which holds while the sample resistance is small compared with the 1 MΩ series resistor. Tutorial 2 measures the current with a second lock-in and computes \(R_{xx} = V_{xx}/I\) exactly.

Now you have three aliases:

docs.title: 5. Try it by hand
docs.text:
Before measuring, check that everything responds. The Manual panel (right) lists every channel you can set. Type 2 into Vbg (1) and press Enter: the gate ramps to 2 V at 5 V/s. To watch the resistance, choose Rxx at the top of the Monitor and click Monitor (2):

Set Vbg back to 0 when you are done.

docs.title: 6. Describe the measurement: a sweep
docs.text:
A measurement in easyMeasure is a sweep: some channels are stepped through values, and at every step others are recorded. Open the Sweep editor tab:

  1. Name: dirac_peak. It goes into the file name.
  2. Points: 161.
  3. Set swept channels: click + sweep channel, choose Vbg, Start -8, Stop 8. That gives 161 points, 0.1 V apart.
  4. Record: tick Rxx and Ileak. Before recording, the pre-sample delay of 0.02 s gives the lock-in time to settle after each step. With a real lock-in, use 3 to 5 time constants. In the Sweep menu (menu bar, at the top of the window):

  1. Validate: easyMeasure computes every point and checks it against the limits. The status line of the editor says ✔ valid: shape 161 = 161 points.
  2. Add & start.

Also worth a look: the Post-sweep tab. Add a constant there, Vbg = 0, and the gate goes back to 0 V when the measurement ends, even if it ends with an error or you abort it. Sweep → Save… stores the sweep as a file for next time. This one is examples/graphene_dirac.json (Sweep → Load…).

docs.title: 7. Watch it run
docs.text:
The Live data tab shows the measurement as it comes in. There is one plot for each recorded channel, a progress bar, and the estimated time left:

There's the Dirac peak, at \(V_{bg} \approx 0.3\) V where the carrier density is zero, and the leakage current stays in the picoampere range. Things to try:

  • the X box chooses the horizontal axis, and ⚙ the colours and options;
  • move the mouse over a plot to read values;
  • Add plot shows another channel, or the same one twice;
  • the toolbar's Pause and Abort work at any point. Abort still runs the post-sweep phase, so the gate returns to 0.

Close the window during a measurement and start it again: the measurement never stopped, and the live view picks it up where it is.

docs.title: 8. Your data
docs.text:
When the sweep ends, the Queue tab lists it in the history:

  • The data is in your data folder, e.g. data/2026-11-11/00001_dirac_peak.emj. The file is written while the measurement runs, so it survives a crash or a power cut. An HDF5 copy (.h5) is written next to it at the end.
  • Open data (or File → Open data file…) opens it in a new tab with the same plots.
  • If you set a PowerPoint file, a slide with the plots and a summary was appended.
  • Loading the data in Python, or in any program that reads HDF5: see Data files.

docs.title: 9. Save your setup
docs.text: Instruments, aliases and everything else you defined form your setup. easyMeasure saves it automatically after every change and restores it when it starts again. To keep a copy, or to use it on another computer, use Setup → Save setup… in the menu bar. The setup of this whole tutorial series is examples/graphene_setup.json.

docs.title: User guide
docs.text:
The user guide explains each part of easyMeasure in full: every button, option and rule. It is the place to look things up.

New to easyMeasure?

Start with the Quick start and the tutorials. They walk through real measurements step by step, with screenshots. Come back here when you want to know everything a part can do.

Each page describes the GUI first. Where the same can be done from Python, it follows in a box marked From Python, which you can skip. The Scripting and Python chapter explains how that works.

You can try everything with the simulated instruments, without any hardware: load examples/graphene_setup.json (Setup → Load setup…), or start the backend with the older demo setup, python -m easymeasure.backend --setup examples/demo_setup.json.

docs.title: The parts
docs.text:
Building a setup

  1. Instruments: adding instruments, addresses, channels, settings, actions, finding what is connected.
  2. Aliases and protection: short names, limits, ramp rates, scaling.
  3. Composite channels: channels computed from others, such as the density and displacement field of a dual-gated sample.
  4. Parameters: named constants (capacitances, gains) that formulas use by name.

Measuring

  1. Sweeps: the sweep editor, dimensions, setpoints, recording, delays, pre- and post-sweep settings.
  2. Point actions and flow control: code at every point; skipping points, ending a sweep early.
  3. The run queue: queueing, pausing, aborting, the history.
  4. User actions: your own one-click buttons ("all gates to zero").
  5. Data files: where data goes, the crash-safe journal, HDF5, loading data in Python.

Watching and reporting

  1. Desktop GUI: the panels, the lock, settings.
  2. Plotting live and stored data: curves, heat maps, sliders.
  3. Monitor and Manual panels: watching and setting channels.
  4. PowerPoint reports: a slide for every sweep.

Working from elsewhere

  1. Remote access and the web app: measuring from home, accounts, roles.

Instruments without a driver

  1. Driver Wizard: a driver from a form, no programming.
  2. Simulated instruments: trying things out, fault injection.

Under the hood

  1. Robustness: what protects a measurement from misbehaving hardware.
  2. Testing: the test suite and stress tests.

Python clients and writing drivers in Python are in the Scripting and Python chapter.

docs.title: The ideas in one paragraph
docs.text: An instrument is a driver connected to a port. It has channels (numbers, arrays such as spectra, or text) and actions. An alias gives an instrument channel a short name and carries its protection: limits, ramp rate and scale. Composite channels compute instrument values from your own variables, or the other way round. A sweep sets channels through any number of nested dimensions and records others at every point. Sweeps and scripts run one at a time from the queue. Every run is written to a crash-safe data file. Instruments, aliases, composites, the monitor list and user actions together form the setup, which is saved as a file and autosaved. Key ideas explains each with a picture of where it lives in the GUI.

docs.title: Aliases and protection
docs.text:
An alias gives one instrument channel a short name and carries its protection: limits, ramp rate and scaling. Protection belongs to the alias, not to the instrument, so the same source can be a gate limited to ±10 V in one setup and a heater limited to 5 V in another.

Instrument channels can be read and written anywhere under their full name (lockin.X, bg.voltage), but such a write is plain: no limits, no ramp. Set what needs protection (gates, magnets, heaters) through an alias: then nothing is set beyond its limits or faster than its ramp rate, in a sweep, the Manual panel or a script. Any channel of an instrument can be aliased, settings too. The alias' access is the channel's (read-only removes writing).

docs.title: Making an alias
docs.text:
In Instruments & channels, select the instrument, then its channel, and click Make alias…. Or, on the Channels (aliased) tab, click Add… and choose the target channel there.

The aliases appear in the Channels (aliased) table, and from then on in every channel list: sweeps, Monitor, Manual, plots.

Select an alias and click Edit… to change it, or Remove to delete it (refused while a composite channel uses it).

docs.title: The fields
docs.text: field meaning Name the alias name, used everywhere: sweeps, monitor, scripts, Manual panel Target the instrument channel, instrument.channel Minimum, Maximum hard limits, in alias units. A value outside is refused, and nothing is written Ramp rate the fastest change allowed, in alias units per second. Empty: jump Ramp step optional: the largest step per write while ramping Scale, Offset alias value = instrument value × scale + offset (amplifier gain, divider, unit change) Unit shown in the front ends and data files Allowed values text channels: the values that may be written; narrows the instrument's own list Read only refuse every write through this alias Description free text, shown as a tooltip

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Limits are checked everywhere a value is set: the Manual panel, scripts, composite channels, and every setpoint of a sweep. A sweep is checked completely before it starts, so it can't fail halfway because a point is out of range. NaN and infinity are never written.

Choose limits from what the sample tolerates, not from what the instrument can do: the breakdown voltage of a gate dielectric, the critical current of a junction, the largest field the sample holder takes.

docs.title: Ramp rates
docs.text:
With a ramp rate, a change moves the instrument there in small, timed steps. Going from 0 to 5 V at 5 V/s takes one second. This protects gates, magnets and superconducting samples from sudden jumps.

  • Sweeps ramp between points, and to the first point, at the alias' rate.
  • Ramps can be aborted.
  • A ramp starts from where the instrument really is. After an instrument action or a direct write, the remembered value is discarded and the start is read back.
  • The Manual panel's ramp box can switch ramping off for a single write (a jump); use with care.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
An amplifier, a divider, or a different unit. The alias is in the units you think in, the instrument in its own:

situation target scale alias unit ×10 voltage amplifier after a DAC output daq.ao0 10 V at the sample current preamplifier at 10⁻⁷ A/V into a voltmeter dmm.Vdc 1e-7 A a lock-in voltage, as a four-probe resistance at 10 nA excitation lockin.X 1e8 Ω a source in millivolts src.V1 1000 mV

Limits and ramp rate are in alias units, after scaling. The graphene setup of the tutorials uses the third line for Rxx.

docs.title: Text channels
docs.text: For a channel whose value is text, such as a measurement mode, Allowed values narrows what can be written: with Vdc, Idc, only those two modes can be set through the alias, even though the meter has more.

docs.title: Built-in channels
docs.text: @time (Unix time) and @elapsed (seconds since the sweep started) can be recorded like any channel.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
Defining and using aliases from a Python client 
c.call("define_alias", name="Vg", target="src.V1", min=-2, max=2, ramp_rate=2.0,
       unit="V", description="gate voltage")
c.call("define_alias", name="Isd", target="dmm.Vdc", scale=1e-7, unit="A")
c.call("define_alias", name="dmm_mode", target="dmm.mode", allowed=["Vdc", "Idc"])

c.call("write_channel", name="Vg", value=0.6)               # ramps
c.call("write_channel", name="Vg", value=0.0, ramp=False)   # jumps
c.call("write_channel", name="Vg", value=5)
# LimitError: Vg: value 5 above maximum 2

c.call("define_alias", name="Vg", target="src.V1", min=-1, max=1, ramp_rate=1,
       replace=True)                                       # change it
c.call("remove_alias", name="Vg")

See Python clients.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Composite channels build channels on top of aliases, such as the carrier density and displacement field of a dual-gated sample.

docs.title: Composite channels
docs.text:
Composite channels are software channels built on aliases, and on each other. There are three types:

type what it is example multivariate write (multi) named variables; hardware channels are formulas of them detuning ε and energy U driving two gates composite read (read) a read-only formula of other channels resistance V / I simple mapping (map) a one-to-one view of one channel, with forward and backward formulas a setpoint in °C on a controller in K

docs.title: Defining one
docs.text:
In Instruments & channels, on the Channels (composite) tab, click Add…. The editor has a type selector, a variables table and the formulas. Check runs every check described below without defining anything, and shows which channels the composite would define; OK checks first and keeps the editor open if the check fails:

Tutorial 2 builds this one step by step: the carrier density n and displacement field D of a dual-gated sample, driving the two gate voltages, in a composite nD. Once defined, the variables are channels like any alias, named nD.n and nD.D: they appear in the Manual panel, can be swept, recorded and monitored. The table lists them below their composite:

Name Type Definition nD Multivariate write Vbg = …; Vtg = … ↳ nD.n variable −2 … 2 1e12/cm² ↳ nD.D variable −0.5 … 0.5 V/nm

docs.title: Multivariate write
docs.text:
Several variables, whose names you choose, drive several channels (the targets): any writable channels with a number - aliases (with their limits and ramp rates), other composite channels, or channels of an instrument (src.V1, written as they are):

From Python 
c.call("define_composite", type="multi", name="gates",
       variables=[{"name": "eps", "min": -0.4, "max": 0.4, "unit": "V", "ramp_rate": 0.5},
                  {"name": "U",   "min": 0,    "max": 0.5, "unit": "V"}],
       targets={"Vx": "U + eps", "Vy": "U - eps"})

Each variable is now a channel of its own, named after the composite: gates.eps and gates.U, with its own minimum, maximum, unit and ramp rate:

From Python 
c.call("read_channel", name="gates.eps")          # nan: never set yet
c.call("set_many", values={"gates.eps": 0.1, "gates.U": 0.3})
# {'Vx': 0.4, 'Vy': 0.2}   (the hardware values that were set)
c.call("read_channel", name="gates.eps")          # 0.1: the value it was last set to
c.call("write_channel", name="gates.U", value=0.1)  # eps stays 0.1 → Vx = 0.2, Vy = 0.0

Names

Inside the composite's own target formulas, the variables go by their short names (U + eps). Everywhere else (the Manual panel, sweeps, scripts, other formulas, the Monitor, data files) they go by the full name gates.eps. So two composites may both have a variable x (a.x, b.x), and a variable never clashes with an alias or a parameter. A composite may not have the name of an instrument (dmm.x would read like an instrument channel).

Setting one variable recomputes only the targets that depend on it, using the other variables' last values.

The first setting

While a variable has never been set, the targets that need it cannot be computed, so setting gates.eps alone fails with a message naming the missing gates.U. Set the variables together the first time. In the Manual panel the variables show NaN until then, with hold forced on: click Set all to zero, or type a value for each, then click Set all. In a script or from Python, use set_many. A sweep sets them together by itself (below).

docs.title: Limits and ramps
docs.text:
Everything is checked before anything is written: the variables' limits, and the limits of every alias the targets end on. A value that would drive Vx beyond its alias limit is refused, and no channel moves.

Ramps keep every channel within its own rate at the same time: the variable's ramp_rate and each target alias' ramp_rate. This also holds along non-linear relations: with targets={"VL": "q**2"}, moving q from −1 to 1 drives VL 1 → 0 → 1, at no point faster than VL's rate.

docs.title: Out of range
docs.text:
Often the region you want in the variables doesn't fit in the box the hardware limits allow: a rectangle in \((n, D)\) is a tilted rectangle in \((V_{bg}, V_{tg})\), and its corners may need more than ±10 V. Out of range in the composite editor (out_of_range in the definition) decides what happens when a combination of the variables would drive a target outside its limits:

Out of range in a sweep set by hand or from a script Skip the point (skip, the default) the point is skipped before any channel is set, as if a point action called skip_point() first: nothing moves and its data stay NaN. Validation says how many points will be skipped refused, with the reason Error (error) the sweep is refused by validation, naming the first bad point refused Clamp to the limit (clamp) the target is set to the nearest end of its range; the point is measured the same

Skip suits maps (the region the hardware can reach is measured, the rest is left empty). Error is for measurements where every point matters. Clamp suits targets where the nearest reachable value is good enough. Note that with Clamp a point is labelled with variable values the hardware did not quite reach.

docs.title: In sweeps
docs.text:
Variables of one composite are always set together:

  • swept in the same dimension, they are set together at every point;
  • swept in different dimensions (nD.n inner, nD.D outer), the outer variable is not written on its own: at every inner point both are set together. So a new D never moves the gates with the old n left over from the previous line, and every combination the hardware sees is one of the sweep's points, checked in advance.

Validation checks every combination the sweep will set (all at once, so even a 1000 × 1000 map takes a fraction of a second) and says how many points of the sweep will be skipped.

A few details:

  • A skipped point runs its pre-sweep point action (it comes first), but nothing after it: no channel is set, no delay, no recording.
  • An outer-dimension variable recorded in its own dimension is recorded as its setpoint.
  • With a non-linear formula, the allowed region can have holes: between two allowed points the formula may need a gate beyond its limit. The ramp between them then moves each gate on a straight line in gate voltage instead of following the formula. That line is always inside the limits, and nobody measures during a ramp.
  • A sweep in which every point is skipped still finishes, with all-NaN data.

docs.title: Formulas
docs.text:
Targets may use any expression of the variables and of the setup's parameters (Vbg = (n - n0 + D/kD) / (2*Cb); the variables by their short names here), including piecewise functions and vectors. The formulas of reads and mappings may use parameters too.

From Python 
c.call("define_composite", type="multi", name="drive",
       variables=[{"name": "amp", "min": 0, "max": 2}],
       targets={"wave": "amp*sin(linspace(0, 2*pi, 64))",       # a 64-point waveform
                "Vb":   "piecewise(amp < 1, 0.1, 0.3)",            # a step
                "Vg":   "interp(amp, [0, 1, 2], [0, 0.5, 0.6])"})   # a table

docs.title: Composite read
docs.text:
A read-only channel computed from others: aliases, variables, mappings, other reads, parameters, or channels of an instrument (lockin.X). The classic case is a resistance from two lock-ins, one measuring the voltage (\(V_{xx}\)) and one the current (\(I\)): a composite read Rxx with the formula Vxx / I and unit Ω. In the editor, choose the type Composite read and type the formula; the line below it lists the channels it may use. Tutorial 2 sets this up step by step.

Reading the channel reads its inputs and evaluates the formula. Other examples: a conductance 1/Rxx, a difference (V1 - V2)/2, a power in dB 10*log10(P).

From Python 
c.call("define_composite", type="read", name="Vdiff", expression="(Vx - Vy)/2", unit="V")
c.call("define_composite", type="read", name="R",
       expression="piecewise(abs(I) > 1e-12, Vg / I, nan)", unit="Ω")
c.call("define_composite", type="read", name="spec_dB", expression="10*log10(spectrum)")

Reads can be recorded in sweeps and monitored like any channel. Vector inputs give vector results. A NaN input (e.g. a variable never set) gives NaN.

docs.title: Simple mapping
docs.text:
A one-to-one software view of one channel. forward gives the target y from x, and backward gives x back from y:

From Python 
c.call("define_composite", type="map", name="Tset_C", target="Tset",
       forward="x + 273.15", backward="y - 273.15",
       min=-273.15, max=26.85, unit="°C")
c.call("write_channel", name="Tset_C", value=-73.15)   # Tset = 200 K
c.call("read_channel", name="Tset_C")                  # reads Tset, applies backward

Reading the mapping really reads the hardware, so a change made to the instrument directly is seen.

docs.title: The inverse check
docs.text:
When a mapping is defined, forward and backward are checked to be each other's inverse over the whole [min, max] range. The range is sampled densely (also logarithmically for wide ranges) and checked within tolerance, which defaults to 1e-6 × range. The error names the worst point:

From Python 
c.call("check_composite", type="map", name="sq", target="Vb",
       forward="x**2", backward="sqrt(y)", min=-1, max=1)
# ChannelError: … at x = -1 forward gives y = 1 and backward gives 1 back …

Piecewise mappings are fine, as long as they are one-to-one:

From Python 
c.call("define_composite", type="map", name="Vg_nl", target="Vg",
       forward="piecewise(x < 0, 2*x, 0.5*x)",
       backward="y/2 if y < 0 else 2*y", min=-1, max=1)

A mapping may also have its own ramp_rate (in its units per second), and a tolerance for formulas that are inverse only to some precision:

From Python 
c.call("define_composite", type="map", name="Vg_mV", target="Vg",
       forward="x/1000", backward="1000*y", min=-2000, max=2000, unit="mV",
       ramp_rate=500, tolerance=1e-6)

If the mapping's range reaches beyond the target alias' limits, the definition returns a warning. Values beyond the alias limits are still refused when set.

docs.title: Nesting
docs.text:
Composites can drive each other. A mapping can target a variable, and a multivariate write can target another composite's variables or a mapping:

From Python 
c.call("define_composite", type="map", name="eps_mV", target="gates.eps",
       forward="x/1000", backward="1000*y", min=-400, max=400, unit="mV")
c.call("define_composite", type="multi", name="outer", variables=["s"],
       targets={"gates.U": "0.2 + s", "eps_mV": "100*s"})
c.call("write_channel", name="outer.s", value=0.1)
# U = 0.3, eps = 0.01 V → Vx = 0.31, Vy = 0.29

On every write:

  • every hardware channel is computed once, even when it is reached through several paths;
  • two requests in one write that give the same channel different values are refused;
  • everything is limit-checked before anything is written;
  • ramps keep every alias, variable and mapping within its own rate.

docs.title: Circular dependencies
docs.text:
Loops are refused when they would be defined, and the old definition is kept:

From Python 
c.call("define_composite", type="read", name="r1", expression="Vx + 1")
c.call("define_composite", type="read", name="r2", expression="r1 * 2")
c.call("define_composite", type="read", name="r1", expression="r2 + 1", replace=True)
# ChannelError: circular dependency: r1 → r2 → r1

A runtime guard also stops a loop that slipped in some other way within a fraction of a second, so a call can never hang the backend. A channel cannot be removed or redefined away while another composite uses it.

docs.title: Sweeping composites
docs.text:
Variables and mappings can be swept like aliases. Variables of one composite that are swept in the same dimension are set together at every point, so even the first point works before they have ever been set:

{"points": 51, "sweep": [{"channel": "gates.eps", "start": -0.2, "stop": 0.2},
                         {"channel": "gates.U",   "start": 0.1,  "stop": 0.3}],
 "record": ["Vx", "Vy", "Vdiff"]}

All combinations are limit-checked before the sweep starts.

docs.title: Checking without defining
docs.text:
check_composite takes the same arguments as define_composite and returns the channels it would define and any warnings, without changing anything:

From Python 
c.call("check_composite", type="multi", name="lazy", variables=["p", "q"],
       targets={"Vb": "p"})
# {'channels': ['lazy.p', 'lazy.q'], 'warnings': ['composite lazy: variable q drives no target'], …}

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
type fields multi name, variables (names or {name, min, max, unit, ramp_rate, description}), targets {channel: formula}, out_of_range (skip (default), error or clamp), description read name, expression, unit, description map name, target, forward (of x), backward (of y), min, max (required), unit, ramp_rate, tolerance, description

A multivariate composite's variables are channels named composite.variable.

docs.title: Data files
docs.text:
Every sweep is written to <data folder>/<date>/<run>_<name>.emj while it runs, for example D:/data/2026-11-11/00042_coulomb_diamonds.emj. When it ends, an HDF5 copy (.h5) is written next to it.

The data folder is chosen when easyMeasure starts for the first time, and can be changed under File → Settings….

docs.title: Opening data in the GUI
docs.text:
• While a sweep runs, the Live data tab shows it, and it stays there when the sweep has ended.
  • Open data in the queue history, or File → Open data file…, opens an earlier run in a new data tab, with the same plots as the live view (Plotting). Partial files from an aborted or crashed run open too.
  • File → Browse recent runs… lists the runs in the data folder.
  • Details in a data tab shows the sweep definition, the metadata and the pre/post-sweep readings.
  • Sweep → Load from data file… loads the sweep that made a file, to run it again or change it.

docs.title: The journal (.emj)
docs.text:
The journal is an append-only sequence of frames, each with a length and a CRC32 checksum:

  • header: the full sweep definition, every setpoint, units, metadata;
  • point: the values recorded at one point;
  • phase: pre/post recordings;
  • event: status changes, notes, and the aborted / continued events of a continued run;
  • footer: final status, points, skipped points, read failures, aborts.

A continued run is a new file that starts with the frames of the run it continues. Its header lists every earlier abort under aborts.

Every frame is flushed immediately and fsync-ed every fsync_interval (0.5 s, see settings). After a crash or a power cut, the file loads up to the last fraction of a second:

  • a torn or corrupted tail is detected and ignored;
  • the rest loads as a partial dataset, with points that were not measured as NaN.

If the disk fails during a run, the sweep keeps running in memory and the error is reported.

docs.title: Loading data in Python
docs.text:
from easymeasure.backend.storage import DataSet

ds = DataSet.load("D:/data/2026-11-11/00001_coulomb_diamonds.emj")   # complete or partial
ds.status                    # 'finished', 'aborted', 'error', 'terminated'; partial file: header status
ds.shape                     # [101, 41]: points per dimension, 0 = innermost
ds.data["I"].shape           # (101, 41)
ds.data["T"].shape           # (41,): recorded in dimension 1
ds.dim_of                    # {'I': 0, 'X': 0, 'T': 1, '@elapsed': 1}
ds.setpoints[0]["Vg"]        # the 101 gate voltages
ds.setpoints[1]["Vb"]        # the 41 bias voltages
ds.pre, ds.post              # {'T': 1.501, 'B': 0.0}: pre/post recordings
ds.header["definition"]      # the sweep definition, ready to queue again
ds.header["units"]           # channel → unit
ds.header["parameters"]      # the setup's parameters at the start: {name: {value, unit, formula}}
ds.footer                    # {'status', 'points', 'skipped_points', 'read_failures', …}
ds.completed_points, ds.total_points

A channel recorded in dimension k has shape (N_k, …, N_{D-1}) + value_shape. A spectrum of 512 points recorded in dimension 0 of a 101 × 41 sweep is a (101, 41, 512) array.

docs.title: Plotting with matplotlib
docs.text:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
ds = DataSet.load(path)
Vg, Vb = ds.setpoints[0]["Vg"], ds.setpoints[1]["Vb"]
plt.pcolormesh(Vg, Vb, ds.data["I"].T, shading="nearest")
plt.xlabel("Vg (V)"); plt.ylabel("Vb (V)"); plt.colorbar(label="I (nA)")
plt.show()

docs.title: Partial and running files
docs.text:
DataSet.load works on a file that is still being written. You get what has been measured so far, with NaN elsewhere:

import numpy as np
ds = DataSet.load(path)
done = ~np.isnan(ds.data["I"])
print("%d of %d points" % (done.sum(), done.size))

Through the backend (the same data, also for remote users):

From Python 
snap = c.call("run_snapshot")                 # the running (or last) sweep
snap = c.call("load_run", path=path)          # any stored run
hdr = c.call("read_run_header", path=path)    # just the header: definition, metadata
runs = c.call("list_runs", limit=20)          # newest files: path, name, size, mtime

docs.title: HDF5
docs.text:
The .h5 copy has the same content in a conventional layout:

path content /data/<channel> recorded arrays (attribute dim: the dimension it was recorded in) /setpoints/<k>/<channel> setpoints of dimension k /filled/<k> boolean mask of the points measured in dimension k /pre, /post pre/post recordings (attributes or datasets) attributes header_json, footer_json, status everything else 
import h5py, json
with h5py.File("00001_coulomb_diamonds.h5") as f:
    I = f["data/I"][...]
    Vg = f["setpoints/0/Vg"][...]
    definition = json.loads(f.attrs["header_json"])["definition"]

Switch the copy off with the setting export_hdf5 = false.

docs.title: Data folder
docs.text:
The data folder is chosen when the GUI first meets a backend, and can be changed in File → Settings. From Python:

From Python 
c.call("set_settings", data_dir="D:/data")    # refused if it cannot be created

Runs are numbered across days (00001, 00002 …). Remote users only reach files inside the data folder.

docs.title: In the GUI
docs.text:
• File → Open data file…, or Open data in the queue history, opens a run in a data tab with the same plots as the live view (see Plotting).
  • The web app lists stored runs, opens them and downloads the .emj / .h5 files.
  • Sweep → Load from data file… loads a run's definition.

docs.title: Driver Wizard
docs.text: Most SCPI instruments, and many older ones, are controlled by text commands. For an instrument like that without a driver, the Driver Wizard builds one without programming. Open it from Backend → Driver wizard…, or the Driver wizard… button under Instruments & channels.

docs.title: 1. Start from
docs.text:
Start from a template, or reopen a driver made with the wizard:

template contains Generic SCPI identification, error queue, reset / clear SCPI source-measure unit source level, mode, compliance, output, NPLC, measured voltage and current SCPI multimeter function, autorange, NPLC, reading Simple line protocol non-SCPI, no error queue

docs.title: 2. Basics
docs.text:
• Driver name: [a-z][a-z0-9_]*, e.g. keysight_e3631a.
  • Description: shown in the driver list.
  • *IDN? check: the reply must contain one of a | b, e.g. E3631A | E3632A. It is checked on connect, and also used to recognise the instrument when scanning ports.
  • Error query: e.g. SYST:ERR?. It is read after every setting, so a refused value raises an error with the instrument's own message. A query the instrument does not understand then fails at once with its message (e.g. -113,"Undefined header") instead of a read timeout.
  • Terminations, timeout, query delay.
  • Interfaces: GPIB, USB, LAN, TCP socket, serial, simulated. The Add instrument dialog lists ports of those kinds.

docs.title: 3. Channels
docs.text:
Add any number of channels of two kinds:

  • data channels: measured or swept values, aliased in the setup;
  • config channels: settings.

Per channel:

field meaning example access r, w or rw rw type float, str or vector (comma-separated numbers) float unit V Get the query; for numbers the first number in the reply is taken VOLT? Set the command, with {value} (or {value:.3f}) where the value goes VOLT {value:.4f} Allowed values a \| b \| c; a drop-down in the front ends P6V \| P25V \| N25V Map value ↔ instrument word Voltage=VOLT \| Current=CURR Scale reading × scale, setting ÷ scale 0.001 (instrument in mA, channel in A)

Replies to a mapped channel are recognised in SCPI short or long form, with 1 / 0 read as ON / OFF.

docs.title: 4. Actions
docs.text: Actions are named command lists, e.g. reset = *RST | *CLS. They run like any driver action.

docs.title: 5. Initialization
docs.text:
• Commands on connect. A command ending in ? is a query whose reply is logged.
  • A Python script run after them. It can use write(cmd), query(cmd), read(), sleep(s), log(msg), options, instrument, np and math. Raise an exception to refuse the connection.
  • Commands on disconnect, e.g. OUTP OFF.
idn = query("*IDN?")
if "E3631A" not in idn:
    raise RuntimeError("not an E3631A: %s" % idn)
write("SYST:REM")
log("connected to %s" % idn.strip())

docs.title: 6. Check, try and save
docs.text:
• Check: errors block saving, warnings don't. The generated Python file can be previewed.
  • Try it: connects to an address you give (SIM::… works too), reads every readable channel once and shows the value, unit and time per channel. It then removes the trial instrument again.
  • Save:
    • writes <home>/drivers/<name>.py;
    • reloads the drivers;
    • offers to add an instrument with the new driver.

Instruments already using the driver are reconnected with the new version, but not during a sweep.

docs.title: Example: a Keysight E3631A triple supply
docs.text:
channel kind access type unit get set output_sel config rw str INST? INST {value} (allowed P6V \| P25V \| N25V) voltage data rw float V VOLT? VOLT {value:.4f} current_limit config rw float A CURR? CURR {value:.4f} Vmeas data r float V MEAS:VOLT? Imeas data r float A MEAS:CURR? output config rw str OUTP? OUTP {value} (map ON=1 \| OFF=0)

The actions are reset = *RST | *CLS, and the error query is SYST:ERR?. After Save, add it like any instrument and alias voltage with limits and a ramp rate.

docs.title: The generated file
docs.text:
The file holds the definition as a Python literal (DEFINITION) and a small class deriving from CommandInstrument (easymeasure/drivers/_command.py). It can be edited by hand, e.g. to override read / write for an unusual channel, and the wizard reopens it through DEFINITION.

Saving from the wizard over a file that was extended by hand warns first, and keeps the old file as <name>.py.bak. A built-in driver name, or a file not made by the wizard, is never overwritten.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
The wizard's backend commands are available to scripts:

From Python 
tmpl = c.call("wizard_templates")[0]["definition"]
d = dict(tmpl, name="my_meter", description="my meter")
c.call("wizard_check", definition=d)          # {'errors': [], 'warnings': [...], 'source': '…'}
c.call("wizard_try", definition=d, address="GPIB0::5::INSTR")
c.call("wizard_save", definition=d)
c.call("wizard_list"); c.call("wizard_load", name="my_meter"); c.call("wizard_delete", name="my_meter")

Over remote access the wizard is admin-only, because it writes code to the backend computer.

docs.title: Desktop GUI
docs.text:
python -m easymeasure.frontend                    # connect to the running backend
python -m easymeasure.frontend --start-backend    # … starting one if none runs

The GUI is only a view: it talks to the backend over a socket and never blocks on it. Close it, kill it or start several on different screens; the measurement does not notice. A reopened GUI picks up the running sweep where it is.

The window is split in two:

  • on the left, the instruments, sweep editor and queue;
  • on the right, the data: the live view and any loaded files;
  • on the far right, the Monitor and Manual docks;
  • at the bottom, the Log.

The read-only Running sweep view can be shown from the View menu.

docs.title: Instruments & channels
docs.text:
The page fits the window without a scroll bar. The first row holds:

  • Instruments: Add…, Edit…, Reconnect, Disconnect, Remove, and Driver wizard…. The Add dialog's address list shows the ports found on the backend computer that fit the driver (see Instruments).
  • Channels (hardware): the selected instrument's channels, with their allowed values and the last value read or set (nothing is read just to fill the table), and its actions. Buttons: Make alias…, Get, Set… (writes the channel as it is: no limits, no ramp) and Run action.

Below them, four tabs:

  • Channels (aliased): the aliases, with their limits and last values.
  • Channels (composite): the composite channels. A multivariate composite is followed by a row per variable, under the name it goes by everywhere else (↳ nD.n), with its range and last value.
  • User Actions: your user actions.
  • Parameters: the setup's parameters.

Drag a tab to change their order; the order is remembered. The splitter between the two rows moves too.

The Setup menu has Save setup… / Load setup… / Merge setup….

docs.title: Messages
docs.text: What a button did, or why it was refused, is shown in the window's status bar at the bottom, not in the page: errors in red stay until the next message, the rest clear after 10 seconds. Every message is also written to the Log dock, so nothing is lost when the next one comes.

docs.title: Checking what you type
docs.text: Every field that takes a formula or code has a Check button: parameters, composite channels, user actions, point actions and the script editor. Check asks the backend, without saving anything: are the names known, is there a circle, does the code compile, do the channels it quotes exist? OK (or Add to queue) checks first, and a dialog closes only when the check passes. Warnings (a channel that does not exist yet, say) are shown in orange but do not stop you.

docs.title: Sweep editor
docs.text:
The editor has any number of dimensions, each laid out in the order of one point:

  1. the actions;
  2. setting the swept channels;
  3. the pre-sample delay;
  4. recording;
  5. the post-sample delay.

An outer dimension also shows where the next inner dimension's loop runs: last, or before recording with record after inner dims. The pre and post phases, error policies and metadata are below.

The Sweep menu works on the sweep in the editor: New, Load… / Save… (JSON), Load from data file… (the definition of a stored run), Validate (limit-checks every setpoint), Add to queue and Add & start. Continue an aborted run… picks a run of the data folder and continues it.

docs.title: Queue
docs.text:
The queue panel has:

  • the controls: Start, Pause, Resume, Abort, Abort all and Stop after current, enabled by what the queue can do now;
  • the queued items, which can be reordered and removed;
  • the history: Rerun selected, Continue… (an aborted or failed sweep, from where it stopped), Open data, and Copy to sweep / script editor;
  • a script editor.

See The run queue.

docs.title: Data views
docs.text: The Live data tab follows the running sweep. File → Open data file… opens stored runs in further tabs. See Plotting.

docs.title: Docks
docs.text:
• Monitor: channels polled at their own intervals.
  • Manual: every writable channel with a spin box and slider.

See Monitor and Manual panels.

The Log dock shows the backend log (all clients see the same) with level filter and search.

docs.title: Menus
docs.text:
• File: Open data file… (Ctrl+O), Browse recent runs…, Settings… (data folder, PowerPoint file, display), Quit (the backend keeps running).
  • Setup: Save setup…, Load setup…, Merge setup… (see Instruments).
  • Sweep: New, Load…, Load from data file…, Save…, Validate, Add to queue, Add & start, for the sweep in the editor (see Sweeps). Using one brings its tab to the front.
  • Backend: Start backend, Reconnect, Restart backend…, Show tray icon, Remote access…, Driver wizard…, Shut down backend….
  • View: show or hide the Monitor, Manual and Log docks and the Running sweep view.

The toolbar has the queue controls, Add slide to PPT and Open data….

docs.title: First start
docs.text:
The first time the GUI meets a backend, it asks for:

  • the data folder, where every run is saved;
  • the PowerPoint file that slides are appended to (empty = none).

Both are prefilled with the current values. Ask me later asks again at the next start. Both stay editable in File → Settings, and a data folder that cannot be created is refused.

docs.title: Display settings
docs.text:
File → Settings → Display:

  • font size: applied at once, also to plot axes;
  • UI scale: an overall scale of 50–300 %, applied on the next GUI start.

Together they suit any screen resolution. The window can be made small: toolbars wrap, and panels scroll only when they must.

Combo boxes stay narrow so toolbars do not grow, but their drop-down lists show long channel names in full.

docs.title: Lock
docs.text:
🔓 Lock (top right corner, Ctrl+L) locks the GUI against accidental changes.

Greyed out:

  • instruments, the sweep editor and the queue;
  • manual control;
  • adding / removing monitors;
  • Add slide to PPT and Settings;
  • the Setup and Sweep menus;
  • the Backend menu, except Reconnect.

Still usable:

  • switching tabs;
  • the plots and all their settings;
  • monitor time spans;
  • opening data files;
  • the log.

Click again to unlock; the state is remembered across restarts. It is a guard against slips, not access control. It affects this window only, not other GUIs, the web page, the tray or scripts.

docs.title: Tray icon
docs.text:
While the backend runs, a tray icon shows its state:

colour state green idle blue running orange paused red error gray unreachable

Its tooltip shows the current run and its progress.

The tray menu can:

  • open the GUI;
  • open the web page (Open in browser, which offers to switch on remote access first if it is off);
  • pause, resume and abort;
  • open the data folder or the log;
  • shut the backend down.

A notification appears when a run ends. The tray is a separate helper process, so it can never affect the backend. Start the backend with --no-tray to disable it.

docs.title: Instruments
docs.text:
An instrument is a driver connected to a port. It exposes:

  • channels: values to read and/or write. A channel is a float (a scalar or an array of any dimension, such as a spectrum or a camera image) or a str;
  • configuration channels: settings such as range, sensitivity, mode or output on/off;
  • actions: commands without arguments, such as reset, trigger or auto-phase.

The drivers that come with easyMeasure are listed under Supported instruments; each has a reference page with every channel.

docs.title: Adding an instrument
docs.text:
In Instruments & channels, click Add… under the Instruments list:

  • Name: a short name of your choice, such as lockin or bg. Its channels are then called lockin.X, bg.voltage and so on.
  • Driver: the kind of instrument. The line below it says what the driver is for.

  • Address: where it is connected. The list shows the ports and devices the backend computer has that this driver accepts:

    • instruments that identified as this driver's kind come first, marked ✓;
    • then the other ports;
    • then ports already in use;
    • then the driver's suggestions, such as its built-in emulator.

    You can also type any address (see Addresses). Refresh scans again; with ask *IDN? it also identifies GPIB, USB and LAN instruments.

  • Options: driver settings, in JSON, such as "reset": true or "call_timeout": 20. Choosing a driver fills in its options with their defaults; most instruments need no change. See Guard options.

The new instrument appears in the list with its state:

state means connected ready disconnected switched off with Disconnect error could not be reached. The Last error column says why

An instrument that cannot be reached is still added, so a typo in the address doesn't lose your settings. Fix the problem, then click Reconnect. Edit… changes the address or options (and reconnects), Remove deletes the instrument (refused while aliases use it). The Calls, Errors and Timeouts columns count the instrument's traffic, which helps when a cable is loose.

No hardware at hand?

Every hardware driver accepts the address SIM::<anything> (NI DAQs: DAQ::SIM) and then talks to a built-in emulator of the instrument. The sim_* drivers simulate a whole sample; see Simulated instruments.

From Python 
c.call("add_instrument", name="lockin", driver="sr830", address="GPIB0::8::INSTR")
c.call("add_instrument", name="smu", driver="keithley2400", address="GPIB0::24::INSTR",
       options={"call_timeout": 20, "verify_writes": True})
c.call("reconnect_instrument", name="lockin")
c.call("update_instrument", name="lockin", address="GPIB0::9::INSTR")   # reconnects
c.call("disconnect_instrument", name="lockin")
c.call("remove_instrument", name="lockin")

The returned description has state and last_error.

docs.title: Addresses
docs.text:
interface address examples needs gpib GPIB0::12::INSTR VISA library + GPIB card driver usb (USB-TMC) USB0::0x0957::0x8B18::MY51141134::0::INSTR VISA library tcpip (VISA LAN) TCPIP0::192.168.1.20::inst0::INSTR, TCPIP0::192.168.1.20::5025::SOCKET VISA library tcp (raw socket) TCP::192.168.1.30::1234 (e.g. a Prologix GPIB-Ethernet adapter) – serial COM3, /dev/ttyUSB0, ASRL3::INSTR adapter driver daq DAQ::Dev1 (the NI MAX device name), DAQ::SIM NI-DAQmx sim SIM::<bus name> – none NONE (instruments without a port, e.g. the simulated ones) –

Each driver lists the interfaces it accepts. An address of another interface is refused when the instrument is added. For example, the GPIB instruments also accept serial and tcp (RS-232, or a Prologix adapter), and the Keysight B2900 also takes USB and LAN.

docs.title: Finding what is connected
docs.text:
The Address list of the Add… dialog already shows what the backend computer has. Tick ask *IDN? and click Refresh to have each GPIB, USB and LAN instrument identify itself.

From Python 
r = c.call("discover_resources", identify=True)
for f in r["found"]:
    print(f["interface"], f["address"], f.get("description", ""), f.get("idn", ""))
print(r["notes"])     # what could not be scanned (no VISA library, no NI-DAQmx …)

Serial ports come with their description (e.g. an FTDI adapter), VISA instruments with their alias, and NI devices with their product type. identify asks each GPIB / USB / LAN instrument *IDN?, except instruments already configured here, which are left alone.

docs.title: Several instruments behind one GPIB adapter
docs.text:
A Prologix GPIB-USB or GPIB-Ethernet adapter is one port shared by several instruments. Add each of them with the adapter's port as address (e.g. COM5), and in the options set "shared": true and its GPIB address, "gpib_addr": 22.

From Python 
for name, drv, addr in (("dmm", "hp34401a", 22), ("src", "yokogawa7651", 3)):
    c.call("add_instrument", name=name, driver=drv, address="COM5",
           options={"shared": True, "gpib_addr": addr})

Before an instrument talks, the port is switched to it (++addr N). The measurement thread has priority over monitor and GUI traffic, so monitoring never slows a sweep down.

docs.title: Channels
docs.text:
Select an instrument, and its channels and actions are listed under Channels (hardware). Get reads the selected channel:

column Config ⚙ marks a configuration channel (a setting, below) Access r readable, w writable Type, Shape float or str; () for a single number, (401,) for a 401-point trace Allowed values for settings with a fixed list of values

Instrument channels, instrument.channel, are channels like all the others: read and written anywhere (sweeps, the monitor, scripts, composite formulas), as far as their access allows. Set… writes the selected one. A write to an instrument channel is plain: no limits, no ramp. For a gate or a magnet, give the channel an alias with Make alias… and use the alias: it carries the limits and the ramp rate.

From Python 
c.call("read_channel", name="lockin.X")
c.call("write_channel", name="bg.voltage", value=0.0)  # as it is: no limits, no ramp
c.call("channel_info", name="lockin.X")
# {'name': 'lockin.X', 'kind': 'hardware', 'access': 'r', 'readable': True,
#  'writable': False, 'dtype': 'float', 'shape': [], 'unit': 'V', 'config': False,
#  'instrument': 'lockin', 'choices': None, …}

docs.title: Configuration channels
docs.text:
Settings such as a range, a time constant or an output switch are channels of kind config, set with Set… (or in the Manual panel, with settings ticked). In a sweep, set them as constants in the pre-sweep or post-sweep settings (see Sweeps), so every data file records how the instrument was set.

From Python 
c.call("write_channel", name="lockin.sensitivity", value="500uv")   # → '500 µV'
c.call("write_channel", name="lockin.time_constant", value="300 ms")
c.call("write_channel", name="smu.nplc", value=10)
c.call("read_channel", name="lockin.sensitivity")

Allowed values. Many settings accept only certain values. The front ends then show a drop-down. Writes are checked and normalised to the listed spelling. Case, blanks, u/µ and Ohm/Ω do not matter, so "500uv" sets "500 µV".

docs.title: Channel lists that follow the instrument
docs.text:
A mode switch can rename channels, change units or make a channel read-only. The backend asks the driver for its channel list again after every configuration write, action and reconnect, and the front ends follow:

From Python 
c.call("write_channel", name="smu.output", value="OFF")    # modes change with output off
c.call("write_channel", name="smu.mode", value="Current")
# voltage is now measured (read-only), current is the source,
# Icompliance [A] became Vcompliance [V]

An alias whose target disappeared reports an error instead of silently reading something else. This applies, for example, to dmm.Vdc after the meter was switched to Iac. Re-point the alias, or switch back.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
Instrument actions, such as auto phase, reset or preset, are listed below the channels. An action is a write-only channel, instrument.action, without a value: writing it runs it. Select one and click ▶ Run action; in scripts and point actions: set('lockin.auto_gain'); in a sweep: a pre- or post-sweep constant with no value. Actions are guarded like every other call but never retried automatically, because a trigger must not fire twice. Afterwards the cached values of that instrument's aliases are discarded, so the next ramp reads back where the instrument really is.

From Python 
c.call("write_channel", name="lockin.auto_phase")
c.call("read_channel", name="lockin.auto_phase")   # refused: an action has no value

docs.title: Talking to the instrument directly
docs.text:
Sometimes you need a command the driver does not offer. A user action or a script can send it: instrument('lockin').raw_query('*IDN?') returns the answer, instrument('lockin').raw_write('OUTX 1') sends a command.

From Python 
c.call("raw_query", instrument="lockin", command="*IDN?")
# 'Stanford_Research_Systems,SR830,s/n48261,ver1.07'
c.call("raw_write", instrument="lockin", command="OUTX 1")

Over remote access this needs the admin role, and every command is logged.

docs.title: Guard options
docs.text:
Every instrument, whatever its driver, takes these options:

option default meaning call_timeout 10 s deadline for every driver call retries 2 retries of a failed read / write retry_delay 0.05 s pause between retries reconnect_after 2 consecutive failures before a reconnect timeout_retries 1 retries after a timeout breaker_threshold 2 hangs before a channel is quarantined breaker_cooldown 10 s quarantine time (doubles on repeated trips) shared driver default the port may be shared with other instruments

Common driver options of the hardware drivers:

option meaning reset *RST on connect check_errors read the error queue after every setting, so a refused value raises the instrument's own message (default on) verify_writes SMUs: read every source value back (worth it on RS-232) gpib_addr GPIB address behind a Prologix adapter timeout, read_termination, baudrate port settings

See Robustness for what happens when an instrument misbehaves.

docs.title: Saving the setup
docs.text:
Instruments, parameters, aliases, composites, the monitor list and user actions together form the setup. Save setup… and Load setup… in the Setup menu write it to a file and read it back. Loading replaces the current setup.

From Python 
c.call("save_setup", path="C:/lab/fridge_setup.json")
c.call("load_setup", path="C:/lab/fridge_setup.json")   # returns a list of problems ([] = fine)

The setup is also autosaved on every change. python -m easymeasure.backend --restore starts with the last one. The file format is in the reference.

docs.title: Merging a setup
docs.text:
Setup → Merge setup… takes parts of another setup file into the current one: a second cryostat's instruments, a colleague's composite channels, a set of user actions. A wizard asks for the file, then shows one page for each kind of item, in the order they depend on each other:

  1. Instruments;
  2. Parameters;
  3. Channels (aliases);
  4. Composite channels;
  5. Actions;

then a Review page, with Merge.

  1. The items of the file. Tick what to take. Merge as gives an item a new name here (here I, which this setup already has, becomes Idmm). Status says at once whether each ticked item can be merged. B cannot: this setup has a different B. Rename it, or untick it to keep using this setup's B.
  2. Also select what these need ticks, on every page, what the ticked items use: here the instruments src, dmm and magnet (the file's magnet differs from this setup's, so it needs a new name on the Instruments page too).

The statuses:

status meaning ✔ merge it can be merged = already here this setup has an identical one: it is left as it is ⚠ merge it can be merged, but look at the message (e.g. an action quotes a channel that will not exist) ✘ problem it cannot be merged as it is; Next stays greyed out until it is fixed or unticked

The problems it finds:

  • Name conflicts. A name already used here (by anything with a name: instrument, alias, parameter, composite channel or variable, action), or two merged items under one name. Give one of them another name in Merge as, or untick it. An unticked item whose name exists here is replaced by the one already here: whatever uses it in the file then uses this setup's one. When that one is different, a warning says so.
  • Missing pieces. An alias needs its instrument, a formula the channels and parameters it uses. Each must be ticked too, or already be here.
  • Inconsistencies. Everything is checked with the backend's own rules, on a copy of the current setup: formulas, writable targets, mappings that must be each other's inverse, parameter formulas that use live channels, and circular references between composite channels or between parameters.

New names are carried through. Renaming the instrument lockin to lockin2 changes the targets of the merged aliases (lockin.X → lockin2.X). Renaming an alias or a parameter changes the formulas that use it, and the names quoted in the merged actions (get('Vxx')). Parameters are also renamed where an action uses them by name. Nothing changes until you click Merge. Then the items are added one by one, in an order that works.

docs.title: Monitor
docs.text:
The Monitor dock shows channels that the backend polls at their own intervals: temperatures, field, a leakage current, the eight readings of a supply. Values are pushed to every GUI and the web app.

Choose the channel at the top of the dock, set the interval, and click Monitor. ✕ on a tile removes it.

From Python 
c.call("monitor_add", channel="T", interval=1.0)
c.call("monitor_add", channel="cyg.VmeasAll", interval=0.5)
c.call("monitor_list")          # channel, interval, last value, last error, time
c.call("monitor_history", channel="T")    # {'T': [[t, value], …]}
c.call("monitor_remove", channel="T")

Every instrument is polled by its own thread, so a hung instrument never stalls the others. Monitoring has lower priority than a running sweep on a shared port.

docs.title: Tiles
docs.text:
Each tile shows the latest value in large type, the polling interval, and a plot over the chosen time span (1 min, 10 min, 1 h or all). Text channels show their text. Errors are shown in the tile until the next good reading.

Vector channels can be shown two ways. Use the tile's selector to switch:

view shows default for vs time one curve per element against time, with a legend for up to 8 vectors up to 16 elements, such as the eight readings of a supply vs index the latest values against the element index longer vectors, such as spectra

2-D channels, such as images, are shown as an image of the latest value.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text: columns: auto, or 1–8 tiles side by side. Auto picks the arrangement that shows every tile largest in the available space. All tiles are shown at once and share the dock's area. Scroll bars appear only when the dock is smaller than the tiles' minimum size. The choice is remembered between sessions.

docs.title: Manual
docs.text:
The Manual dock lists every writable scalar channel:

  • aliases;
  • composite variables and mappings;
  • instrument settings, with settings ticked.

Each channel has a spin box, and a slider when it has a minimum and a maximum.

  • Writes are protected and ramped: alias limits and ramp rates apply. While a ramp runs, further changes to that channel are coalesced, so only the latest value is sent after it. The ramp box switches ramping off (jumps).

  • ■ Stop ramps lights up (red, with the channel names) while a ramp is running, whether it was started here, in another window, the web page or a Python client. It stops every such ramp where it is: the channel keeps the value it had reached, and the panel shows it. Ramps inside a sweep, a script or a user action are not affected; Abort stops those.

    * Right click → Set from expression…: a function of the present value x, e.g. x + 0.01 or x/2. * Read back (↻) reads the present value. * The mouse wheel only acts on a focused control, so scrolling the panel never moves an instrument. * The filter box narrows the list by name or composite.

docs.title: Composite variables: Set all to zero, hold and Set all
docs.text:
Variables of a multivariate composite are listed, indented, under a header with the composite's name, by their short names (n for nD.n). The header has three controls:

  • Set all to zero sets every variable to 0 together, with limits and ramps as usual. This is the easy way to start.
  • hold: while ticked, edits only mark the variables (blue) and are not sent.
  • Set all sends the held values together; the hardware channels are computed once from all of them.

Before the first setting. Until the variables of a composite have been set, they have no value, and the panel says so:

  • each variable shows NaN, and its slider is greyed out;
  • the header says not set yet, and hold is ticked and cannot be unticked: a variable can only be set alone once the others have a value;
  • Set all is greyed out until every variable has a value typed in (each is held, blue); Set all to zero works at once.

Once the variables are set, hold unticks itself and everything works as usual.

See Composite channels and tutorial 2.

docs.title: User actions and parameters
docs.text:
Your user actions are buttons at the top of the panel: ▶ name runs one (asking first if it is marked ask before running). While it runs its button turns orange (■ name); clicking it then aborts it.

The setup's parameters are listed at the bottom, under Parameters. Type a new value for a value parameter and press Enter: formula parameters follow, and no instrument moves. Formula parameters show their value and formula.

docs.title: Instrument settings
docs.text: Tick settings to also list the instruments' configuration channels (in italics, grouped by instrument). Settings with allowed values (modes, ranges, output on/off) appear as drop-downs.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
A parameter is a named number that belongs to your setup: a gate capacitance, a geometry factor, the value of a bias resistor, an amplifier gain. Instead of typing 0.6 into five formulas, you define Cb = 0.6 once and write Cb everywhere. When the number changes (a new device, a better calibration), you change it in one place.

A parameter is either:

  • a value, a number you set; or
  • a formula of other parameters, such as Ct/Cb or 2*pi*f0. A formula may use only other parameters, never a live channel, and parameters may not refer to each other in a circle.

docs.title: Defining parameters
docs.text:
In Instruments & channels, on the Parameters tab, click Add…:

  1. Name: letters, digits and _; not the name of a channel, a composite or a function such as sin.
  2. Value or formula: type a number (0.6, 1e6) for a value, anything else for a formula of other parameters (Ct/Cb). The line below says which it took.
  3. Unit and an optional description, shown as tooltips.

Check asks the backend what the parameter would be, without defining it: its value, or why it is refused (an unknown name, a circle, a mapping it would break). OK checks first and keeps the dialog open if the check fails.

The table lists every parameter with its present value, its formula, and what uses it:

Edit… (or a double-click) changes one, Remove deletes it. A parameter that a formula, a composite or another parameter uses cannot be removed; the message says which ones use it.

docs.title: Setting a value
docs.text:
A value parameter can also be changed in the Manual panel, in the Parameters group at the bottom: type the value and press Enter. Formula parameters are shown there with their value and formula, and follow at once.

Setting a parameter moves no instrument. Composite channels use the new value the next time they set something: after changing Cb, setting nD.n again puts the gates where the new Cb says.

A parameter is a channel: a value parameter is read and written (rw) like any other, by set('Cb', 0.58) in a script, write_channel, a sweep constant, or even as a swept channel; a formula parameter is read-only (r) and follows the ones it uses. When several channels are written together, the parameters are set first, so the composites in the same write already use the new values.

docs.title: Using parameters
docs.text:
Wherever a formula is written, a parameter can be used by its name:

where example the targets of a multivariate composite Vbg = (n - n0 + D/kD) / (2*Cb) a composite read Rxx = Vxx / I * geom the forward and backward formulas of a mapping x / gain, y * gain user actions, point actions and scripts set('Vbg', V0), params.Cb

A parameter can also be read like any channel: get('Cb'), recorded in a sweep, shown in the Monitor.

In actions and scripts, each parameter is available:

  • by its name, with its value at the start of the action: set('Vbg', V0 + dV);
  • as params.Cb or params['Cb'], always the present value; dict(params) gives them all.

A parameter whose name the script API already uses (state, np, get …) is only available through params.

Mappings are checked again

A mapping is checked to be its own inverse when it is defined. If its formulas use a parameter, it is checked again whenever that parameter changes, and a value that would break it is refused (the old one stays).

docs.title: In data files
docs.text: Every data file records the parameters as they were when the sweep started, in its header: ds.header["parameters"] is {name: {"value", "unit", "formula"}}. So months later you can still tell which capacitance a map of \(n\) and \(D\) was computed with.
