docs.title: In setup files
docs.text: Parameters are saved with the setup, under "parameters", in an order where every formula comes after the parameters it uses. When a setup is loaded, a parameter that is wrong (a circle, an unknown name) is reported and left out, and the rest load.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
Parameters from a Python client 
c.call("define_parameter", name="Cb", value=0.6, unit="1e12 cm^-2/V")
c.call("define_parameter", name="ratio", formula="Ct/Cb")
c.call("define_parameter", name="Ct", definition="1.2")   # as typed: a number or a formula
c.call("check_parameter", name="k", definition="ratio * 2")
# {'name': 'k', 'formula': 'ratio * 2', 'current': 4.0, 'warnings': []}   nothing defined
c.call("write_channel", name="Cb", value=0.58)       # formulas follow
c.call("read_channel", name="ratio")
c.call("list_parameters")
# [{'name': 'Cb', 'value': 0.58, 'current': 0.58, 'unit': ..., 'used_by': ['ratio', 'nD']}, ...]
c.call("remove_parameter", name="ratio")

Defining and removing parameters needs the admin role over remote access; setting a value needs the operator role.

docs.title: Plotting live and stored data
docs.text: The Live data tab follows the running sweep. File → Open data file… opens stored runs, complete or partial, in further tabs with exactly the same plots.

docs.title: The data view
docs.text:
At the top is the run: number, name, status, points done of total, elapsed time and the estimated remaining time. Below it is a grid of plots, one per recorded channel to start with.

button does Add plot another plot (e.g. the same channel twice, as a map and as a line) columns how many plots side by side; auto picks the arrangement that shows every plot largest Add slide to PPT a slide of this run now (see PowerPoint) Copy sweep to editor the run's definition into the sweep editor Details header, metadata, pre/post values, footer Reload (stored runs) read the file again (a run still being written grows)

Every plot is shown at once. The plots share the available area. Scroll bars appear, in either direction, only when the area is smaller than the plots' minimum size.

docs.title: One plot
docs.text:
Each plot's toolbar has:

  • channel: any recorded channel;
  • mode:
    • Auto;
    • Curve;
    • Heatmap (for 2-D data, the default);
    • Stacked curves (2-D data as a set of offset lines);
  • X and Y: which axes to plot. Any sweep axis or value axis can be chosen, for example the bias instead of the gate as X, or the wavelength axis of a spectrum. Y is greyed out for 1-D data;
  • ⚙: colormap, auto levels, follow latest, stack offset;
  • ✕: close the plot.

Sliders. Every axis that is not X or Y becomes a slider below the plot: the outer sweep dimensions of a 3-D scan, the second spectrum dimension, and so on. With follow latest the sliders track the point being measured. Move a slider to look back, and tick follow latest again to return.

Two plots of the same 3-D data, each showing a different pair of axes, with a slider for the third:

Heat maps. Drag the histogram or colour bar to set the levels; auto levels returns to the data range. Colormaps: viridis, plasma, inferno, magma, cividis, turbo, gray, hot, jet, CET-L17, and the diverging RdBu_r, coolwarm, seismic and CET-D1 for signed data.

Redraws are coalesced, so a fast sweep does not load the GUI, and hidden plots are not redrawn.

docs.title: Typical views
docs.text: data view 1-D sweep (I vs Vg) Curve 2-D map (I vs Vg, Vb) Heatmap, X = Vg, Y = Vb; or Curve with a slider on Vb 2-D map, line by line Stacked curves, with an offset spectrum vs field Heatmap, X = frequency (from the instrument), Y = B camera image vs voltage Heatmap, X/Y = image axes, slider = voltage 3-D scan Heatmap of two axes, slider on the third

docs.title: The web app
docs.text: The web app's data tab has the same plots: curve / heat map / stacked curves, X/Y choice, sliders, follow latest, colormaps, colour levels by dragging the colour bar, zoom and pan. They redraw at most about 15 times a second, and only when visible.

docs.title: Plotting in Python
docs.text: See Data files for loading a run and plotting it with matplotlib.

docs.title: Point actions and flow control
docs.text:
Point actions are optional Python snippets that run at every point of a dimension. Typical uses are triggering a meter before recording, waiting for a magnet, logging a value, or stopping a curve once a threshold is crossed. Each dimension has four of them, at the positions shown in the order at each point:

action runs pre_sweep before the swept channels are set post_sweep after setting, before pre_delay pre_record after pre_delay, just before recording post_record just after recording, before post_delay

In the sweep editor, tick an action next to Actions: and its code box appears at its place in the sequence. The + action box offers common snippets, and the drop-down next to it (Skip this point, …) inserts the flow-control calls, and Check checks the code without running it (syntax, and the channels it quotes):

Unticked code is kept in the definition but not run. In the sweep's file, the actions are under hooks:

{"points": 101, "sweep": [{"channel": "Vg", "start": -0.5, "stop": 0.5}],
 "record": ["I"],
 "hooks": {"pre_record":  {"enabled": true, "code": "set('dmm.trigger')"},
           "post_record": {"enabled": true,
                           "code": "if values['I'] > 1e-6: log('high at %s' % (index,))"}}}

docs.title: What the code sees
docs.text:
Everything of the script API (get, set, set_many, sleep, wait_until, action, log, state, np …), plus:

name meaning k the dimension (0 = innermost) i the index of this point in the dimension index the indices of this and the outer dimensions, e.g. (i, j) setpoints the dimension's channel → value at this point values (post_record only) what was just recorded: channel → value

Code is compiled once per sweep. An error in an action stops the sweep, and the post phase still runs.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Trigger a meter in a triggered mode before every reading (pre_record):

set('dmm.trigger')

Wait for a magnet to reach its field (post_sweep of the field dimension):

wait_until(lambda: get('magnet.status') == 'HOLDING', timeout=600, interval=0.5)

Wait for the temperature to settle (post_sweep of a temperature dimension):

target = setpoints['Tset']
wait_until(lambda: abs(get('T') - target) < 0.01, timeout=1800, interval=2)
sleep(60)                      # and let the sample follow

Log values above a threshold (post_record):

if abs(values['I']) > 1e-6:
    log('high current %.3g A at Vg = %.3f' % (values['I'], setpoints['Vg']))

Keep a running count across points (state persists):

state['n_high'] = state.get('n_high', 0) + (values['I'] > 1e-9)

Auto-range a lock-in when it overloads (post_record, with the simulated lock-in, whose sensitivity is a number in volts):

if abs(values['X']) > 0.9 * float(get('lockin.sensitivity')):
    set('lockin.auto_gain')
    sleep(1)

docs.title: Flow control
docs.text:
Think of the dimensions as nested for loops. Three calls change the flow. Each action's + action helper in the editor offers them first.

call entry in the helper like effect skip_point() Skip this point continue the rest of this point (and its inner dimensions, unless they already ran) is skipped; its data are NaN; next point of the same dimension skip_line() Skip this line break this point and the remaining points of this dimension are skipped (NaN); the outer dimension continues (in the outermost dimension the sweep is done) end_sweep() Terminate the entire sweep exit the sweep ends with status terminated; called in post_record it keeps the point just recorded

Stop an I–V curve once the current exceeds 1 µA (post_record):

if abs(values["I"]) > 1e-6:
    end_sweep()

In a 2-D map, finish a line early once the device has switched (post_record of the inner dimension). The next bias value starts at once:

if values["R"] > 1e6:
    skip_line()

Skip setpoints that are known to be bad (pre_sweep):

if 0.10 < setpoints['Vg'] < 0.12:      # a charge jump in this range
    skip_point()

A terminated sweep is a normal end:

  • the post phase runs;
  • the file, the HDF5 copy and the slide are written as usual;
  • every point not reached is NaN;
  • the log says where it ended, and the file footer has terminated_at.

Skipped points count as done for the progress; the footer has skipped_points.

The calls cannot be swallowed by an except Exception in the action. Outside per-point actions, such as in the pre/post hooks or in scripts, they are an error.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: Point actions are Python running in the backend. Over remote access, sweeps with point actions or pre/post hook code need the admin role. Operators can run sweeps without code.

docs.title: PowerPoint reports
docs.text:
When a run ends, a summary slide is appended to the PowerPoint file. This happens whether the run ended normally, by error, by abort or by end_sweep(). The slide has:

  • a figure with one panel per recorded numeric channel (up to six): lines for 1-D data, heat maps for 2-D data;
  • the run summary:
    • start time, duration, status and points done;
    • the error, if any;
    • each dimension's swept channels and ranges and its recorded channels;
    • pre/post values and the pre-sweep constants;
    • metadata and the file path.

docs.title: Setting it up
docs.text:
File → Settings → PowerPoint file, or the first-start dialog:

From Python 
c.call("set_settings", ppt_path="D:/lab/notebook.pptx", auto_ppt=True,
       ppt_colormap="viridis")
setting meaning ppt_path the .pptx slides are appended to ("" = no slides); created if missing auto_ppt append a slide automatically at the end of every run ppt_colormap colormap of the heat maps

A sweep with "ppt": false in its definition gets no automatic slide.

docs.title: Slides on demand
docs.text:
Add slide to PPT (toolbar and data views) adds a slide for the running run, or any loaded data file, at once:

From Python 
c.call("make_ppt")                                # the running / last run
c.call("make_ppt", path="D:/data/2026-11-11/00042_map.emj")
c.call("make_ppt", path=run, ppt_path="D:/lab/talk.pptx")   # into another file

docs.title: The file may be open in PowerPoint
docs.text:
On Windows the slide is inserted into the open presentation through PowerPoint itself (via pywin32, installed automatically on Windows), and the presentation is saved. You can keep the lab notebook open all day.

The slide goes to <name>_pending.pptx next to it, so it is never lost, only if that is impossible. This happens, for example, when the file is locked by a sync client or open on another computer.

docs.title: Remote users
docs.text: Operators can add slides, and the web app can download the PowerPoint file.

docs.title: The run queue
docs.text:
Sweeps and scripts run one at a time from the queue. You can line up a night's worth of measurements and look at the results in the morning. The Queue tab shows it:

  • Queued: what waits. The first line is the item running now (current).
  • History: what has run, with its status and data file.
  • Script: the script editor (see Queue scripts).

docs.title: Adding to the queue
docs.text:
In the Sweep menu (for the sweep in the editor):

  • Add to queue puts the sweep at the end of the queue.
  • Add & start does the same and starts the queue.

The sweep is validated when it is added: a sweep that would exceed a limit is refused right there, not at 3 a.m. Later changes in the editor do not change a sweep that is already queued.

Start queue runs what is queued, one item after the other. When the queue runs empty it goes back to idle by itself; a sweep added after that waits for the next Start queue. Use up / down to change the order of waiting items, Remove to drop one, Clear queue to drop all.

docs.title: Pause, abort, stop
docs.text:
button effect Pause / Resume the running item halts at the next point (sweeps) or line (scripts), with everything left as it is, and continues from there Abort current ends the running item. A sweep's post-sweep settings still run, so the gates still go back to zero Abort all ends the running item, empties the queue, and stops running user actions Stop after current lets the running item finish, then stops the queue stop queue on error when an item fails, the queue stops instead of going on with the next

The same buttons are on the main toolbar, so they are at hand whichever tab is open. Buttons that don't apply right now are greyed out.

docs.title: History
docs.text:
Every finished, aborted or failed item stays in the History, with its status:

  • finished: ran to the end.
  • terminated: ended itself, with end_sweep() (see tutorial 3).
  • aborted: you pressed Abort.
  • error: something went wrong; the log has the reason.

Select an item, then:

  • Rerun selected queues the same sweep or script again, from the start, into a new data file.
  • Continue… (an aborted or error sweep) goes on from where it stopped: see below.
  • Copy to sweep editor (or Copy to script editor) loads it, so you can run a variation.
  • Open data opens its data file in a new data window.

docs.title: Continuing an aborted sweep
docs.text:
A sweep that was aborted, or that stopped on an error, can be continued from the first point it did not measure. Select it in the History and press Continue…, or use Sweep → Continue an aborted run… to pick any data file of the data folder. That includes a file whose run was cut off without its end, for example by a crash or a power cut (its status is incomplete).

The dialog says why and when the run stopped, how many points it measured, and the setpoints of the next point. It asks:

field what it does Wait after setting the channels (s, default 0) every swept channel is ramped to the next point, then the sweep waits this long before it measures again. Use it to let a sample settle, or a temperature recover, after the post-sweep settings changed things at the abort run the pre-sweep settings and hook again first (on by default) the pre phase runs again before the sweep goes on: its constants are set again and its hook runs again. Untick it when the pre phase should not repeat, for example when it starts a long cool-down

Continue now queues the continuation and starts the queue. Add to queue only queues it.

What you get:

  • A new data file, with a new run number. It starts with a copy of everything the aborted run measured, and the sweep appends to it. The aborted file is not changed.
  • The same data as a run that was never aborted. No point is measured twice and none is left out. Points are visited in the same order, with the snake directions kept. A dimension recorded after its inner loop is recorded once. Skipped points stay skipped. @elapsed goes on from where it stopped.
  • Every abort, recorded in the file.
    • The header has aborts, a list with one entry per abort. Each entry has the run, the file, the status and reason, when it stopped, the points measured by then, the last index, when it was continued, the wait and rerun_pre.
    • The header also has continued_from, the file this run continued, and first_run, the run number the sweep started as.
    • The events have an aborted and a continued event for each abort, in order.
    • If the pre phase ran again, its new recordings are in a pre_rerun event; the pre-sweep values of the first run stay as they were.
    • The footer counts the aborts.
  • No limit on the number of continuations. A continued run that is aborted again can be continued again. Its new file carries all the earlier aborts, and the data stay contiguous.

While a continued run goes on, the live data view, the GUI and web status bars and the tray show the points measured before the abort together with the new ones. The progress starts at the breakpoint, not at zero, and the time remaining comes from the rate since the run was continued. The data window lists the aborts under Details.

A run cannot be continued when it finished or was terminated with end_sweep(). It also cannot be continued when a channel it sweeps or records no longer exists. Continuing also refuses the file of the run that is going on now.

Files that go missing or change:

  • A file that is deleted, moved or damaged cannot be continued, and the dialog says so. A file whose last frame was cut off by a crash is not damaged in this sense: it continues from its last complete point.
  • A file deleted or replaced after its continuation was queued. The item checks the file again right before it runs. If the file is gone or is now a different run, the item ends with an error that says why. It writes no data file.
  • Once the continuation has started, the old file is no longer needed. It has been copied. The files of earlier aborts can also be deleted, because the newest file holds all the data. Their names stay in aborts as a record.
  • The same file cannot be queued for continuation twice. If it was continued before, the dialog warns that continuing it again measures the remaining points a second time. To go on with the newest data, continue the newest run instead.
  • An abort during the wait, before any new point, leaves a new file with the same data and one more entry in aborts. It can be continued like any other.
From Python 
info = c.call("continue_info", path=item["path"])
info["continuable"], info["points"], info["total"], info["next_setpoints"]
c.call("continue_sweep", path=item["path"], wait=30, rerun_pre=True, start=True)

from easymeasure.backend.storage import DataSet
ds = DataSet.load(path)
for a in ds.header.get("aborts", []):
    print(a["run"], a["status"], a["error"], a["points"], "of", a["total"])

docs.title: Scripts in the queue
docs.text: A script is a Python program that runs from the queue like a sweep, for example a loop that runs the same sweep at several temperatures. Scripts are an advanced topic with their own chapter: Queue scripts.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
Queueing and controlling from a Python client

With a Python client c:

id1 = c.call("queue_add", item={"kind": "sweep", "definition": sweep1})
id2 = c.call("queue_add", item={"kind": "sweep", "definition": sweep2}, start=True)
c.call("queue_move", item_id=id2, position=0)     # run it first
c.call("queue_remove", item_id=id1)
c.call("pause"); c.call("resume"); c.call("abort"); c.call("abort_all")
c.call("queue_stop")                              # stop after the current item
c.call("queue_options", stop_on_error=True)

st = c.call("queue_state")
st["state"], st["current"], len(st["queued"])     # 'running', {...}, 3
st["can"]       # which controls apply now: {'start': False, 'pause': True, ...}
for item in st["history"]:
    print(item["id"], item["kind"], item["name"], item["status"], item.get("path"))

The queue is idle, running, paused or aborting. The GUI and the web page enable their buttons from can.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: Over remote access, operators can queue, control and continue sweeps. Scripts, and sweeps with code in their point actions, need the admin role, because they run Python on the measurement computer.

docs.title: Remote access and the web app
docs.text:
The backend itself only listens on 127.0.0.1. For access from other computers it starts a gateway process, which speaks HTTPS and secure WebSockets and forwards authenticated, permitted requests to the backend over localhost:

browser / RemoteClient ──TLS 1.2+ (WSS, compressed)──▶ gateway ──localhost──▶ backend

docs.title: Switching it on
docs.text:
python -m easymeasure.remote adduser alice --role admin    # asks for a password
python -m easymeasure.backend --remote                     # backend + gateway on port 8443

Or in the GUI: Backend → Remote access…. There you can switch it on, see who is connected, and add, change or remove accounts. Remote access stays on across backend restarts until it is switched off. The tray's Open in browser offers to switch it on.

Then open https://<computer>:8443 in a browser.

docs.title: The web app
docs.text:
The web app mirrors the GUI:

  • instruments and channels, with actions, configuration channels, aliases, composites and user actions;
  • the sweep editor: load and save JSON files from your computer, load from a stored run, validate, queue;
  • the queue, with history and rerun;
  • live data and stored runs, with the same N-D plots: curve, heat map and stacked curves, X/Y choice, sliders, follow latest, colormaps, colour levels by dragging the colour bar, and zoom and pan;
  • monitor tiles, with columns and per-element curves for vector channels;
  • the Manual panel: spin box, slider, right-click expression, Set all to zero, hold + Set all;
  • the log, and downloads of data files and the PowerPoint file.

It reconnects by itself when the network, gateway or backend restarts, and it works on a phone. Light and dark themes follow the system, or Backend → Settings… in the web app.

docs.title: Accounts
docs.text:
python -m easymeasure.remote adduser bob --role operator
python -m easymeasure.remote passwd bob
python -m easymeasure.remote role bob viewer
python -m easymeasure.remote deluser bob
python -m easymeasure.remote users

Passwords have at least 10 characters and are stored scrypt-hashed. Account changes take effect at once, also for running gateways. Sessions of a removed user, or of a user whose password or role changed, are closed.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
role may viewer watch everything (state, monitor, live and stored data, logs, queue), read channels, download data operator + write channels (aliases and composites, with their limits and ramp rates; parameters), run instrument actions and user actions (writing them), monitor, queue / start / pause / abort sweeps, PPT slides, reconnect instruments. Not an instrument's own channels (src.V1, settings such as lockin.sensitivity): those are written without limits, so an operator can read them but not set them, sweep them or use them as sweep constants; the backend refuses it, and the web app does not offer them admin + scripts and sweep hook code (Python on the backend computer = full control), user actions' code, Driver Wizard, instruments, aliases and limits, raw commands, setups, settings, shutdown

Operators cannot run code:

  • sweeps with pre/post hook code or point actions are refused for them;
  • mapping and composite formulas go through a sandboxed evaluator, with an allow-list of math functions, no attribute or file access, and size limits on arrays and powers.

Remote users only reach files inside the data folder. Switching remote access, the tray and account management are only possible on the backend computer. The command reference gives each command's minimum role.

docs.title: Certificate (Let's Encrypt)
docs.text:
Without a configured certificate, the gateway generates a self-signed one. Browsers warn once: compare the SHA-256 fingerprint shown in the dialog, or by python -m easymeasure.remote cert. Python clients pin it with fingerprint=.

With a DNS name pointing to the backend computer (e.g. lab.example.org), the gateway can serve a real certificate. Browsers then connect to https://lab.example.org without a warning. In Backend → Remote access… → Certificate:

  1. Set the gateway Port to 443, the standard HTTPS port, so the address needs no port number. Remote access remembers it.
  2. On Windows, Open Windows firewall… allows incoming TCP 80 and the gateway port (one rule, easyMeasure remote access; Windows asks for administrator rights). The router must forward both ports to this computer.
  3. Enter the domain name, and an e-mail address for Let's Encrypt's expiry warnings. Agree to the Let's Encrypt Subscriber Agreement and press Get Let's Encrypt certificate.

Let's Encrypt checks that the name points here by fetching a token from http://<domain>/.well-known/acme-challenge/…. easyMeasure answers on port 80 for the few seconds of the check, so nothing else may use port 80 then. On Windows this means IIS, or the World Wide Web Publishing Service. Progress and any error (e.g. "nothing reached port 80 of this computer") show in the dialog. The test certificate box uses Let's Encrypt's staging server first, without its rate limits.

The certificate (<home>/remote/tls/acme/<domain>/fullchain.pem + privkey.pem) is used at once: a running gateway picks up changed certificate files within 30 s, without dropping connections. It is renewed automatically 30 days before it expires; the gateway checks hourly while it runs.

Use certificate files… takes any other certificate, such as one from your institution (PEM chain + key). Use self-signed goes back.

From the command line:

python -m easymeasure.remote letsencrypt lab.example.org --email me@example.org --agree-tos
python -m easymeasure.remote letsencrypt lab.example.org --email me@example.org --agree-tos --staging
python -m easymeasure.remote letsencrypt --renew [--force]

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• TLS only: version 1.2 or later, forward-secret AEAD ciphers, no compression or renegotiation.
  • Accounts and lock-out. Failed logins lock out the address (after 5 failures) and the account (after 10, from anywhere) for 30 s, doubling up to 1 h. Error messages never reveal whether a user exists.
  • Sessions:
    • 256-bit random tokens, kept by the browser in a __Host- cookie (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict);
    • only their hashes are stored;
    • they expire after 12 h without a connection, or 7 days in total;
    • they end at once on account changes.
  • Browser hardening:
    • a strict Content-Security-Policy;
    • Origin checks against cross-site WebSocket hijacking;
    • clickjacking and MIME-sniffing protection;
    • no data inserted as HTML.
  • Limits:
    • per connection: message size, request rate, unanswered requests;
    • per user and per address: connections;
    • TLS-handshake and first-request timeouts against slow-loris.

A client that accepts no data for 90 s is dropped. Idle connections are never dropped. * Isolation. The gateway is a separate process. Nothing from the network is parsed inside the backend before it has been authenticated and checked. A crash of the gateway cannot affect a running measurement; the backend restarts it. * Audit log (~/.easymeasure/logs/remote.log): logins, lock-outs, denied commands, every command that changes something (with user and address), downloads.

On Windows, allow Python through the firewall when asked (private networks). Only forward the port on your router or firewall if you need access from outside your network; a VPN in front of it is better still. All limits are in ~/.easymeasure/remote/config.json:

python -m easymeasure.remote config                       # show
python -m easymeasure.remote config max_ws_per_user=8 rate=50

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
• Backend frames are forwarded byte-for-byte, so arrays stay raw binary end to end.
  • WebSocket compression shrinks partially filled maps and JSON.
  • A slow connection makes the backend drop monitor and sweep-point events for that client instead of queueing them; the live view resynchronises.

On a local network a request takes well under a millisecond, and a 2 MB map takes about 40 ms.

docs.title: Robustness
docs.text: A measurement may run for days, with instruments that hang, drop commands, return garbage, lose their USB connection or crash their drivers. easyMeasure is built so that none of this takes the measurement, the backend or the data down with it.

docs.title: Separate processes
docs.text:
• The backend owns the instruments and runs measurements. It does not depend on any front end.
  • GUIs, the tray icon and the remote gateway are separate processes. Killing a frozen GUI never touches the backend; a reopened GUI picks up the running sweep. A crash of the gateway cannot affect a running measurement, and the backend restarts it.
  • Clients talk to the backend over framed JSON with raw numpy buffers, with no pickle. Every client has bounded queues:
    • live data for a slow client is dropped above 16 MB, and the client is told to resynchronise;
    • a client whose socket accepted nothing for 60 s, or has more than 64 MB waiting (a frozen GUI), is disconnected;
    • idle connections are never closed.

docs.title: Guarded instrument calls
docs.text:
Every driver call goes through an InstrumentHandle:

  • Deadline. It runs on a dedicated worker thread with a hard deadline (call_timeout). A driver that hangs forever is abandoned, its port is invalidated and a fresh worker is started.
  • Port arbitration. It runs inside a transaction on its port.
  • Contained exceptions. Every exception is caught and converted to an InstrumentError, including SystemExit, KeyboardInterrupt and MemoryError raised by buggy driver code.
  • Retries. Failed reads and writes are retried (retries). After reconnect_after consecutive failures the instrument is reconnected. Actions are never retried, because a trigger must not fire twice.
  • Validation. The result is converted to the channel's declared type and shape; a wrong one is an error, not data.
  • Circuit breaker. A channel that times out breaker_threshold times in a row is quarantined. It fails fast for breaker_cooldown seconds, doubling on repeated trips, so one pathological channel cannot block the rest of its instrument.

docs.title: Guard options
docs.text:
Per instrument, in its options:

option default meaning call_timeout 10 s deadline per call (channels may set their own) retries 2 retries of a failed read / write retry_delay 0.05 s pause between retries reconnect_after 2 consecutive failures before a reconnect timeout_retries 1 retries after a time-out breaker_threshold 2 consecutive time-outs before a channel is quarantined breaker_cooldown 10 s quarantine time (doubles on repeated trips)

docs.title: Ports
docs.text:
Every physical port is one Resource:

  • a second instrument asking for an exclusively owned port is refused;
  • ports declared shared are arbitrated by a fair, re-entrant lock per I/O sequence. When ownership changes, the new owner's select() runs (e.g. ++addr 5 on a Prologix adapter);
  • the measurement thread gets priority over monitor and GUI traffic, so monitoring never slows a sweep down.

docs.title: Protection of the sample
docs.text:
• Limits are checked before anything is written. For sweeps, every setpoint is checked before the first one is set.
  • NaN and infinity are never written.
  • Ramps are time-based and abortable. They start from where the instrument really is, since the cached value is discarded after actions and raw writes.
  • Composite channels move all their targets together, each within its ramp rate.
  • The post phase of a sweep runs after errors and aborts, to bring things back to a safe state.

docs.title: Safety faults
docs.text:
Some instruments can report a fault that endangers the hardware, such as a magnet quench (ami430). Such a fault is not an ordinary error:

  • it is never retried, and never turned into a NaN reading or a skipped point, whatever the sweep's on_read_error and on_set_error say;
  • the backend checks these instruments by itself (a watchdog, every poll_interval seconds), even when no sweep or monitor reads them;
  • when one is detected, the backend aborts the running sweep or script (its status is aborted or error, with the fault as the reason), stops the run queue so that nothing else starts unattended, aborts running user actions, and sends instrument_fault to every front end. The desktop GUI shows a warning window, the web app an error message;
  • the instrument's last error reads FAULT: … until the fault is cleared. The driver refuses what is unsafe meanwhile (for a magnet: changing the field), and reports the fault only once.

After clearing the fault on the instrument, start the queue again by hand.

docs.title: Scripts and code
docs.text:
• Abort reaches scripts on every line, so even while True: pass stops.
  • Composite and mapping formulas are evaluated by a sandboxed evaluator, with an allow-list of functions, no attribute or file access, and bounded array sizes and powers.
  • Dependency loops between composite channels are refused when defined, and a runtime guard stops any that slip through, so a call cannot hang the backend.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
• The journal is append-only and CRC-checked, and is fsync-ed every 0.5 s. After a crash it loads up to the last fraction of a second.
  • If the disk fails mid-run, the sweep keeps running in memory and the error is reported.
  • An aborted or crashed sweep can be continued from the first point it did not measure. The run goes into a new file that holds the old data and the new data together, and lists every abort.
  • PowerPoint slides that cannot be written to the target go to a _pending file.

docs.title: Seeing it work
docs.text:
python -m easymeasure.backend --setup examples/faulty_setup.json

Then run examples/sweep_faulty.json. The instruments drop commands, garble replies, hang, disconnect and raise random exceptions, and sim_chaos does worse. The sweep completes. The log shows each retry, reconnect and quarantine, and the instrument list shows each instrument's statistics.

The stress tests go much further.

docs.title: Simulated instruments
docs.text: easyMeasure can be learned, demonstrated and tested without hardware. There are two kinds of simulation.

docs.title: Simulated instruments
docs.text:
These are drivers of their own, built to be measured: a simulated quantum dot, a magnet that ramps in real time, a camera whose spot moves with two voltages. examples/demo_setup.json uses all of them.

driver simulates sim_source 4-channel DC source, SCPI over a shared SIM:: bus sim_dmm DMM measuring a simulated quantum dot (Coulomb diamonds) on the same bus sim_lockin lock-in: X, Y, R, θ and a 2-vector XY. With sample = graphene, a dual-gated bilayer graphene Hall bar driven through a 1 MΩ series resistor; measure = current makes it the current lock-in, with source naming the driving lock-in's amplitude sim_smu source-measure unit: sources a gate voltage, measures the gate leakage (breakdown near 8 V) sim_vna vector network analyzer: S11 traces of a superconducting resonator against power and field sim_spectrum 1-D trace per reading; the peak shifts with field and voltage sim_camera 2-D image per reading; the spot moves with two voltages sim_awg vector-valued write channel (waveform) sim_magnet field that ramps in real time; status RAMPING / HOLDING sim_temperature setpoint with first-order thermal lag sim_chaos pathological: wrong types, random shapes, hangs forever, slow, raises SystemExit / KeyboardInterrupt / MemoryError, flaky writes, binary garbage

The simulated instruments share one simulated world, so their readings are consistent. The dot's current depends on src.V1 and src.V2, the spectrum on the magnet's field, and so on.

From Python 
c.call("add_instrument", name="src", driver="sim_source", address="SIM::GPIB0")
c.call("add_instrument", name="dmm", driver="sim_dmm",    address="SIM::GPIB0")  # same bus
c.call("add_instrument", name="magnet", driver="sim_magnet", address="NONE")

docs.title: Fault injection
docs.text:
Every simulated driver takes options that make it misbehave like real hardware:

option effect error_rate a command is lost (time-out) garble_rate a corrupted reply, or a value of the wrong type hang_rate, hang_time a call hangs (for hang_time seconds) disconnect_rate the instrument drops off the bus exception_rate the driver raises a random exception nan_rate a NaN reading latency every call takes this long seed make the faults reproducible From Python 
c.call("add_instrument", name="flaky", driver="sim_dmm", address="SIM::GPIB0",
       options={"error_rate": 0.05, "hang_rate": 0.01, "hang_time": 30, "seed": 1})

examples/faulty_setup.json uses these options on every instrument, plus sim_chaos. Run examples/sweep_faulty.json with it to watch the robustness machinery at work.

docs.title: Emulated hardware
docs.text:
Every hardware driver can talk to a built-in emulator of its instrument instead of a port. Give it the address SIM::<anything>, or DAQ::SIM for the NI DAQs:

From Python 
c.call("add_instrument", name="smu", driver="keithley2400", address="SIM::smu")
c.call("add_instrument", name="lockin", driver="sr830", address="SIM::li")
c.call("add_instrument", name="daq", driver="ni63xx", address="DAQ::SIM",
       options={"model": "USB-6363"})

The emulators (easymeasure/drivers/emulators/) implement the instruments' command tables from their programming manuals:

  • short and long SCPI forms;
  • optional nodes;
  • the error queue and *ESR?.

Their physics is good enough to see something:

  • an SMU drives a resistor, with compliance clamping;
  • a lock-in sees a phase-shifted signal;
  • the DAQ has loop-back wiring: aiK sees aoK, and each digital line is wired to the one half a port away;
  • the Cygnus supply has resistive loads (option load_ohm).

Use emulators to rehearse a measurement before the instrument is connected, to check a setup file, or to develop against a driver. The driver reference pages list each driver's channels as reported by its emulator.

docs.title: Sweeps
docs.text: A sweep steps some channels through values in any number of nested dimensions and records other channels at every point. The Sweep editor tab builds it. The Quick start makes a first one, and tutorial 1 a two-dimensional one.

docs.title: The sweep editor
docs.text:
From top to bottom:

  • Name (1) of the sweep and its data file, a Comment (stored as metadata), and what to do on errors (see Errors).
  • Dimensions: the list of dimensions on the left, the selected one on the right. For each: the number of Points (2), the channels it sets (Set swept channels, 3), the delays, the channels it records (Record, 4), and the optional point actions. They are laid out in the order they happen at every point.
  • Pre-sweep and Post-sweep tabs: settings applied before the first point and after the last (see Pre and post phases).
  • The status line at the bottom, which shows what the Sweep menu did.

The Sweep menu, in the menu bar, works on the sweep in the editor:

  • New starts an empty sweep. Load… / Save… read and write it as a .json file, and Load from data file… loads the sweep of an earlier measurement, for a rerun or a variation.
  • Validate (5) checks the sweep and shows its number of points and shortest duration.
  • Add to queue and Add & start (6) queue it.

A sweep is stored as a plain dictionary, the same as a JSON file. The examples below show that form, since it is compact: each key is a box of the editor. The full list of keys is in the sweep definition reference.

From Python 
sweep = {"name": "iv",
         "dimensions": [{"points": 101,
                         "sweep": [{"channel": "Vb", "start": -0.3, "stop": 0.3}],
                         "record": ["I"]}]}
c.call("validate_sweep", definition=sweep)      # {'ok': True, 'shape': [101], …}
c.call("queue_add", item={"kind": "sweep", "definition": sweep}, start=True)

In a queue script, run_sweep(sweep) runs it and returns the data.

docs.title: Dimensions
docs.text:
Dimension 1 is the innermost (fastest) loop. + dimension adds another one around it, and ▲ inner / ▼ outer reorder them. (In the file, the dimensions are a list, so dimension 1 is the first entry, index 0.)

A 2-D map of current against gate and bias voltage, where the gate is stepped for every bias value:

{"name": "coulomb_diamonds",
 "dimensions": [
   {"points": 101, "sweep": [{"channel": "Vg", "start": -0.6, "stop": 0.6}],
    "record": ["I", "X"]},
   {"points": 41,  "sweep": [{"channel": "Vb", "start": -0.3, "stop": 0.3}],
    "record": ["T", "@elapsed"]}]}

It behaves like:

for Vb in linspace(-0.3, 0.3, 41):          # dimension 2 (outer)
    set Vb; record T, @elapsed
    for Vg in linspace(-0.6, 0.6, 101):     # dimension 1 (inner)
        set Vg; record I, X

A channel recorded in a dimension is stored with one axis for that dimension and one for each outer dimension: I and X are 101 × 41 maps, and T is a 41-point line. There is no limit on the number of dimensions. A 3-D map just adds a third entry.

docs.title: Setpoints
docs.text:
Each row of Set swept channels gets its values in one of three ways. The table's Mapping and Values columns are to the right of Start and Stop; scroll or widen the window. Custom sweeps has worked examples.

Linear: start / stop:

{"channel": "Vg", "start": -0.5, "stop": 0.5}

Explicit values:

{"channel": "B", "values": [0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4]}

The dimension's points must match the number of values.

Mapping: an expression of i (index), N (points), t = i/(N-1), start, stop and x (the linear value from start to stop):

{"channel": "Vg", "start": 0, "stop": 1, "mapping": "start + (stop - start)*t**2"}
{"channel": "B",  "start": -3, "stop": 3, "mapping": "sign(x)*x**2/3"}
{"channel": "f",  "start": 1e3, "stop": 1e6, "mapping": "start*(stop/start)**t"}

The first example is quadratic spacing, denser near the start. The second is denser near zero field. The third is logarithmic.

docs.title: Several channels in one dimension
docs.text:
Every channel listed in a dimension's sweep steps together, which is useful for a diagonal cut or a compensated gate:

{"points": 201,
 "sweep": [{"channel": "Vx", "start": -0.5, "stop": 0.5},
           {"channel": "Vy", "start": 0.5,  "stop": -0.5},
           {"channel": "Vg", "start": 0, "stop": 0.2, "mapping": "0.1 + 0.4*(x - 0.1)"}],
 "record": ["I"]}

Variables of one composite channel swept in the same dimension are set together at every point.

docs.title: Vector channels
docs.text:
A channel whose value is an array, such as an AWG waveform, needs a mapping that returns the array for each point:

{"channel": "wave", "start": 0, "stop": 1,
 "mapping": "x*np.sin(np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 64))"}

docs.title: Recording
docs.text:
Any readable channel can be recorded: aliases, raw instrument.channel references, composite channels, configuration channels and the built-ins @time and @elapsed. Array channels are stored with their own shape appended:

{"name": "spectrum_vs_field",
 "dimensions": [{"points": 61, "sweep": [{"channel": "B", "start": -1.5, "stop": 1.5}],
                 "record": ["spectrum", "peak", "image"]}]}

spectrum (a trace per reading) becomes a 61 × length array, image (a 2-D camera frame) a 61 × h × w array. The live view shows them with sliders for the extra axes.

docs.title: Delays
docs.text:
{"points": 101, "sweep": [{"channel": "Vg", "start": -0.5, "stop": 0.5}],
 "record": ["X"], "pre_delay": 0.3, "post_delay": 0}

pre_delay runs after setting and before recording. For a lock-in, use about 3 to 5 time constants. post_delay runs after recording. The shortest duration of a sweep, from its delays, is in validate_sweep(...)["min_duration"].

docs.title: Snake scans
docs.text:
{"points": 101, "sweep": [{"channel": "Vg", "start": -0.5, "stop": 0.5}],
 "record": ["I"], "snake": true}

With snake the dimension alternates its direction on each pass of the outer loop: up, down, up, and so on. This avoids a long ramp back to the start, and hysteresis shows up as a difference between the even and odd lines.

docs.title: The order at each point
docs.text:
Every point of a dimension runs:

  1. pre_sweep action
  2. set the swept channels (ramped at their alias rates)
  3. post_sweep action
  4. pre_delay
  5. pre_record action
  6. record
  7. post_record action
  8. post_delay
  9. the inner dimensions

With "record_after_inner": true (outer dimensions only) the inner dimensions run before step 5. You then record, for example, the temperature after each line rather than before it. The editor lays every dimension out in this order. The actions are optional code snippets; see Point actions.

docs.title: Pre and post phases
docs.text:
"pre":  {"hook": "log('starting at T = %.3f K' % get('T'))",
         "constants": [{"channel": "src.output", "value": "ON"},
                       {"channel": "lockin.sensitivity", "value": "1e-2"}],
         "record": ["T", "B"]},
"post": {"record": ["T"],
         "constants": [{"channel": "Vg", "value": 0}, {"channel": "Vb", "value": 0}],
         "hook": ""}
  • Pre phase: hook, then constants, then record. This happens before the first point.
  • Post phase: record, then constants, then hook. This always runs: after the last point, after an error and, by default (run_post_on_abort), after an abort. Use it to bring the sample back to a safe state.

Constants are a natural place for configuration channels (ranges, modes, output on/off). A constant can also be an action, of an instrument (dmm.reset) or your own (gates_to_zero), without a value: it runs at that place in the order. A sweep whose pre-sweep constants switch a mode, such as smu.mode = Current before a current sweep, is validated again after the constants were applied. A sweep that still does not fit stops before its first point.

Hook code is Python using the script API. Over remote access, a sweep with hook code needs the admin role.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
"on_read_error": "nan",     // a failed reading: store NaN and go on (or "abort")
"on_set_error": "abort",    // a failed setting: stop the sweep (or "skip" the point)
"run_post_on_abort": true

The guarded instrument layer already retries transient errors and reconnects instruments, so these policies only see what survived that.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Before a sweep starts, every setpoint is computed and limit-checked: alias limits, composite variables, and mapping ranges. A sweep that would exceed a limit anywhere never starts:

From Python 
bad = {"name": "x", "dimensions": [{"points": 11,
       "sweep": [{"channel": "Vg", "start": 0, "stop": 5}], "record": []}]}
c.call("validate_sweep", definition=bad)
# SweepDefinitionError: Vg: value 2.5 above maximum 2   (the first setpoint beyond the limit)

validate_sweep returns the shape, total points, minimum duration, warnings and the normalised definition. Sweep → Validate calls it.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
"metadata": {"sample": "D17", "cooldown": 3, "comment": "after thermal cycle"}

The metadata goes into the data file header and the PowerPoint slide. "ppt": false skips the slide for this sweep.

docs.title: Complete example: I–V curve with a source-measure unit in current mode
docs.text:
{"name": "iv",
 "dimensions": [{"points": 101,
   "sweep": [{"channel": "Isrc", "start": 0, "stop": 1e-6}], "record": ["Vmeas"]}],
 "pre":  {"constants": [{"channel": "smu.mode", "value": "Current"},
                        {"channel": "smu.Vcompliance", "value": 2},
                        {"channel": "smu.output", "value": "ON"}]},
 "post": {"constants": [{"channel": "Isrc", "value": 0},
                        {"channel": "smu.output", "value": "OFF"}]}}

Here Isrc is an alias of smu.current, and Vmeas is an alias of smu.voltage. This is examples/sweep_iv_current.json; the other examples/sweep_*.json files show vector channels (sweep_awg_vector.json), a 3-D camera scan (sweep_camera_3d.json) and spectra against field (sweep_spectrum_vs_field.json).

docs.title: Loading a sweep from a data file
docs.text: Every data file holds the full definition of its sweep. In the editor, Load from data file… opens it for a rerun or a variation. From Python, use c.call("read_run_header", path=...)["definition"].

docs.title: The test suite
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[test]"
python -m pytest -q tests          # a few minutes; GUI tests run offscreen
python -m pytest -q tests/test_composites.py -k loops     # one file / test
file covers test_codec_exprs.py the wire codec (fuzzed), the expression sandbox test_resources_instruments.py fair / priority locks, port arbitration, hung / crashing / garbage-returning drivers, circuit breaker test_channels.py, test_composites.py limits, ramp rates, scaling; composite writes, reads, mappings, nesting, loops test_sweep.py N-D sweeps with vector and image data, mappings, hooks, flow control, abort / pause test_storage.py crash recovery of truncated or corrupted files, disk failure during a sweep, HDF5 test_robustness.py scripts (including an un-cooperative infinite loop), a frozen client, a SIGKILLed frontend, a backend restart under a live GUI test_server.py the protocol, events, many clients test_drivers.py, test_cygnus.py, test_ni63xx.py every hardware driver against its emulator test_dynamic_channels.py allowed values; channel lists that change with modes, also in sweeps test_actions.py, test_user_actions.py instrument actions, user actions test_interfaces.py addresses, interfaces, discovery test_driver_wizard.py the wizard: templates, generated drivers, try-it, save / reload test_gui.py the desktop panels, offscreen test_remote.py, test_acme.py the gateway and the certificate client (see below) test_web_ui.py the web app in Chromium (Playwright) test_docs.py this documentation's generated pages

docs.title: Driver tests
docs.text:
tests/test_drivers.py runs every hardware driver against its emulator. It checks:

  • that every command a driver sends exists in the instrument's command table;
  • that settings round-trip through all their allowed values;
  • that mode switches rename channels and change units;
  • that refused values come back with the instrument's own error message;
  • that a noisy serial line is survived;
  • that several instruments can share one GPIB adapter;
  • that an I–V sweep in current-source mode runs from the example setup.

docs.title: Remote access tests
docs.text:
tests/test_remote.py checks the gateway:

  • TLS versions and pinning, security headers, static-file traversal and cookie flags;
  • generic login errors and brute-force lock-out;
  • WebSocket authentication and Origin checks;
  • every role's permissions, end to end;
  • sessions closed on account changes;
  • malformed, oversized and non-WebSocket traffic;
  • rate, in-flight and connection limits;
  • slow-loris sockets, a client that never reads, and idle connections;
  • backend and gateway restarts (sessions survive), and a SIGKILLed gateway (the backend restarts it);
  • downloads, the expression sandbox and performance.

tests/test_acme.py runs the Let's Encrypt client against a local fake ACME server.

docs.title: Web app tests
docs.text:
tests/test_web_ui.py drives the web app in Chromium. It needs:

pip install -e ".[webtest]"
python -m playwright install chromium

docs.title: Stress tests
docs.text:
python examples/stress_test.py --minutes 10                    # faulty hardware
python examples/remote_stress_test.py --minutes 10 --browser   # remote access under attack

stress_test.py runs a backend process with the faulty setup. Six clients hammer it with:

  • reads, out-of-limit writes and configuration-channel writes;
  • every instrument action, including ones that fail, hang forever or raise SystemExit;
  • sweeps (some with actions in their hooks) and scripts;
  • pause / abort, malformed requests and abrupt disconnects.

A frozen client and a client sending random bytes join in.

At the end it checks that:

  • the backend is alive and responsive;
  • every protected value is within its limits;
  • a normal sweep still completes;
  • every data file loads.

It also reports the backend's memory over time.

remote_stress_test.py runs the faulty-hardware stress test while legitimate remote clients work and attackers:

  • guess passwords;
  • send random, malformed and oversized messages;
  • send forbidden commands and sandbox escapes;
  • flood requests and open slow-loris sockets;
  • in one case, never read.

It checks that:

  • nothing forbidden ever succeeded;
  • the probe client never failed;
  • both processes survived with bounded memory;
  • a remote sweep still completes.

A 10-minute run on a 2-core machine at load 12 sent 130 000 fuzz messages, 590 password guesses, 11 700 forbidden requests and 155 000 rate-limited requests. Results:

  • no forbidden request succeeded;
  • 0 of 1545 probe pings failed (p50 7 ms, p99 0.4 s through the gateway);
  • the gateway stayed at 180–215 MB.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[docs]"
mkdocs build --strict

The pages for drivers, commands, expressions, the command line and the Python API are generated from the code (docs/gen_reference.py), so they cannot go stale. tests/test_docs.py checks that the generator covers every driver and command.

docs.title: User actions
docs.text:
User actions are your own named snippets of Python, run with one click, such as gates_to_zero, magnet_down or outputs_off. They can control any channel. They are part of the setup, so they are saved, loaded and autosaved with it.

A user action is itself a channel: a write-only one with a plain name (letters, digits and _, like an alias). Writing it runs it, from anywhere: its button, set('gates_to_zero') in a script or another action, a pre- or post-sweep constant without a value, or write_channel from Python. Its name is unique among all names of the setup (aliases, composites, parameters, instruments).

set_many({'VL': 0, 'VR': 0})      # limits and ramp rates apply as always
set('B', 0)
print('gates and field at 0')

Each action is also a button at the top of the Manual panel: ▶ runs it, and while it runs, the same button aborts it.

The code can use the setup's parameters: by name (set('Vbg', V0), the value when the action starts) or as params.V0 (the present value). set('Cb', 0.6) (or params.Cb = 0.6) changes a value parameter.

docs.title: The Actions panel
docs.text:
Instruments & channels → User Actions (a tab; desktop and web) lists your actions with their description and last run: finished ✔ / aborted ■ / error ✘, time and duration. Hover a failed run to see its error.

button does ▶ Run (or Enter, or double click on the web) run the selected action now ■ Abort stop the running action(s) at the next line, sleep or ramp step Add… / Edit… the editor: name, description, ask before running, code; insert channel name… puts a channel name at the cursor; Check checks the name and the code (OK checks too) Remove, ↑ ↓ delete, reorder

Add… opens the editor:

Tick ask before running for actions that should be confirmed first, such as "outputs off" during a cooldown. Tutorial 3 makes the gates_to_zero button step by step.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
From Python 
c.call("define_user_action", name="gates_to_zero",
       code="set_many({'Vx': 0, 'Vy': 0})\nset('Vg', 0)",
       description="all gates to 0 V", confirm=True)

c.call("write_channel", name="gates_to_zero")          # runs it
# {'name': 'gates_to_zero', 'status': 'finished', 'error': None, 'elapsed': 0.41, …}

c.call("list_user_actions")
c.call("define_user_action", name="zero_gates", code="…", rename_from="gates_to_zero")
c.call("move_user_action", name="zero_gates", position=0)
c.call("remove_user_action", name="zero_gates")

write_channel waits for the end and returns how it ended (finished or aborted). A failure raises, like any write that fails; the last result of every action, failures included, is in list_user_actions.

docs.title: How they run
docs.text:
• Immediately, not through the queue, like a write from the Manual panel. A paused sweep does not hold an action back.
  • With the same namespace as scripts: get, set, set_many, sleep, wait_until, instrument, print, log, np, math and state (the same dict as scripts).
  • Alias and composite limits and ramp rates apply to every set; channels of instruments are written as they are.
  • Each run has its own abort control. Abort, or abort all, stops it at the next line, sleep or ramp step. Run from a script or a sweep, aborting those stops it too.
  • One run of the same action at a time: running it again while it runs is refused.

Sweeps cannot be started from an action; queue them instead.

docs.title: Actions calling actions
docs.text:
set('gates_to_zero')
set('B', 0)

An action runs another by writing it, set('name'). An error or abort in the inner one stops the outer one too. An action that ends up calling itself is refused, with the chain in the message (action loop1 calls itself (loop1 → loop2 → loop1)).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Outputs off (with ask before running):

for k in range(1, 9):
    set('cyg.output%d' % k, 'OFF')
set('smu.reset')

Bring a cryostat to base temperature and report:

set('Tset', 0.01)
wait_until(lambda: get('T') < 0.05, timeout=7200, interval=10)
log('at base: %.1f mK' % (1000 * get('T')))

Park the gates where the last good sweep left them:

set_many(state.get('parking', {'Vx': 0, 'Vy': 0}))

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: Defining an action is writing code that runs on the backend computer, so over remote access it needs the admin role. Running and aborting actions is an operator right.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
page contents Backend commands every command with signature, minimum remote role and description (generated) Sweep definition every field of a sweep Setup file the JSON format of setups Script API the functions available in scripts, hooks, point actions and user actions Expressions functions and constants allowed in formulas (generated) Command line --help of every program (generated) Settings and files backend settings, gateway configuration, where files live Instrument drivers one page per driver: interfaces, options, channels, actions (generated) Python API every module, class and function (generated from the docstrings)

The generated pages are rebuilt from the code at every documentation build.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text: Installed with easyMeasure: easymeasure-backend, easymeasure (the GUI) and easymeasure-remote; every program also runs as python -m <module>. The help texts below are generated from the programs.

docs.title: Backend
docs.text:
python -m easymeasure.backend or easymeasure-backend

usage: easymeasure-backend [-h] [--host HOST] [--port PORT] [--home HOME] [--setup SETUP]
                           [--restore] [--quiet] [--no-tray] [--remote [PORT]] [--no-remote]
                           [--force]

Run the easyMeasure backend service.

    python -m easymeasure.backend [--port 47811] [--host 127.0.0.1]
                                  [--setup my_setup.json | --restore]

The backend is independent of any frontend: frontends may be started, closed or
killed at any time without affecting a running measurement.

options:
  -h, --help       show this help message and exit
  --host HOST      interface to listen on
  --port PORT      TCP port (default 47811)
  --home HOME      state directory (default ~/.easymeasure)
  --setup SETUP    setup file to load at start
  --restore        restore the automatically saved setup of the last session
  --quiet          no console logging
  --no-tray        do not show the system-tray indicator
  --remote [PORT]  also start the internet gateway (HTTPS/WSS, default port 8443); see python -m
                   easymeasure.remote
  --no-remote      do not start the gateway even if remote access is enabled
  --force          start even if another backend seems to be running

docs.title: Desktop GUI
docs.text:
python -m easymeasure.frontend or easymeasure

usage: easymeasure [-h] [--start-backend] [--home HOME]

options:
  -h, --help       show this help message and exit
  --start-backend  start a detached backend if none is running
  --home HOME      state directory (default ~/.easymeasure)

docs.title: Remote access
docs.text:
python -m easymeasure.remote or easymeasure-remote

usage: python -m easymeasure.remote [-h] [--home HOME]
                                    {serve,adduser,passwd,role,deluser,users,cert,letsencrypt,status,config}
                                    ...

Remote access: run the gateway and manage accounts.

    python -m easymeasure.remote serve [--port 8443] [--host 0.0.0.0]
    python -m easymeasure.remote adduser NAME [--role viewer|operator|admin]
    python -m easymeasure.remote passwd NAME
    python -m easymeasure.remote role NAME ROLE
    python -m easymeasure.remote deluser NAME
    python -m easymeasure.remote users
    python -m easymeasure.remote cert [--regenerate]
    python -m easymeasure.remote status

Usually the backend starts the gateway itself (``python -m easymeasure.backend
--remote``) and restarts it if it ever stops.  Changes to accounts take effect
immediately, also for running gateways (sessions of a removed user, or of a user
whose password or role changed, are closed).

    letsencrypt         get (or renew) a Let's Encrypt certificate

  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --home HOME           state directory (default ~/.easymeasure)

docs.title: Backend commands
docs.text:
Everything the front ends do goes through these commands, so a script can do the same. Call them with keyword arguments:

from easymeasure.client import BackendClient
c = BackendClient.connect()
c.call("write_channel", name="Vg", value=0.2)

or in-process on a Backend object (be.write_channel(name="Vg", value=0.2)). Role is the minimum role a remote user needs (local only: refused through the internet gateway). Commands marked ⚡ are served by a separate thread pool, so they answer even while every instrument is busy.

docs.title: Expressions
docs.text: Formulas appear in several places: sweep mappings, composite channel targets, reads and mappings, Set from expression… in the Manual panel. They are evaluated by a sandboxed evaluator (easymeasure.common.exprs): only the names below, arithmetic, comparisons, and / or / not, a if c else b, indexing and list / tuple literals. No attribute access (except np.<function> from the list), no imports, no files; array sizes and powers are bounded.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: limit value source length 4000 characters largest array 10,000,000 elements largest integer from ** / << 4096 bits

docs.title: Piecewise functions
docs.text:
piecewise(x < 0, -x, x < 1, x**2, 1)   # cond1, value1, cond2, value2, …, default
piecewise(x > 0, sqrt(x))                # no default: NaN where no condition holds
-x if x < 0 else 2*x                      # scalar
where(x < 0, -x, 2*x)                     # elementwise
interp(x, [0, 1, 2], [0, 10, 0])          # table, linear in between

piecewise works on scalars and arrays (elementwise, with broadcasting). Invalid operations (log(-1), 0/0) give NaN / inf without warnings.

docs.title: Names per context
docs.text: where names sweep mapping x (linear value from start to stop), i (index), N (points), t = i/(N-1), start, stop composite multivariate write target the composite's variables composite read any channel: aliases, variables, mappings, other reads composite mapping forward: x; backward: y Set from expression… x (the present value)

docs.title: Script API
docs.text:
Python code runs in the backend in five places, all with the same namespace:

  • queued scripts;
  • a sweep's pre/post hooks;
  • point actions;
  • user actions;
  • run_script_now.

The few differences are listed at the end.

docs.title: Channels
docs.text: Every channel is read with get and written with set, whatever its kind: an alias, a composite channel (nD.n), a parameter, a user action, @time, or a channel, setting or action of an instrument (dmm.V, lockin.sensitivity, dmm.reset). Its access (r, w, rw) is respected: get of an action or set of a read-only channel raises.

docs.title: get(name)
docs.text:
Read any readable channel: an alias, a composite channel, a parameter, instrument.channel, @time or @elapsed. Returns a float, a numpy array or a string.

I = get('I')
spec = get('spectrum')          # numpy array
mode = get('dmm.mode')          # 'Vdc'

docs.title: set(name, value=None, ramp=True)
docs.text:
Write any writable channel. An alias or composite channel keeps its limits (checked first) and, with ramp, is approached at the ramp rate(s); a channel of an instrument is written as it is (no limits, no ramp); a value parameter takes the value. Writing an action runs it; it needs no value. The call waits for the end of the ramp (or of the action) and returns the value set.

set('Vg', 0.25)
set('Vg', 0, ramp=False)        # jump
set('lockin.sensitivity', '1e-3')
set('bg.voltage', 0)            # the instrument's channel: no limits, no ramp
set('Cb', 0.6)                  # a value parameter
set('lockin.auto_gain')         # an instrument action
set('gates_to_zero')            # a user action

docs.title: set_many({name: value, …}, ramp=True)
docs.text:
Set several channels together, e.g. all variables of a composite (required for their first setting). Everything is limit-checked before anything is written, and the ramp moves all of them together. Parameters are set first, actions run last. Returns every value set.

set_many({'gates.eps': 0.0, 'gates.U': 0.3})

docs.title: sleep(seconds)
docs.text: An abortable sleep. Always use it instead of time.sleep, so pause and abort work.

docs.title: wait_until(condition, timeout=60, interval=0.2)
docs.text:
Polls condition() until it is true. Returns True, or False after timeout seconds. It does not raise.

if not wait_until(lambda: get('magnet.status') == 'HOLDING', timeout=600):
    log('magnet did not settle')

docs.title: check()
docs.text: Honour pause / abort now. This is rarely needed, because abort is checked on every line anyway.

docs.title: instrument(name)
docs.text:
A guarded proxy of the instrument:

member does .raw_query(cmd) send a command, return the reply .raw_write(cmd) send a command .call(method, *args, **kwargs) call a driver method, guarded .state connected, disconnected, error … 
smu = instrument('smu')
log(smu.raw_query('*IDN?'))

docs.title: Sweeps and actions
docs.text: function does where run_sweep(definition) run a sweep synchronously and return its data: a DataSet with .status (finished, aborted, error, terminated), .data, .setpoints, .value_axes, .path queued scripts load_sweep(path) a sweep definition (a dict) from a .json file saved by the sweep editor, or from a data file (.emj, .h5); change it, then run_sweep() it everywhere skip_point(), skip_line(), end_sweep() flow control point actions

docs.title: Output and state
docs.text: name log(msg), print(…) write to the backend log (and the GUI's log dock) warn(msg) the same, as a warning state a dict kept in the backend between scripts, hooks and user actions params the setup's parameters, read-only: params.Cb, params['Cb'], dict(params) (present values). Each parameter is also a name of its own (Cb), with its value when the script or action started, unless that name is taken by the API np, math, time modules

docs.title: Point-action extras
docs.text: name k the dimension i the index in it index the indices of this and the outer dimensions setpoints channel → value at this point values (post_record) what was just recorded

docs.title: Differences between the places
docs.text: scripts hooks point actions user actions runs from the queue at the start / end of a sweep at every point at once, on request run_sweep ✓ – – – user_action – – – ✓ flow control – – ✓ – pause at the next line with the sweep with the sweep not affected abort queue abort sweep abort sweep abort abort_user_action / abort all remote role admin admin admin admin to define, operator to run

docs.title: Backend settings
docs.text:
Kept in <home>/backend_settings.json. Change them in the GUI (File → Settings) or with set_settings:

c.call("set_settings", data_dir="D:/data", fsync_interval=0.5)
setting default meaning data_dir – default: ~/.easymeasure/data ppt_path "" append slides here when a run ends ("" = off) auto_ppt True append a slide automatically at the end of every run export_hdf5 True write an .h5 copy next to the journal at the end fsync_interval 0.5 seconds between fsyncs of the data file (data lost on a crash) driver_paths [] extra directories with driver files autosave_setup True save the setup to /autosave_setup.json on every change ppt_colormap viridis colormap of the heat maps on slides remote_access False start the internet gateway with the backend folders_confirmed False the GUI asked for the data folder / PowerPoint file once

docs.title: Remote gateway configuration
docs.text:
Kept in <home>/remote/config.json; see Remote access. Show or change it with python -m easymeasure.remote config [key=value …] (JSON values).

key default meaning host 0.0.0.0 interface to listen on ("127.0.0.1" = this computer only) port 8443 HTTPS / WSS port (443: no port number in the address) certfile – PEM certificate chain; None = self-signed (auto-generated) keyfile – private key of certfile cert_names [] extra host names / IPs for the self-signed certificate acme – Let's Encrypt: {domain, email, staging, directory, http_port} (set by 'letsencrypt'; the gateway renews the certificate) cert_check_s 30 how often the gateway looks for a new certificate file session_idle_hours 12 a session with no connection for this long expires session_max_days 7 absolute session lifetime (log in again after that) max_sessions_per_user 20 logged-in sessions per account max_ws_total 64 simultaneous live connections max_ws_per_user 16 live connections per account max_conn_per_ip 64 TCP connections per client address max_msg_bytes 8388608 largest message a client may send rate 200 requests per second per connection (sustained) burst 600 requests a connection may send at once before rate applies max_in_flight 64 unanswered requests per connection login_max_failures_ip 5 failed logins from one address before it is locked out login_max_failures_user 10 failed logins for one account (from anywhere) lockout_s 30 first lockout; doubles each time lockout_max_s 3600 longest lockout first_request_timeout 15 TLS connection that sends no request in time is closed tls_handshake_timeout 10 seconds for the TLS handshake heartbeat_s 20 WebSocket ping interval (detects dead peers only) trust_proxy False take the client address from X-Forwarded-For allowed_origins [] extra browser origins allowed to connect

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
<home> is ~/.easymeasure (override with the environment variable EASYMEASURE_HOME, or --home on the command line).

file contents <home>/backend.json port and access token of the running backend (clients read it) <home>/backend_settings.json backend settings <home>/autosave_setup.json the setup, saved on every change (--restore) <home>/data/<date>/<run>_<name>.emj / .h5 data, unless data_dir is set <home>/drivers/ drivers made with the Driver Wizard (and your own) <home>/logs/backend.log backend log (rotating) <home>/logs/remote.log remote access audit log <home>/remote/config.json, users.json gateway configuration, accounts (hashed passwords) <home>/remote/tls/ gateway certificates (self-signed, Let's Encrypt acme/<domain>/)

docs.text: port used by 47811 (localhost only) backend ↔ GUIs and BackendClient (--port) 8443 (configurable, e.g. 443) remote gateway, HTTPS / WSS 80 (a few seconds) Let's Encrypt HTTP-01 challenge

docs.title: Setup file
docs.text:
A setup contains:

  • the instruments;
  • the parameters;
  • the aliases;
  • the composite channels;
  • the monitor list;
  • the user actions.

It is saved as JSON (save_setup), loaded with load_setup or python -m easymeasure.backend --setup file.json, and autosaved on every change to <home>/autosave_setup.json (restored by --restore).

{
  "format": "easyMeasure-setup-1",
  "instruments": [
    {"name": "src", "driver": "sim_source", "address": "SIM::GPIB0", "options": {"gpib_addr": 1}},
    {"name": "smu", "driver": "keithley2400", "address": "GPIB0::24::INSTR",
     "options": {"call_timeout": 20, "verify_writes": true}}
  ],
  "aliases": [
    {"name": "Vg", "target": "src.V1", "min": -2, "max": 2, "ramp_rate": 2.0, "unit": "V",
     "description": "gate"},
    {"name": "I", "target": "dmm.reading", "unit": "nA"}
  ],
  "composites": [
    {"type": "multi", "name": "gates",
     "variables": [{"name": "eps", "min": -0.4, "max": 0.4, "unit": "V", "ramp_rate": 0.5},
                   {"name": "U", "min": 0, "max": 0.5, "unit": "V"}],
     "targets": {"Vx": "U + eps", "Vy": "U - eps"}},
    {"type": "read", "name": "Vdiff", "expression": "(Vx - Vy)/2", "unit": "V"},
    {"type": "map", "name": "Tset_C", "target": "Tset", "forward": "x + 273.15",
     "backward": "y - 273.15", "min": -273.15, "max": 26.85, "unit": "°C"}
  ],
  "monitor": [{"channel": "T", "interval": 1.0}, {"channel": "I", "interval": 0.5}],
  "actions": [
    {"name": "gates_to_zero", "code": "set_many({'Vx': 0, 'Vy': 0})",
     "description": "all gates to 0 V", "confirm": false}
  ]
}

docs.title: Sections
docs.text: key entries format always "easyMeasure-setup-1" instruments {name, driver, address, options}; see each driver for its options parameters {name, value \| formula, unit, description}; see Parameters aliases {name, target, min, max, ramp_rate, ramp_step, scale, offset, unit, allowed, read_only, description}; see Aliases composites {type: multi \| read \| map, …}; see Composite channels monitor {channel, interval} actions {name, code, description, confirm}; see User actions

docs.title: Loading
docs.text:
load_setup returns a list of problems. An empty list means everything loaded:

  • instruments that cannot connect are added anyway and reported;
  • parameters are loaded together, whatever their order; one that is wrong (a circle, an unknown name) is reported and left out;
  • aliases whose instrument is missing are reported;
  • composites are loaded in dependency order, whatever their order in the file;
  • a user action whose code does not compile is reported.

With replace=False, the setup is added to what is there instead of replacing it.

A composite needs its type. The variables of a multi composite are channels named after it: above, gates.eps and gates.U. Setups written before this naming used the bare variable names in sweeps, scripts and other formulas; rename them there (eps → gates.eps).

docs.title: Sweep definition
docs.text:
A sweep is a JSON-compatible dict. See the Sweeps tutorial for explanations and examples. validate_sweep returns the normalised form, with every default filled in.

{
  "name": "gate_bias_map",
  "dimensions": [
    {"points": 101,
     "sweep":  [{"channel": "Vg", "start": -0.5, "stop": 0.5},
                {"channel": "Vc", "start": 0, "stop": 1, "mapping": "start+(stop-start)*t**2"},
                {"channel": "wave", "mapping": "np.sin(np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 64))*t"},
                {"channel": "Vx", "values": [0, 0.1, 0.3]}],
     "record": ["I", "spectrum"],
     "pre_delay": 0.05,
     "post_delay": 0.0,
     "snake": false,
     "record_after_inner": false,
     "label": "",
     "hooks": {"pre_record": {"enabled": true, "code": "set('dmm.trigger')"}}},
    {"points": 21, "sweep": [{"channel": "Vb", "start": -0.3, "stop": 0.3}],
     "record": ["T"]}
  ],
  "pre":  {"hook": "log('starting')", "constants": [{"channel": "dmm.mode", "value": "Vdc"}],
           "record": ["T"]},
  "post": {"record": ["T"], "constants": [{"channel": "Vg", "value": 0}], "hook": ""},
  "on_read_error": "nan",
  "on_set_error": "abort",
  "run_post_on_abort": true,
  "ppt": true,
  "metadata": {"sample": "D17", "comment": "..."}
}

docs.title: Top level
docs.text: field type default meaning name str "sweep" used in the file name and slide title dimensions list (required) at least one; index 0 is the innermost (fastest) loop pre dict {} pre phase: hook → constants → record post dict {} post phase: record → constants → hook; always runs on_read_error "nan" / "abort" "nan" a failed reading: store NaN, or stop the sweep on_set_error "abort" / "skip" "abort" a failed setting: stop the sweep, or skip the point run_post_on_abort bool true run the post phase after an abort too ppt bool true append a PowerPoint slide at the end (if a file is configured) metadata dict {} free key/values, stored in the header and shown on the slide

docs.title: Dimension
docs.text:
field type default meaning points int ≥ 1 (required) number of points (at most 10 000 000; whole sweep at most 100 000 000) sweep list [] swept channels (below); empty = repeat points times record list of names [] channels recorded at every point of this dimension pre_delay s ≥ 0 0 after setting, before recording post_delay s ≥ 0 0 after recording snake bool false alternate the direction on each pass of the outer loop record_after_inner bool false (outer dimensions) run the inner dimensions before recording label str "" a name for the dimension, shown in the editor hooks dict all off point actions: pre_sweep, post_sweep, pre_record, post_record, each {"enabled": bool, "code": str} (a bare string counts as enabled code)

A channel may be recorded in only one dimension.

docs.title: Swept channel
docs.text:
Each entry has channel (an alias, composite variable, mapping or writable channel) and one of:

fields setpoints start, stop linspace(start, stop, points) values the list (its length must be points) mapping (+ optional start, stop) an expression of i, N, t = i/(N-1), start, stop, x (the linear value) and numpy; required for vector / array channels

Any writable channel with a number can be swept: an alias, a variable or mapping of a composite, a value parameter, or a channel of an instrument (written as it is, without limits or ramp). Text channels and actions cannot be swept.

Variables of one multivariate composite are set together, also when they are swept in different dimensions: the outer ones are then set with the inner ones at every inner point. A combination that would drive a target of the composite out of range is skipped, refused or clamped according to the composite's out_of_range (Composite channels). Skipped combinations are counted in the validation warnings and in the footer's out_of_range_skipped.

docs.title: Pre / post phase
docs.text: field type meaning hook str Python code (script API), run first (pre) or last (post) constants list of {channel, value} written once, in order; settings are typical. An action (dmm.reset, a user action) runs: no value needed record list of names channels recorded once, stored in the file's pre / post

docs.title: Recording names
docs.text:
• aliases, composite channels, instrument.channel references (configuration channels included);
  • @time: Unix time of the recording;
  • @elapsed: seconds since the sweep started.

docs.title: Order at each point
docs.text:
pre_sweep → set swept channels → post_sweep → pre_delay → pre_record → record
          → post_record → post_delay → inner dimensions

With record_after_inner, the inner dimensions run right after pre_delay.

docs.title: Flow-control calls (point actions only)
docs.text: call like effect skip_point() continue rest of the point skipped, its data NaN skip_line() break the rest of this dimension's line skipped end_sweep() exit status terminated; post phase runs

docs.title: Data shape
docs.text: A channel recorded in dimension k of a sweep with points (N_0, …, N_{D-1}) is stored as an array of shape (N_k, …, N_{D-1}) + value_shape.
