docs.title: easymeasure
docs.text:
easyMeasure - a generic framework for multi-dimensional automated measurement.

The package is split into:

  • easymeasure.backend - the long-running measurement service (instruments, channels, sweeps, run queue, storage, logging). It runs in its own process and survives frontend crashes.
  • easymeasure.client - a small thread-based client used by scripts/tests.
  • easymeasure.frontend - the PySide6 GUI, which talks to the backend only through non-blocking sockets.
  • easymeasure.common - shared code (wire codec, errors, safe expressions).
  • easymeasure.report - figure rendering and PowerPoint generation.

docs.title: code_stamp
docs.text:
code_stamp() -> float

Newest modification time of the package sources.

The GUI compares its own stamp with the backend's to warn when the running backend still executes older code (e.g. after a git pull).

docs.title: easymeasure.backend
docs.text:
easyMeasure backend: instruments, channels, sweeps, queue, storage.

Typical in-process use::

from easymeasure.backend.service import Backend
be = Backend()
be.load_setup(path="examples/demo_setup.json")
be.queue_add({"kind": "sweep", "definition": {...}}, start=True)

As a service (what the GUI uses)::

python -m easymeasure.backend

docs.title: easymeasure.client
docs.text:
Thread-based client for the backend (scripts, notebooks, tests).

from easymeasure.client import BackendClient
c = BackendClient.connect()            # uses ~/.easymeasure/backend.json
c.call("read_channel", name="Vg")
c.on_event = lambda kind, data: print(kind)   # status events (queue, sweep start/end ...)
c.subscribe(["monitor"])                      # ... or ask for more, "*" for everything

An idle client is never disconnected. A client is only dropped when the backend has data waiting for it and its socket has accepted nothing for 60 s (a frozen GUI); the reader thread here always drains the socket, so that cannot happen.

The GUI uses its own Qt-native, non-blocking client (easymeasure.frontend.connection); this one blocks the calling thread.

Over the internet use RemoteClient (same interface, through the TLS gateway; see easymeasure.client.remote).

docs.title: easymeasure.drivers
docs.text:
Instrument drivers.

One module per driver; the module name is the driver name used in setups ("driver": "keithley2400"). The backend's ~easymeasure.backend.registry.DriverRegistry discovers every module here (names starting with _ and sub-packages are helpers, not drivers) plus <home>/drivers (drivers made with the Driver Wizard, see ._command) and the user's own driver directories (driver_paths setting).

Hardware drivers keithley2400, keysight_b2901, keysight_b2902 (source-measure units), sr830 (SR830 / SR850 lock-in amplifiers), hp34401a (6.5 digit DMM), ni6211 (NI USB-6211 multifunction DAQ), ni63xx (NI USB-63xx X Series DAQs, channels by model), yokogawa7651 (DC voltage / current source), hp4145 (HP 4145A/B and 4155/4156 in 4145 syntax, user mode), cygnus16430 (Cygnus 16430 8-channel 150 V / 40 mA supply), scpi_generic (any SCPI device, configured by options).

Simulated instruments (sim_*) Demo / test devices with fault injection, see .simbus.

The SCPI hardware drivers also talk to built-in emulators (.emulators) when given a SIM::<name> address, so setups can be tried without hardware.

docs.title: easymeasure.frontend
docs.text:
PySide6 frontend for easyMeasure.

The GUI never talks to instruments: everything goes through the backend over a non-blocking socket (.connection). Closing or killing the GUI has no effect on the backend.

docs.title: easymeasure.remote
docs.text:
Remote access to the backend over the internet: an HTTPS/WSS gateway, the browser frontend it serves, user accounts and the access policy.

Quick start (on the backend computer)::

python -m easymeasure.remote adduser alice --role admin
python -m easymeasure.backend --remote          # backend + gateway on port 8443

then open https://<computer>:8443 in a browser, or from Python::

from easymeasure.client import RemoteClient
c = RemoteClient("https://lab-pc:8443", "alice", password, fingerprint="AB:CD:...")

See easymeasure.remote.gateway for the security design and easymeasure.remote.policy for what each role may do.

docs.title: easymeasure.tray
docs.text:
System-tray indicator for a running backend.

Started automatically by python -m easymeasure.backend (disable with --no-tray). It runs as a separate process and talks to the backend like any other client, so the tray can never affect the backend; it exits on its own when the backend goes away.

The icon colour shows the state (green idle, blue running, orange paused, red error/aborting, gray not reachable); the tooltip shows the current run and its progress. Menu: open the GUI, open the web page (starting remote access if it is off), pause / resume / abort, open the data folder or the log, shut the backend down. A notification pops up when a run ends.

docs.title: easymeasure.backend.channels
docs.text:
Channels: one namespace, one way to read and write.

Every name in a setup is a channel (or the name of the thing that owns some):

============== ========================== ========================================== kind name access ============== ========================== ========================================== hardware instrument.channel what the driver says (r, w, rw) config instrument.setting what the driver says (a configuration channel) action instrument.action w: writing it runs the action alias Vg the target's, without w if read-only variable composite.variable rw (multivariate composite) map name rw (one-to-one mapping) read name r (composite read: a formula of channels) parameter name rw for a value, r for a formula user_action name w: writing it runs the user's code special @time r ============== ========================== ==========================================

get, set, set_many, check_value and info take any of them; the access is respected and nothing else is special-cased. Names are unique across all kinds (aliases, parameters, composites and their channels, user actions, instruments): a name that is taken is refused when it is defined.

Writing a hardware channel is a plain write: no limits, no ramp. Protection (min / max, ramp_rate, ramp_step, scale / offset, allowed, read_only) belongs to aliases. Writing an action (instrument or user) runs it; the value, if any, is ignored.

Composite channels (.composites) are formulas of channels: multivariate writes (variables driving several targets), composite reads and one-to-one mappings. Their targets and inputs may be any channel of the right access (aliases, other composite channels, hardware channels). They nest; a dependency loop is refused when it would be defined. Setting a composite channel computes everything it drives, checks every value against its limits before anything is written, and moves all targets together so that no ramp rate is exceeded, also along non-linear relations.

docs.title: easymeasure.backend.composites
docs.text:
Composite (virtual) channels: definitions and their checks.

Three kinds, all built from user formulas (easymeasure.common.exprs, so piecewise functions work: piecewise(x < 0, -x, x), a if c else b, where, interp tables):

multi – multivariate write Variables x, y, … (each with its own name, min, max, unit and ramp rate) are channels of their own, named after the composite: the variables eps and U of gates are the channels gates.eps and gates.U (in the Manual panel, sweeps, scripts and other formulas). Its own formulas use the short names. Every target (an alias, a mapping, or a variable of another multivariate composite) is a formula of the variables::

    {"type": "multi", "name": "gates",
     "variables": [{"name": "eps", "min": -1, "max": 1, "unit": "V", "ramp_rate": 0.1},
                   {"name": "U", "min": 0, "max": 2}],
     "targets": {"VL": "U/2 + eps", "VR": "U/2 - eps"}}

Setting a variable writes the targets that depend on it (with the last set
value of the others).  Reading a variable gives the value it was last set to,
NaN before that.

``out_of_range`` says what happens when a combination of the variables would
drive a target outside its own range (an alias' limits …):

* ``"skip"`` (default): a sweep skips that point (as ``skip_point()`` before
  the swept channels are set); a direct write is refused;
* ``"error"``: refused everywhere; a sweep containing such a point fails
  validation;
* ``"clamp"``: the target is set to the nearest end of its range.

read – composite read A formula of other channels (aliases, mappings, variables, other reads)::

    {"type": "read", "name": "R", "expression": "V / I if I != 0 else nan", "unit": "Ω"}

map – simple mapping A one-to-one software channel for one hardware channel (alias, mapping or variable): forward gives the target value y from x, backward gives x from y; min/max (required) is the range of x. That backward(forward(x)) == x everywhere in the range is checked when the mapping is defined::

    {"type": "map", "name": "T", "target": "Vheater", "forward": "sqrt(x/10)",
     "backward": "10*y**2", "min": 0, "max": 50, "unit": "mW"}

The dependency graph (writes and reads) is checked for cycles by the ~easymeasure.backend.channels.ChannelManager whenever a composite is added or replaced.

docs.title: easymeasure.backend.instrument
docs.text:
Instrument abstraction layer.

Two classes matter:

Instrument Base class for drivers. A driver declares its channels (CHANNELS) and implements read(channel) / write(channel, value) (or per-channel _read_<name> / _write_<name> methods). Drivers are written in the obvious, naive way - all the paranoia lives in InstrumentHandle.

InstrumentHandle The guarded wrapper the rest of the backend uses. Every driver call:

* runs on a dedicated worker thread with a hard deadline - a driver that hangs
  forever is abandoned, its port invalidated and a fresh worker started;
* runs inside a resource transaction (port arbitration);
* has every exception (including ``SystemExit`` / ``KeyboardInterrupt`` raised
  by buggy driver code) caught and converted to :class:`InstrumentError`;
* is retried with recovery / reconnection according to the instrument options;
* has its result validated and coerced to the declared type and shape.

Channel values are either numeric (stored as float or numpy.ndarray of float64 of any dimension) or strings.

Static description of an instrument channel.

shape: () for scalars, otherwise a tuple whose entries are fixed sizes or -1 for "any size". None means "unknown / anything".

allowed: optional list of the accepted values (strings for str channels, numbers for scalar float channels). Writes are checked against it (text ignoring case and blanks, numbers to 1e-9 relative) and normalised to the listed spelling; front ends show a combo box instead of a text field.

A driver may return a different channel list from Instrument.get_channels after a configuration channel was written (e.g. a mode switch renames the reading channel or changes its unit): the backend asks again after every configuration write and action, and tells the front ends when it changed.

Logging system.

  • Everything goes to a rotating log file (~/.easymeasure/logs/backend.log).
  • The most recent records are kept in a ring buffer so a (re)connecting frontend can show recent history.
  • Listeners (the IPC server) are notified of every record; a failing listener is never allowed to break logging.

docs.title: easymeasure.backend.monitor
docs.text:
Monitor: continuously polls selected channels and streams the values.

Each monitored channel has its own interval. Channels are polled by a small pool of worker threads (one per instrument, so a slow/hung instrument never delays the others). Values are kept in a per-channel ring buffer (so a reconnecting frontend gets recent history) and pushed to listeners.

docs.title: easymeasure.backend.parameters
docs.text:
Parameters: named numerical constants of a setup.

A parameter is either a value (a number set by hand: a gate capacitance, a geometry factor, a bias resistor) or a formula of other parameters (Cb/e, 2*pi*f0). Formulas may use only parameters (never live channels), and may not refer to each other in a circle.

Parameters read like channels (get('Cb'), a sweep may record them, a composite read may use them) but cannot be written as channels: a value parameter is set with set_parameter (the Parameters panel or the Manual panel), a formula parameter only by changing its formula. Composite channels (targets, read formulas, mapping formulas) and actions may use parameters in their formulas; they use the value the parameter has at that moment, so changing a parameter does not move any hardware by itself - the next write uses the new value.

docs.title: easymeasure.backend.registry
docs.text:
Driver registry.

Every instrument driver lives in its own Python source file. A driver module must define a subclass of easymeasure.backend.instrument.Instrument; if it defines several, the one named in a module-level DRIVER variable is used. The driver is identified by its module name (e.g. sim_dmm).

Drivers are discovered in the easymeasure.drivers package and in any additional directories given to DriverRegistry (driver_paths in the backend settings), so users can keep their own drivers outside the library. Import errors are captured and reported instead of crashing the backend.

docs.title: easymeasure.backend.resources
docs.text: Resource management: low-level ports (COM / GPIB / USB / Ethernet / simulated).

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
• Each physical port is represented by exactly one Resource object, so two instruments can never open the same port independently and fight over it.
  • By default a resource is exclusive: a second instrument asking for it gets a ResourceBusyError.
  • Shared ports (a GPIB bus behind a Prologix adapter, an RS-485 chain, a multi-channel controller ...) can be requested with shared=True. Access is then arbitrated: every I/O sequence must run inside with resource.transaction(owner): which grants a fair, FIFO, re-entrant lock. When ownership switches from one instrument to another an optional selector callback of the new owner is run (e.g. send ++addr 12).
  • Resources can be invalidated (e.g. after a hung call). The next transaction transparently reopens the port; stale handles held by abandoned threads are closed and ignored.

docs.title: Address formats
docs.text:
================================= =========================================== COM3 / ASRL3::INSTR serial port (pyserial, or pyvisa for ASRL) /dev/ttyUSB0 serial port (pyserial) GPIB0::12::INSTR pyvisa USB0::0x1234::...::INSTR pyvisa TCPIP0::1.2.3.4::inst0::INSTR pyvisa TCP::192.168.1.5::5025 raw TCP socket (built-in, no pyvisa needed) SIM::<name> simulated byte port (see drivers/simbus.py) DAQ::<device> NI-DAQmx device (DAQ::Dev1); no byte port, but one owner, so two drivers cannot share a DAQ card NONE or empty instrument without a port (DLL/software) ================================= ===========================================

Each address belongs to one interface (interface_of): gpib, usb, tcpip (VISA LAN), tcp (raw socket), serial, daq, sim, none or other (any other VISA type). Drivers list the interfaces they accept (Instrument.INTERFACES); ResourceManager.discover finds the ports of this computer by interface, optionally with their *IDN?.

docs.title: FairLock
docs.text:
FairLock()

Re-entrant, FIFO-within-priority lock with timeout.

Plain threading.RLock is not fair: a fast loop (e.g. the monitor) can starve a sweep. Here waiters are served in arrival order, except that waiters with a better priority (the measurement thread) go first, so monitoring and GUI traffic never slow a running sweep down.

docs.title: easymeasure.backend.runqueue
docs.text:
Run queue: the backend state machine.

States::

idle  --start-->  running  --pause-->  paused  --resume--> running
  ^                  |  \---abort--> aborting --(item ends)--+
  +---- queue empty / stop / abort_all -----------------------+

Items are either sweeps ({"kind": "sweep", "definition": {...}}) or scripts ({"kind": "script", "code": "..."}) and are executed strictly sequentially on one dedicated thread. Whatever an item does, the queue thread survives it.

docs.title: easymeasure.backend.scripting
docs.text:
Execution of user scripts (queue items, pre/post sweep hooks).

Scripts are plain Python run in the backend with a small API in their namespace:

===================== ========================================================= get(name) read any readable channel (Vg, gates.eps, dmm.V, a parameter, @time) set(name, value) write any writable channel: an alias with its limits and ramp, src.V1 as it is, a parameter; set('dmm.reset') or set('zero_gates') runs an action set_many({n: v}) write several together (e.g. variables of one composite) sleep(s) abortable sleep (always use this instead of time.sleep) wait_until(f, timeout, interval) poll f() until true check() honour pause / abort log(msg)/print write to the backend log instrument(name) guarded instrument proxy: .raw_query, .raw_write, .call run_sweep(defn) run a sweep definition synchronously; returns its DataSet (.status, .data, .setpoints, .path) load_sweep(path) a sweep definition (dict) from a JSON file saved by the sweep editor, or from a data file params the setup's parameters: params.Cb, params['Cb']; each parameter is also available by its name (value at the start) np, math, time modules state a dict persisting between scripts in the same backend ===================== =========================================================

Abort/pause are honoured not only inside API calls but on every executed line of the script (via a thread-local trace function), so even while True: pass can be aborted.

docs.title: easymeasure.backend.server
docs.text:
TCP server exposing the Backend to frontends.

Design goals: the backend must never be slowed down or blocked by a frontend, and frontends may connect / disconnect / crash at any time.

  • Each client has a reader thread and a writer thread with a bounded queue.
  • Commands are executed on a thread pool, so a slow instrument call never blocks other requests (or other clients).
  • Events (monitor values, sweep points, log lines) are droppable: if a client is too slow its queue overflows, events are dropped and the client receives a resync event telling it to re-request a snapshot. Replies are never dropped.
  • Authentication: a random token, advertised in ~/.easymeasure/backend.json.

Messages (all codec frames)::

client -> server  {"type": "hello", "token": "...", "client": "gui"}
server -> client  {"type": "welcome", "version": ..., "pid": ...}
client -> server  {"type": "req", "id": 7, "cmd": "read_channel", "args": {...}}
server -> client  {"type": "resp", "id": 7, "ok": true, "result": ...}
                  {"type": "resp", "id": 7, "ok": false, "error": "...", "kind": "..."}
server -> client  {"type": "event", "event": "monitor", "data": {...}}

docs.title: File format (.emj - easyMeasure journal)
docs.text:
An append-only sequence of self-checking frames, preceded by the 8-byte magic b"EMJ1\r\n\x1a\n"::

b"F"  u8 type  u32 payload_length  u32 crc32(payload)  payload

payload is an easymeasure.common.codec frame (JSON + raw arrays, no pickle). Frame types:

  • HEADER - sweep definition, setpoints, metadata (first frame)
  • POINT - values recorded at one recording event: {"k": dim, "i": index, "v": {channel: value}, "e": {channel: error}, "t": time}
  • PHASE - pre/post sweep recordings
  • EVENT - status changes, notes
  • FOOTER - final status

Every frame is flushed to the OS immediately and fsync-ed at least every fsync_interval seconds (and at every phase change), so a crash or power loss loses at most that window. A torn last frame is detected by its length/CRC and ignored on recovery; everything before it is usable. Loading a partial file gives arrays filled with NaN where no data was taken.

export_hdf5 converts a journal into a conventional HDF5 file for analysis.

docs.title: JournalWriter
docs.text:
JournalWriter(path: Path, fsync_interval: float = 0.5)

Append-only, self-checking journal.

A failed write (disk full, network share hiccup, USB disk unplugged ...) never loses data that the measurement produced: the torn bytes are truncated away and the frame is kept in a pending queue that is retried on every subsequent write and on close. pending tells how many frames are not on disk yet.

docs.title: DataSet
docs.text:
DataSet(header: dict)

N-dimensional data of one sweep run.

header contains (among others):

  • shape: list of dimension sizes, dim 0 = innermost (fastest)
  • dims: per dimension {"sweep": [names], "record": [names], "label": ...}
  • setpoints: {dim: {channel: array of shape (N_k, *channel_shape)}}
  • definition: the full sweep definition (dict)

Data arrays: data[name] for a channel recorded in dimension k has shape (N_k, N_{k+1}, ..., N_{D-1}) + value_shape with float64 (NaN = missing) or object dtype for strings.

docs.title: easymeasure.backend.sweep
docs.text:
Generic multi-dimensional sweep definition and execution engine.

Definition (JSON-compatible dict)::

{
  "name": "gate_bias_map",
  "dimensions": [                       # dimension 0 = innermost / fastest
    {"points": 101,
     "sweep":  [{"channel": "Vg", "start": -0.5, "stop": 0.5},
                {"channel": "Vc", "start": 0, "stop": 1, "mapping": "start+(stop-start)*t**2"},
                {"channel": "wave", "mapping": "np.sin(np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 64))*t"},
                {"channel": "Vx", "values": [0, 0.1, 0.3, ...]}],
     "record": ["I", "spectrum"],
     "pre_delay": 0.05,                 # after setting, before recording
     "post_delay": 0.0,                 # after recording
     "snake": false,                    # alternate direction on each pass
     "record_after_inner": false,       # (outer dims) record after the inner loop
     "hooks": {"pre_record": {"enabled": true, "code": "set('dmm.trigger')"}}},
    {"points": 21, "sweep": [{"channel": "Vb", "start": -0.3, "stop": 0.3}],
     "record": ["T"]}
  ],
  "pre":  {"hook": "log('starting')", "constants": [{"channel": "mode", "value": "AC"}],
           "record": ["T"]},
  "post": {"record": ["T"], "constants": [{"channel": "Vg", "value": 0}], "hook": ""},
  "on_read_error": "nan",               # or "abort"
  "on_set_error": "abort",              # or "skip"
  "run_post_on_abort": true,
  "metadata": {"sample": "D17", "comment": "..."}
}

Every point of a dimension runs, in this order::

pre_sweep hook -> set the swept channels -> post_sweep hook -> pre_delay
  -> pre_record hook -> record -> post_record hook -> post_delay
  (-> the inner dimensions; with record_after_inner they run before pre_record)

The four hooks are optional Python snippets (like the pre/post-sweep hook, see .scripting), each switched on with enabled. Besides the script API they see k (dimension), i (index in it), index (indices of this and the outer dimensions), setpoints (the dimension's channel -> value at this point) and, in post_record, values (what was just recorded).

Three special calls change the flow (think of nested for loops):

skip_point() (continue) ends the point at once: the rest of its sequence (and, unless they already ran, its inner dimensions) is skipped, the data recorded at this point stay NaN, and the sweep continues with the next point of the same dimension. skip_line() (break) does the same for this point and all remaining points of this dimension's line; the outer dimension continues (for the outermost dimension the sweep is done). end_sweep() (exit) stops the whole sweep: status terminated, the post-sweep phase still runs, unvisited points stay NaN. Called in post_record it keeps the point just recorded (e.g. stop when a threshold is crossed and see that point); the skips discard it.

Variables of one multivariate composite are set together. When they are swept in different dimensions (n inner, D outer), the outer ones are not written on their own: they are set together with the inner ones at every inner point, so the hardware only ever sees whole combinations. A combination that would put a target of the composite out of range is skipped (skip_point() before anything is set) when the composite's out_of_range is "skip"; validation counts such points and, for "error", refuses the sweep.

Mapping expressions may use i (index), N (points), t = i/(N-1), start, stop, x (= linear value between start and stop) and numpy. A mapping is mandatory for vector/tensor channels.

Recorded data of a channel recorded in dimension k is assembled into an array of shape (N_k, ..., N_{D-1}) + value_shape. Special record channel: @time (unix time of the recording event), @elapsed (seconds since start).

A user action is a write-only channel with a plain name: writing it runs it (write_channel(name="zero_gates"), set('zero_gates') in a script or another action, a pre-sweep constant, a Manual-panel button). docs.title: easymeasure.client.remote
docs.text:
Blocking client for a backend reached over the internet through the gateway.

Same interface as easymeasure.client.BackendClient::

from easymeasure.client import RemoteClient
c = RemoteClient("https://lab-pc.example.org:8443", "alice", getpass.getpass(),
                 fingerprint="87:68:0C:...")       # from: python -m easymeasure.remote cert
c.call("read_channel", name="Vg")
c.on_event = lambda kind, data: print(kind)
c.close()

Certificate checking: give fingerprint (pins the gateway's self-signed certificate - the usual case) or cafile (a private CA), or neither for a certificate from a public CA. verify=False disables checking and makes the connection vulnerable to interception; only use it on a trusted network.

The connection is TLS-encrypted and compressed (permessage-deflate). An idle client stays connected indefinitely; requests are limited by the gateway's rate limits and your account's role (c.role, c.allowed).

docs.title: easymeasure.common.codec
docs.text:
Wire codec for the backend <-> frontend link.

A message is any JSON-like Python object (dict/list/str/float/int/bool/None) which may additionally contain numpy.ndarray (numeric/bool dtypes), numpy scalars, tuples and bytes. Arrays are not JSON-encoded: they are replaced by a small placeholder and their raw memory is appended after the JSON header, so large 2-D maps travel efficiently.

Frame layout (all integers little-endian)::

u32  frame_length          (number of bytes that follow)
u32  json_length
json_length bytes of UTF-8 JSON
concatenated raw buffers referenced from the JSON

No pickle is used anywhere, so a malformed or hostile frame cannot execute code.

docs.title: easymeasure.common.exprs
docs.text:
Small, sandboxed expression evaluator for user formulas.

Used for sweep mapping functions (start + (stop-start)*t**2), composite channel definitions (0.5*x + 0.1), composite read-back formulas and the manual-control "set from expression".

Piecewise functions: piecewise(x < 0, -x, x < 1, x**2, 1) (the value of the first true condition; a final odd argument is the "otherwise" value, else NaN), a if cond else b, where(cond, a, b) and tables with interp(x, xs, ys).

Because these formulas can arrive from remote (web) users, this module is a security boundary, built as an allow-list rather than a deny-list:

  • only arithmetic, comparisons, conditionals, indexing, tuples/lists and calls of allow-listed functions are accepted (no attribute access except np.<fn> / math.<fn> from a fixed list and a few data properties such as .real);
  • no builtins are reachable, no names except the variables, math functions and constants; no lambdas, comprehensions, f-strings or starred arguments;
  • resource bombs are defused: **, *, % and << go through guarded helpers (no 9**9**9 or 'a'*10**9) and array constructors refuse to build more than MAX_ELEMENTS elements.

docs.title: easymeasure.drivers._command
docs.text:
Command-based instruments described by data: the engine behind the Driver Wizard.

A definition (a plain dict, JSON-compatible) describes an instrument that is controlled by text commands - most SCPI instruments, and many older ones:

.. code-block:: python

{"name": "my_meter", "description": "...",
 "idn_query": "*IDN?", "idn_match": "34461",       # identification (optional)
 "options": {"timeout": 5.0, "read_termination": "\n", "write_termination": "\n"},
 "error_query": "SYST:ERR?",                       # read after every setting
 "init": {"commands": ["*CLS"], "script": "..."},  # run on connect
 "shutdown": {"commands": []},                     # run on disconnect (best effort)
 "channels": [
    {"name": "volt", "access": "r", "dtype": "float", "unit": "V",
     "get": "READ?"},
    {"name": "func", "access": "rw", "dtype": "str", "config": True,
     "get": "FUNC?", "set": 'FUNC "{value}"',
     "allowed": ["DC V", "AC V"], "map": {"DC V": "VOLT:DC", "AC V": "VOLT:AC"}}],
 "actions": [{"name": "reset", "commands": ["*RST"], "description": "..."}]}

Channels access r / w / rw; dtype float, str or vector (comma-separated numbers, read-only); config marks a setting. get is the query whose reply is the value (numbers: the first number in the reply; text: the reply without quotes), set the command with {value} (or {value:.3f}) where the value goes. allowed lists accepted values (drop-down in the front ends); map translates a value into the instrument's word ("Voltage": "VOLT") and back - replies are recognised in SCPI short or long form, and 1/0 match ON/OFF. scale multiplies readings and divides settings (instrument in mA, channel in A: scale 0.001). timeout overrides the call deadline.

Initialization init.commands are sent in order on connect (a command ending in ? is a query; its reply is logged). init.script is Python run afterwards with write(cmd), query(cmd), read(), sleep(s), log(msg), options, instrument and np/math; raise an exception to refuse the connection (e.g. a wrong model).

Driver files generated by the wizard (<home>/drivers/<name>.py) hold the definition as a Python literal plus a class; the class may be extended by hand (override read / write for special channels), and the wizard reopens the file through its DEFINITION.

docs.title: easymeasure.drivers._smu
docs.text:
Common logic of the source-measure unit drivers (not a driver itself).

Each SMU output has a mode:

Voltage the voltage channel is the source (read/write), the current channel is measured (read-only) and the compliance is a current limit (channel Icompliance, unit A); Current the other way round, compliance Vcompliance in V.

The channel list follows the mode (the backend re-reads it after every setting), so the front ends show a read-only measured channel and the right compliance name and unit. Changing the mode needs the output switched off; reading the measured quantity while the output is off gives NaN (nothing is measured, and some SMUs would otherwise switch the output on by themselves).

Option verify_writes reads every new source value back (one extra query) and retries when it did not arrive - worth it on RS-232 lines, where a command can be lost without the instrument noticing.

docs.title: easymeasure.drivers.ami430
docs.text:
American Magnetics Model 430 (and 420) superconducting magnet power supply programmer.

The magnet's configuration (coil constant, current limit, ramp rates, the persistent switch's heater current and times, quench detection) lives in the programmer, set once on its front panel; this driver only reads it. What it does is drive the magnet safely:

Field Writing field sets the target and starts the ramp (RAMP) and returns at once, like the front panel: status reads RAMPING, then HOLDING. A sweep waits with a point action, e.g. wait_until(lambda: get('magnet.status') == 'HOLDING'). Reading field gives the magnet's field (in persistent mode the field it was left at).

Persistent switch (IsPersistentSwitchInstalled = Yes) The field can only be changed in driven mode (switch heater on). In persistent mode a field write is refused: the supply would only change the current in its leads. The actions do the two transitions in the order that cannot quench the magnet, step by step, checking the programmer's own state before every step:

``enter_persistent``
    1. the supply must hold the field (``HOLDING`` / ``PAUSED``); wait
       ``settle_time`` s, and until the magnet voltage has decayed below
       ``max_magnet_voltage``;
    2. switch heater off (``PSwitch 0``); wait while the switch cools
       (``COOLING SWITCH``);
    3. ramp the leads to zero (``ZERO``, option ``zero_leads``) and wait for
       ``AT ZERO``.  Status: ``PERSISTENT``.

``exit_persistent``
    1. ramp the supply to the magnet's persistent current (target = the
       persistent field, ``RAMP``) and wait for ``HOLDING``;
    2. heat the switch (``PSwitch 1``) **only** if the supply current matches
       the magnet current within ``match_tolerance`` A - heating at the wrong
       current forces the difference into the magnet and can quench it;
    3. wait while the switch heats (``HEATING SWITCH``), then hold the field
       (``RAMP``).  Status: ``HOLDING``, driven.

Each action checks its preconditions, starts the procedure and returns; the
procedure then advances whenever the driver talks to the programmer - every
read, and the backend's watchdog every ``poll_interval`` s - so the field can be
watched meanwhile.  ``status`` reads ``ENTERING PERSISTENT`` /
``EXITING PERSISTENT`` until it is done, ``operation`` says which step it is on
(or why it stopped).  A step that does not complete in time, or a programmer
that does something unexpected (paused from the front panel, ...), stops the
procedure where it is safe, without heating the switch.  The ``pause`` action
stops the supply and the procedure.

Quench The programmer detects quenches itself (and then takes the supply to zero). The driver checks its state at every call and at every watchdog poll; a quench raises ~easymeasure.common.errors.InstrumentFault, which ends a running sweep or script, stops the run queue and the user actions, and is reported to every front end. Until the quench is cleared (clear_quench, or RESET QUENCH on the front panel) field writes and the persistent actions are refused; reading still works.

Model 420: the same command set, over RS-232. Model 430: Ethernet (TCP::<ip>::7180) or RS-232. Both send \r\n line ends.

docs.title: easymeasure.drivers.cygnus16430
docs.text:
Cygnus 16430: 8-channel programmable supply, 0 – 150 V / 0 – 40 mA per channel (Cao RQM Lab, firmware cygnus-16430-firmware).

USB CDC virtual serial port (address COM5 / /dev/ttyACM0; the baud rate does not matter), SCPI-style ASCII as implemented in the firmware's scpi.c: VOLT n,v / CURR n,i / OUTP n,ON|OFF with channels 1 … 8, MEAS:VOLT? n / MEAS:CURR? n readback, RATE V|I,SF ADC speed, FILT:VOLT|CURR n,α IIR filter. The firmware has a one-slot error register (SYST:ERR? → 0 or -1,"message") and does not answer a query it rejects; the driver only sends valid commands and checks the register after every setting, so a refused value raises the firmware's own message.

Each output is a one-quadrant source: a voltage setpoint with a current limit (constant voltage until the limit, then constant current) and its own output relay. Channels (k = 1 … 8)

================== ===== ==================================================== voltage<k> V voltage setpoint, 0 … 150 V (swept); reads the setpoint Vmeas<k> V measured output voltage Imeas<k> A measured output current Ilimit<k> A current limit, 0 … 40 mA (config) output<k> ON / OFF: the output relay (config) voltAll V all 8 setpoints as a vector (written at once, VOLTA) IlimitAll A all 8 current limits as a vector (written at once, CURRA) VmeasAll V all 8 measured voltages ImeasAll A all 8 measured currents Vrate Irate ADC filter word SF 13 … 255 for all voltage / current readings (13: fastest, 255: lowest noise) (config) Vfilter Ifilter IIR filter α (0 … 1], 1 = off, set on every channel (config) ================== ===== ====================================================

Readback is round-robin over the 8 channels: a channel's reading is refreshed every 8·24·SF/32768 s (76 ms at SF 13, 1.5 s at SF 255). With option settle (default on) a reading of a channel whose setpoint, limit or relay just changed waits until fresh conversions (and, with a filter, ~99 % of the filter's step response) are in.

Actions: all_off (every relay off), reset (*RST: outputs off, setpoints zero, filters cleared), auto_calibrate (CAL:AUTO, the firmware's current-trim refresh; all outputs must be off; takes a while). SIM::<name> uses the built-in emulator (port of the firmware's parser, resistive loads: option load_ohm).

docs.title: easymeasure.drivers.e8358a
docs.text:
Agilent (Keysight) E8358A PNA series vector network analyzer, 300 kHz - 9 GHz (also the E8356A / E8357A, 3 / 6 GHz: the same commands).

Measurements The four S-parameters of channel 1 (option channel) are read as whole frequency sweeps: S21 (log magnitude, dB), S21_phase (degrees), S21_re / S21_im (the complex value), and the same for S11, S12, S22. Their x axis is frequencies (Hz), which the plots and data files use. The driver creates a measurement (EM_S21 ...) on the analyzer the first time a parameter is read, shows it in window 1, and keeps it; option parameters (e.g. "S21,S11") creates them when connecting, so the first sweep already measures them all.

One sweep per point Reading a measurement channel triggers a single sweep of every measurement (SENSe:SWEep:MODE SINGle, or GROups with the average count when averaging is on, so a reading is always a fresh, complete average) and waits for it to end (*OPC / *ESR?). All channels of that sweep are read from it: recording S21 and S21_phase at a point costs one sweep, not two. The next reading of a channel already read starts the next sweep. The analyzer then stays in HOLD, showing the last sweep; the continuous action lets it sweep freely again (for looking at the front panel). Every measurement on the analyzer is swept, also ones made at its front panel: the delete_traces action (a first pre-sweep constant) removes them all, settings unchanged, so a sweep measures only what it records. A sweep that has not ended after 3 × sweep time × sweeps + sweep_timeout s is an error.

Settings f_start / f_stop / f_center / f_span, points (1 - 16001), if_bandwidth (the PNA's list, 1 Hz - 40 kHz), sweep_type (LIN / LOG), averaging and average_count, output (RF on / off) and correction (the calibration of the channel, if one is applied) are configuration channels; power (dBm) is a data channel, so it can be aliased and swept. A setting the analyzer refuses (a frequency out of range, ...) raises with its own message.

Connect over LAN (TCPIP0::<ip>::inst0::INSTR or the SCPI socket TCPIP0::<ip>::5025::SOCKET) or GPIB. SIM::e8358a is an emulator.

docs.title: easymeasure.drivers.emulators
docs.text:
Instrument emulators: simulated hardware that speaks the real command language.

The hardware drivers (keithley2400, keysight_b2901 ...) are tested against these emulators. The command tables are written from the instruments' programming manuals in SCPI notation ([:SOURce[1]]:VOLTage[:LEVel]), and a command the manual does not define is answered like a real instrument would: an entry in the error queue and no reply. So the tests check the exact command strings a driver sends, not just that it "works with itself".

A driver given a SIM::<name> address attaches its emulator to that simulated bus (see ensure_emulator), so a setup can be tried out without hardware.

docs.title: easymeasure.drivers.hp4145
docs.text:
HP 4145A/B semiconductor parameter analyzer, and HP/Agilent 4155/4156 in 4145 syntax mode, driven in HP-IB user mode (direct control of the SMUs).

User mode (US) sets each SMU directly - DV (force voltage), DI (force current), DS (disable) - and measures with TV / TI, point by point, which is what a sweep framework needs. Everything the analyzer's own sweep engine does (SS, MD ...) is not used.

Per SMU n (1 … 4, option smus; same mode logic as the keithley2400):

================== ====== ============================================================= mode<n> config Voltage (force V, measure I) / Current (force I, measure V) voltage<n> V forced (Voltage mode) or measured; ±100 V current<n> A measured (Voltage mode) or forced; ±100 mA Icompliance<n> config current limit in Voltage mode (A) … Vcompliance<n> config … voltage limit in Current mode (V) output<n> config ON (programmed with DV/DI) / OFF (DS) range<n> config source range: AUTO or a fixed one ================== ====== =============================================================

Plus vs1, vs2 (voltage sources, ±20 V) and vm1, vm2 (voltmeters) unless option vs_vm is false, and integration (short / medium / long, IT).

The SMUs' power envelope is checked before anything is sent (the analyzer would just flag an error): 100 mA up to 20 V, 50 mA up to 40 V, 20 mA up to 100 V, for the forced value against the compliance. Both quantities of an SMU are measured with TV / TI, so the forced value reads back as measured. While an SMU's output is OFF its readings are NaN; changing its mode needs the output OFF. A reading flagged "overflow" is ±inf, "oscillation" NaN.

The analyzer has no setting queries in user mode: the driver remembers what it programmed. On (re)connect it assumes every SMU is OFF and does not touch the outputs (a reconnect in the middle of a measurement leaves the bias alone); set output<n> to ON to (re)program an SMU.

4155/4156: the driver switches the analyzer into the 4145 syntax command mode by itself if it is not there yet (CMD?: 0 = SCPI, 1 = FLEX, 2 = 4145 syntax): from FLEX it returns to SCPI with :PAGE, from SCPI it selects 4145 syntax with :SYST:LANG COMP, and checks CMD? after each step (option force_4145_syntax = false leaves the mode alone). Address e.g. GPIB0::17::INSTR. SIM::<name> uses the built-in emulator (option emulate_model = 4145B or 4155C).

Not verified against the manual text (the scanned manuals were not readable): the mode switch commands above, the VS / VM channel numbers 5 and 6, the DS <ch> form and the exact reply layout of TV / TI (the driver takes the status from the first character and the number from the end, which covers the documented variants).

docs.title: easymeasure.drivers.ni6211
docs.text:
National Instruments USB-6211 multifunction DAQ (also USB-6210/6215, through NI-DAQmx).

Needs NI's NI-DAQmx driver runtime (from ni.com); the nidaqmx Python package is installed with easyMeasure. The address names the device as shown in NI MAX: DAQ::Dev1. DAQ::SIM (or option simulate) uses a built-in emulation of the card (no NI software needed); NI MAX can also create a simulated USB-6211 that this driver drives like a real one.

Channels

================== ==== ================================================== ai0 … ai15 V analog inputs: mean of samples samples taken at rate; with terminal = DIFF only ai0 … ai7 (ai8 … ai15 are the negative inputs) ai V vector of all analog inputs from one simultaneous scan ao0, ao1 V analog outputs, ±10 V (read back: last value written) di0 … di3 digital inputs P0.0 … P0.3 (PFI 0 … 3), 0 / 1 do0 … do3 digital outputs P1.0 … P1.3 (PFI 4 … 7), 0 / 1 ctr0, ctr1 edge counters (rising edges since connect / reset) ================== ==== ==================================================

Settings: rate (samples/s per input: a single input aiK is acquired alone, up to 250 kS/s; the ai vector acquires all scanned inputs, together at most 250 kS/s), samples (per reading, averaged; 1 = a single on-demand conversion, fastest), terminal (RSE / NRSE / DIFF) and ai_range (±10 / ±5 / ±1 / ±0.2 V). Option ai_channels (e.g. "0-3") limits the exposed inputs and those of the ai vector (a higher rate for it).

docs.title: easymeasure.drivers.ni63xx
docs.text:
National Instruments USB-63xx X Series multifunction DAQ (NI-DAQmx).

One driver for the USB-6341, 6343, 6346, 6349, 6351, 6353, 6356, 6361, 6363 and 6366 (BNC, screw / spring terminal, mass termination and OEM variants): the model (option and configuration channel model; auto = what the device reports) decides the channel list — number of analog inputs and outputs, digital lines, input / output ranges, terminal configurations and rate limits, from NI's specifications (._nidaq_models).

Needs NI's NI-DAQmx driver runtime (from ni.com); the nidaqmx Python package is installed with easyMeasure. Address: the device name in NI MAX, DAQ::Dev1. DAQ::SIM… (or option simulate) uses the built-in emulation of the chosen model (auto → USB-6363); NI MAX can also create a simulated device that the driver drives like a real one.

Channels (counts for the model)

====================== ==== =================================================== ai0 … V analog inputs: mean of samples samples at rate; DIFF uses the pairs aiK/aiK+8 (K = 0…7, 16…23), so only those K exist; simultaneous models (6346, 6349, 6356, 6366) are differential only ai V vector of all scanned inputs from one scan ao0 … V analog outputs (±10 V, or ±5 V with ao_range) dio0 … digital port 0 lines P0.K, 0 / 1 pfi0 … pfi15 PFI lines as digital lines (PFI 0…7 = P1, 8…15 = P2) ctr0 … ctr3 rising edges on the counter's default source (PFI 8 / 3 / 0 / 5) since its first reading or reset_counters ====================== ==== ===================================================

Every digital line is an input until written: writing makes it an output driving that level (reading it then returns the driven level); the action release_digital makes all of them inputs (high impedance) again. A counter reserves its source PFI line, which then cannot be used as a digital line.

Settings (configuration channels): model, rate (samples/s per input: a single input aiK is acquired alone, up to the single-input rate; the ai vector acquires all scanned inputs, which on multiplexed models share the aggregate rate), samples (per reading, averaged; 1 = one on-demand conversion, fastest), terminal (RSE / NRSE / DIFF), ai_range and ao_range (those of the model). Option ai_channels (e.g. "0-3") limits the exposed inputs and those of the ai vector (which then allows a higher rate for it).

docs.text:
Generic SCPI instrument configured entirely by options (no code needed).

Example options::

{"idn_contains": "KEITHLEY",
 "init": ["*RST", ":SOUR:FUNC VOLT"],
 "channels": [
    {"name": "V", "access": "rw", "get": ":SOUR:VOLT?", "set": ":SOUR:VOLT {value:.6g}",
     "unit": "V"},
    {"name": "I", "access": "r", "get": ":MEAS:CURR?", "unit": "A", "index": 1},
    {"name": "trace", "access": "r", "get": ":TRAC:DATA?", "shape": [-1]},
    {"name": "output", "access": "rw", "dtype": "str", "get": ":OUTP?", "set": ":OUTP {value}",
     "config": true}
 ],
 "actions": [{"name": "trigger", "command": "*TRG"},
             {"name": "reset", "command": ["*RST", "*CLS"]}]}

index picks one element of a comma separated reply. Vector channels parse comma separated replies into arrays. Works with any port type (VISA, serial, TCP).

docs.title: easymeasure.drivers.sim_lockin
docs.text:
Simulated lock-in amplifier (no port; address NONE).

Option sample chooses what it measures:

  • dot (default): the differential conductance of the simulated quantum dot (gate / bias from the options gate and bias);
  • graphene: a dual-gated bilayer graphene Hall bar (gates from back_gate / top_gate, normally two sim_smu instruments bg and tg). The AC current is driven by a lock-in's sine output through a bias_resistor: I = V_out / (bias_resistor + R_2t), where the two-terminal resistance R_2t (3 Rxx + 2 contacts) is not negligible when the sample is insulating, so the current is not constant. measure chooses what this lock-in sees: voltage (X = I · Rxx, the four-probe voltage) or current (X = I, a current input). The driving output is this lock-in's own amplitude, or with source = "<other lock-in>.amplitude" that of another lock-in.

Both see the field of field (a sim_magnet). Besides scalar channels it offers XY - a 2-element vector reading.

docs.title: easymeasure.drivers.sim_vna
docs.text:
Simulated vector network analyzer (no port; address NONE).

Measures the reflection S11 of a superconducting resonator (see SimWorld.resonator_s11): the dip deepens and narrows with power as the two-level-system losses saturate, moves down at high power (Kerr effect), and moves down and broadens in a magnetic field (option field: a sim_magnet). Low power and a wide IF bandwidth give noisy traces, like the real thing.

Each reading is a whole frequency sweep: S11 (magnitude, dB) and S11_phase (degrees), with their frequency axis in frequencies - the plots use it as the x axis. Used in the tutorials.

docs.title: easymeasure.drivers.simbus
docs.text:
Simulated byte ports (SIM::<bus> addresses) and fault injection.

A simulated port behaves like a real line-oriented port: the driver writes commands and reads replies through the normal Resource API, so the whole I/O path (arbitration, timeouts, garbled replies, reconnection) is exercised. Several simulated devices may sit on one bus; like a Prologix GPIB adapter, ++addr N selects which one receives subsequent commands.

Faults are injected by FaultInjector, configured through driver options::

error_rate      probability that a command is silently dropped (-> read timeout)
garble_rate     probability that a reply is corrupted
hang_rate       probability that the port blocks for ``hang_time`` seconds
hang_time       how long a "hang" lasts (default 30 s, i.e. longer than any deadline)
disconnect_rate probability that the port "drops" and must be reopened
exception_rate  probability that the driver raises a random Python exception
nan_rate        probability that a numeric reading is NaN
latency         artificial delay per command (seconds)

docs.title: easymeasure.drivers.sr830
docs.text:
Stanford Research Systems SR830 / SR850 DSP lock-in amplifier (and SR810).

The model is detected from *IDN?; the differences (reference modes, the current-input gain, reserve names, how noise is read) are handled here. Address e.g. GPIB0::8::INSTR, or ASRL1::INSTR / COM1 for RS-232 (set the instrument to 9600 baud; replies end with CR: option read_termination = "\r"). SIM::<name> uses the built-in emulator.

Channels measured (read-only): X, Y, R (V, or A with a current input), theta (deg), Xn, Yn (noise, V/√Hz or A/√Hz), aux_in1 … aux_in4 (V)

sources (read/write, may be aliased and swept): ``sine_out`` (V rms,
0.004 … 5), ``frequency`` (Hz; read-only with an external reference),
``phase`` (deg), ``aux_out1`` … ``aux_out4`` (V, ±10.5)

settings: ``reference`` (Internal / External), ``sensitivity``,
``time_constant``, ``rolloff`` (low-pass filter slope 6 … 24 dB/oct),
``coupling`` (AC / DC), ``ground`` (Float / Ground), ``line_filter``

docs.title: easymeasure.drivers.yokogawa7651
docs.text:
Yokogawa 7651 programmable DC source (voltage or current).

The 7651 only sources; it does not measure. Its single source channel follows the mode setting:

========= =========== ================================== ================== mode channel ranges compliance ========= =========== ================================== ================== Voltage voltage 10 mV, 100 mV, 1 V, 10 V, 30 V Icompliance (A, 5 … 120 mA) Current current 1 mA, 10 mA, 100 mA Vcompliance (V, 1 … 30 V) ========= =========== ================================== ==================

Settings: mode, range (AUTO or a fixed range), the compliance, output (ON / OFF). A range takes up to 120 % of its nominal value (the 30 V range up to 32 V).

With range = AUTO the driver picks the smallest range that holds the new value. While the output is ON it only ever switches to a larger range, never down, so a sweep does not glitch the output by changing range on the way down. Changing the mode needs the output OFF.

Every setting is followed by E (execute) and confirmed by reading the output data (OD) back: a value the instrument did not take raises an error (option check_errors). Address e.g. GPIB0::1::INSTR; SIM::<name> uses the built-in emulator.

Commands used (7651 HP-IB/GP-IB command set): F1/F5 (function), R2 … R6 (range), S<value> (set), E (execute), O1/O0 (output), LV<V>/LA<mA> (limits), OD (output data), OC (status) and OS (settings).

docs.title: easymeasure.drivers.emulators.ami430
docs.text:
Emulated American Magnetics Model 430 programmer with a superconducting magnet.

Commands and queries are those of the Model 430 manual (remote interface reference): STATE?, FIELD:MAGnet?, CONFigure:FIELD:TARGet, RAMP, PAUSE, ZERO, PSwitch, QUench ... and the IEEE-488.2 *IDN?, *CLS, SYSTem:ERRor?.

The magnet behaves like one, in (scaled) real time:

  • the supply ramps its current at the segment-1 rate while the magnet is driven (switch heater on), at the faster "PSw P/S ramp rate" while the switch is cold (then only the current in the leads changes, the magnet keeps its persistent current);
  • PSwitch 1 heats the switch for the heated time (STATE 9), PSwitch 0 cools it for the cooled time (STATE 10); ramping is refused meanwhile;
  • when the switch turns resistive the supply current is forced into the magnet: a difference of more than mismatch_quench A quenches the magnet, as heating a switch at the wrong current can do;
  • a quench (quench() from a test, or a mismatch) sets STATE 7 and QUench? 1, zeroes the supply and lets the magnet current decay; QUench 0 clears it (the supply then PAUSEs).

Options: time_scale (simulated seconds per real second), coil (T/A), limit (A), rate (segment-1 rate, A/s), psw_rate (A/s), heat_time, cool_time (s), switch (a persistent switch is installed), units (0 = kG, 1 = T), rate_units (0 = per second, 1 = per minute), inductance (H), mismatch_quench (A), auto_zero (ramp the leads to zero after cooling, as the front panel does), greeting (the TCP welcome lines), model (430 or 420).

docs.title: easymeasure.drivers.emulators.cygnus
docs.text:
Emulated Cygnus 16430 8-channel supply (Cao RQM Lab firmware, Core/Src/scpi.c).

The command handling is a port of the firmware's dispatch_line: the exact verbs (VOLT n,v, OUTP? n, MEAS:VOLT? n ... no SCPI long/short forms), a one-slot error register read by SYST:ERR? (0 or -1,"<message>"), and - like the firmware - no reply at all to a query it rejects (bad channel, unknown command), so a driver mistake shows up as a timeout plus an error.

Every output drives a resistive load (option load_ohm, default 10 kΩ, or a list of 8): with the relay on the channel regulates the voltage until the current reaches its limit (then the voltage drops, constant current); with the relay open the readback is the unloaded output node (setpoint, no current). Readings follow the round-robin ADC: a channel's value is refreshed every 8 · 24 · SF / 32768 s (SF = RATE), so a reading right after a change is the old one (option emulate_latency, default on).

docs.title: easymeasure.drivers.emulators.hp4145
docs.text:
Emulated HP 4145B (or 4155C in 4145 syntax mode) in HP-IB user mode.

Commands: ID, US, IT1-IT3, BC, DR<n>, DV ch,range,value,comp, DI ch,range,value,comp, DS [ch], TV ch, TI ch (and CMD? on the 4155). SMUs 1-4 drive a resistor each (option load_ohm) and clamp at their compliance; VM1 / VM2 (channels 5, 6 for TV) read VS1 / VS2 (channels 5, 6 for DV). A measurement answers <status><channel><V|I><value>, e.g. NAI+1.0000E-03 (status N normal, C in compliance). Commands that are not allowed or out of range set errors and change nothing; commands the emulator does not know go to unknown.

Option emulate_model: 4145B (default) or 4155C; emulate_cmd_mode: the 4155's command mode at power-on (0 = SCPI, 1 = FLEX, 2 = 4145 syntax). In SCPI mode it understands :SYSTem:LANGuage COMPatibility (-> 4145 syntax), in FLEX mode :PAGE (-> SCPI); 4145 commands are ignored outside 4145 syntax mode. emulate_switch_delay: seconds a mode change takes (CMD? reports the old mode meanwhile); emulate_no_lang: the SCPI language command is refused.

docs.title: easymeasure.drivers.emulators.lockin
docs.text:
Emulated SR830 / SR850 lock-in amplifier (command set of the manuals' chapter 5).

Option emulate_model = "SR830" (default) or "SR850". The emulated sample returns a signal proportional to the sine output with a fixed phase, and the aux inputs read back half of the aux outputs (a "loop-back cable").

docs.title: easymeasure.drivers.emulators.nidaqmx_sim
docs.text:
A stand-in for the nidaqmx package emulating one NI USB DAQ per device name.

Only the part of the nidaqmx API the ni6211 / ni63xx drivers use is provided, with the same names, argument conventions and return shapes as nidaqmx 1.x (task.read() gives a float for one channel, a list per channel for several, lists of samples for timed reads). Each card is a USB-6211 unless define makes it another model of .._nidaq_models (channel counts, ranges, rates, digital port layout). The card is wired as a loop-back test box: aiK sees aoK (for every output), the other inputs carry 0.1 V × index plus a little noise, every counter counts a 1 kHz clock; USB-6211: port0 (digital inputs) reads port1 (outputs); X Series: every digital line is wired to the line half a port away (P0.0 ↔ P0.4 on an 8-line port), an input reads what its partner drives, otherwise 0 (pull-down).

Errors follow DAQmx: invalid channels, ranges, rates or a resource that is already reserved (a digital line used by two tasks, an X Series counter's source PFI used as a digital line) raise errors.DaqError with DAQmx's codes.

docs.title: easymeasure.drivers.emulators.pna
docs.text:
Emulated Agilent PNA series network analyzer (E8356A / E8357A / E8358A), for the e8358a driver.

The command set is the PNA programming guide's (firmware A.07): measurements are created by name on a channel (CALCulate{ch}:PARameter[:DEFine] 'name',S21), selected (CALC:PAR:SEL) and read as complex data (CALC:DATA? SDATA); the sweep is configured under SENSe{ch} and the source under SOURce{ch}. A sweep is started with SENSe:SWEep:MODE SINGle (or GROups with a group count, for averaging) and takes about points / IF bandwidth seconds per direction; *OPC sets the operation-complete bit of *ESR? when it has finished.

The device under test is a hanger resonator on a transmission line: a dip in S21 at f0 (option emulate_f0, default 5 GHz), a cable delay, losses, and noise that grows with the IF bandwidth and falls with power and averaging. S12 = S21 and S22 = S11 (a reciprocal, symmetric device).

Option time_scale divides the time a sweep takes (tests use a large one).

docs.text:
Checking what is typed into a code or formula field, with the backend.

Every editor of code or formulas (parameters, composite channels, user actions, point actions, scripts) has a Check button, and its OK (or Add / Run) checks first: the dialog closes only when the check passes. The backend answers - it knows the channels, the parameters and the rules - so the front ends never repeat those rules. Without a connection only the local checks run.

BackendCheck wires that up: give it how to build the request, how to show the answer, and what to do once it passed.

docs.text:
Non-blocking, Qt-native connection to the backend.

Everything happens through Qt signals on the GUI thread; nothing here ever waits. Requests take callbacks::

docs.title: easymeasure.frontend.setup_merge
docs.text:
Merging part of a saved setup into the current one (no Qt, no backend calls).

A SetupMerge holds the items of a setup file (instruments, parameters, aliases, composite channels, user actions) next to the current setup (as the backend describes it in get_state). The user selects items, may give them new names, and SetupMerge.validate says, per item, whether merging it works:

  • names: one namespace for everything (instruments, aliases, composites and their channels, parameters, user actions): a name already used in the current setup is a conflict, unless the item there is identical (then it is simply skipped); two merged items may not get the same name either;
  • dependencies: an alias needs its instrument, a formula the channels and parameters it uses - selected too, or already in the current setup;
  • consistency: everything is checked by the backend's own rules, run here offline on a copy of the current setup (ChannelManager with stand-in instruments): writable targets, formulas, circular references between composites or parameters, mappings that must be each other's inverse.

New names are carried through: renaming the instrument lockin to lockin2 rewrites the targets of the merged aliases (lockin.X -> lockin2.X), renaming an alias, composite channel or parameter rewrites the formulas that use it and the names quoted in user actions (get('Vxx'); parameters also as bare names in action code). SetupMerge.commands lists the backend commands that perform the merge, in an order that works.

Nothing here talks to the backend; the dialog (merge_dialog.py) sends the commands.

docs.title: easymeasure.frontend.panels.manual_panel
docs.text:
Manual panel: set any aliased / composite channel and instrument setting directly.

Instrument settings (configuration channels such as a mode, range or time constant) are listed below the aliases when "settings" is ticked. Channels with a list of allowed values get a combo box instead of a text field / spin box.

Each channel row has a spin box, a slider (when the alias has both a minimum and a maximum) and a context menu on the spin box (right click) to enter a math expression of the present value x (e.g. x + 0.01, x/2, 0.1*pi).

Variables of a multivariate composite channel are grouped (indented) under the composite's name. A group has "hold", "Set all" and "Set all to zero": while hold is ticked, edits only mark the variables and "Set all" sends them in one go (the hardware channels are computed once from all of them). "Set all to zero" sets every variable to 0 together, the usual way to start.

Until a group's variables have been set for the first time they have no value: they show NaN, their sliders are greyed out and hold is forced on. The group is started with "Set all to zero", or by typing a value for every variable and clicking "Set all" (enabled once none shows NaN).

The setup's parameters are listed in their own group: a value parameter can be edited (it is written like any channel; it moves no instrument), a formula parameter shows its value. The user actions are buttons at the top: ▶ runs one (writes it), and while it runs its button aborts it.

Writes go through the backend's protected path (limits, ramp rates). While a channel is still ramping, newer requests for it are coalesced: only the latest value is sent once the previous write has finished. Mouse-wheel changes are ignored unless the widget has keyboard focus, so scrolling the panel can never move an instrument by accident.

docs.title: easymeasure.remote.acme
docs.text:
Certificates from Let's Encrypt (or any ACME server, RFC 8555) for the gateway.

obtain() proves control of a domain name with the HTTP-01 challenge: for the few seconds of the check it answers http://<domain>/.well-known/acme-challenge/<token> on port 80 of this computer, so the domain must point to this computer and port 80 must be reachable from the internet (router / firewall). The result is a certificate chain and key in <home>/remote/tls/acme/<domain>/ that the gateway uses (and reloads when they change); renew_if_due renews it 30 days before it expires.

Only the standard library and cryptography are used. The account key (ECDSA P-256, ES256) is kept per ACME server in <home>/remote/tls/acme/.

Command line: python -m easymeasure.remote letsencrypt DOMAIN --email ADDR --agree-tos [--staging] and ... letsencrypt --renew; progress goes to <home>/remote/acme.json (shown in Backend → Remote access).

docs.title: easymeasure.remote.gateway
docs.text:
Internet-facing gateway: HTTPS + secure WebSocket in front of the backend.

::

browser / RemoteClient ──TLS 1.2+ (WSS, permessage-deflate)──▶ gateway ──localhost TCP──▶ backend

The gateway runs in its own process. Nothing that arrives from the network is parsed inside the backend process before the gateway has authenticated the user, validated the message and checked the user's role, and a crash, hang or memory blow-up caused by a hostile peer can only take down the gateway (which the backend restarts), never the instrument backend or a running measurement.

On the WebSocket each message is one codec frame without its 4-byte length prefix (the WebSocket already delimits messages).

Each live remote connection gets its own backend connection, so the backend's per-client machinery (event subscriptions, droppable events for slow clients, stall detection) works unchanged. Frames from the backend are forwarded byte-for-byte (no re-encoding); WebSocket flow control propagates back-pressure from a slow browser to the backend, which then drops monitor/sweep-point events for that client instead of buffering them.

Security measures (see easymeasure.remote.policy for the roles):

  • TLS only, 1.2+ with forward-secret AEAD ciphers; no plaintext port.
  • Accounts with scrypt-hashed passwords; login brute-force lock-out per address and per account; generic error messages; constant-time checks.
  • Sessions: 256-bit random tokens (only their SHA-256 kept in memory), cookie __Host-em (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict) or Authorization: Bearer for scripts; idle and absolute expiry; revoked when the account changes.
  • Cross-site WebSocket hijacking blocked by an Origin check; strict CSP and other security headers; only files of the bundled web app are served.
  • Limits: connections per address, sessions per user, live connections, message size, request rate, unanswered requests, TLS-handshake and first-request timeouts. Idle connections are never dropped (heartbeats only detect dead peers).
  • Audit log <home>/logs/remote.log: logins, lock-outs, denied commands and every command that changes something.

docs.title: easymeasure.remote.policy
docs.text:
What remote users may do.

Three roles, each including the rights of the one before:

viewer Watch everything: state, monitor, live and stored data, logs, queue. Reads channels (an instrument query) but changes nothing. operator Run measurements within the configured setup: write channels (aliases, composite channels, parameters: their limits and ramp rates are always enforced by the backend), run instrument actions and the user actions an admin defined (writing them), monitor channels, queue / start / pause / abort sweeps, add PPT slides, reconnect instruments. Not the instruments' own channels (instrument.channel, settings too): they are written without limits, so setting or sweeping them - directly, as a sweep channel or a constant - needs the admin role (RESTRICT; the backend refuses it, it knows which names are those channels). Reading them is fine. Cannot run Python code (scripts, sweep hooks), change instruments, aliases or their limits, send raw instrument commands, change backend settings or touch files outside the data directory. admin Everything a local user can do, including scripts and hook code - which means full control of the backend computer. Give this role sparingly.

Commands that only make sense on the backend computer itself (tray icon, remote access control) are never available remotely.

docs.text:

What the backend must refuse for this role in every request (it knows the channels and the data files; the gateway does not): raw_writes - writing an instrument's own channels (write_channel, set_many, the channels a queued sweep writes); code - continuing a run whose sweep has hook code (the gateway checks the code of the sweeps it is sent itself).

LoginThrottle(max_ip: int = 5, max_user: int = 10, base: float = 30.0, cap: float = 3600.0, window: float = 900.0, max_entries: int = 100000)

Failed logins lock out the client address and the account name separately.

After max_ip failures from one address (or max_user failures for one account, from anywhere) further attempts are refused - without checking the password, so a locked-out attacker learns nothing - for base seconds, doubling with every further lockout up to cap. Failures are forgotten after window seconds without one. A successful login clears the address (not the account: a distributed attack keeps the account protected).

Seconds until a login attempt is allowed again (0 = now).

docs.title: easymeasure.remote.tlsutil
docs.text:
TLS for the remote gateway.

Without a configured certificate a self-signed ECDSA P-256 certificate is created on first start (<home>/remote/tls). Browsers will warn about it once; Python clients pin its SHA-256 fingerprint (python -m easymeasure.remote cert). For a browser without warnings, configure a real certificate (e.g. Let's Encrypt) with certfile / keyfile in the remote config, or let .acme get one from Let's Encrypt. A running gateway picks up changed certificate files.

Only TLS 1.2+ with forward-secret AEAD ciphers is accepted; TLS compression and renegotiation are disabled.

docs.title: easymeasure.remote.users
docs.text:
User accounts for remote access (<home>/remote/users.json).

Passwords are stored as salted scrypt hashes (N=2^15, r=8, p=1; ~32 MB and tens of milliseconds per check, which makes offline guessing expensive). The file is written atomically with owner-only permissions and re-read automatically when it changes, so accounts can be added or removed while the gateway runs. Removing a user, changing their role or password ends their open sessions.

docs.title: ami430 – American Magnetics 430 / 420 magnet power supply programmer
docs.text:
Superconducting magnet supply

property value driver name ami430 module easymeasure.drivers.ami430 interfaces TCP socket (tcp), serial (serial), GPIB (gpib), VISA LAN (tcpip), other VISA (other), simulated bus (sim) recognised by *IDN? AMERICAN MAGNETICS suggested addresses SIM::ami430 (built-in emulator) shared port by default no

American Magnetics Model 430 programmer (and the older Model 420) for superconducting magnets. The magnet's configuration (coil constant, current limit, ramp rates, the persistent switch's heater current and times, quench detection) is set once on the programmer's front panel. The driver only reads it. What the driver does is make sure the magnet is driven safely.

Address. Model 430 over Ethernet: TCP::<ip address>::7180, or the RS-232 port. Model 420: its RS-232 port, e.g. COM3. The programmer's field units (kG or T) and ramp-rate units are read and converted; field is always in T and ramp_rate in T/min.

docs.title: Setting the field
docs.text:
Setting field starts the ramp and returns at once, like pressing RAMP on the front panel. status reads RAMPING, then HOLDING. A sweep that steps the field waits at every step with a point action:

wait_until(lambda: get('magnet.status') == 'HOLDING', timeout=3600)

docs.title: Persistent switch
docs.text:
IsPersistentSwitchInstalled (a setting, Yes / No) says whether the magnet has a persistent switch. Option auto (the default) takes it from the programmer's configuration. With Yes:

  • the field can only be changed in driven mode (switch heater on). In persistent mode, setting field is refused: the supply would only change the current in its leads, while the magnet keeps its field;
  • Enter Persistent (enter_persistent) and Exit Persistent (exit_persistent) switch between the two modes.

Each action does its steps in the order that cannot quench the magnet. Before every step it reads the programmer's state again:

Enter Persistent Exit Persistent 1. The supply must hold the field (HOLDING). Wait settle_time seconds, and until the magnet voltage is below max_magnet_voltage. 1. Ramp the supply to the magnet's persistent current, and wait until it holds there. 2. Turn the switch heater off, and wait while the switch cools (COOLING SWITCH). 2. Heat the switch, only if the supply current matches the magnet current within match_tolerance A. 3. Ramp the leads to zero (option zero_leads), and wait for AT ZERO. Status: PERSISTENT. 3. Wait while the switch heats (HEATING SWITCH), then hold the field. Status: HOLDING.

Heating the switch at the wrong supply current forces the difference into the magnet at once, which can quench it. That is why exiting never heats the switch before the currents match.

An action starts the procedure and returns. The procedure then goes on by itself (the backend checks the magnet every poll_interval seconds), and you can watch the field and the status meanwhile. status reads ENTERING PERSISTENT or EXITING PERSISTENT until it is done, and operation shows the current step. A script waits for it:

set('magnet.enter_persistent')
wait_until(lambda: get('magnet.status') == 'PERSISTENT', timeout=3600)

If a step does not finish in time, or the programmer does something unexpected (paused from the front panel, a ramp refused …), the procedure stops in a safe state, without heating the switch. operation then says why. The pause action stops the supply and the procedure. Field writes and the other action are refused while a procedure runs, and while the switch is heating or cooling.

docs.title: Quench
docs.text:
The programmer detects a quench itself and takes the supply to zero. The driver checks for one at every call, and the backend checks every poll_interval seconds, even when nothing reads the magnet. When a quench is detected:

  • the running sweep or script is aborted (its data file says why), the run queue stops, and running user actions are aborted;
  • every front end shows the fault, and the instrument's last error reads FAULT: …;
  • until the quench is cleared, field writes and the persistent actions are refused. Reading the field still works, so you can watch it decay.

Clear it with the clear_quench action (or RESET QUENCH on the front panel) once the magnet is safe. Then start the queue again. See Robustness.

docs.title: Add it
docs.text:
c.call("add_instrument", name="magnet", driver="ami430", address="SIM::ami430")

(SIM::ami430 is the driver's built-in emulator; use the instrument's real address for hardware.)

docs.text:
option default timeout 5 reset False check_errors True read_termination \r\n write_termination \r\n IsPersistentSwitchInstalled auto settle_time 10 max_magnet_voltage 0.05 match_tolerance 0.05 zero_leads True status_interval 0.25

docs.text:

docs.title: cygnus16430 – Cygnus 16430: 8 × (0–150 V, 0–40 mA) supply with output relays (USB serial)
docs.text:
8-channel supply

property value driver name cygnus16430 module easymeasure.drivers.cygnus16430 interfaces serial (serial), simulated bus (sim) recognised by *IDN? Cygnus-16430 suggested addresses SIM::cygnus16430 (built-in emulator) shared port by default no

Cygnus 16430: an 8-channel supply, 0–150 V and 0–40 mA per output, with an output relay each, over USB serial (firmware cygnus-16430-firmware).

Address: its USB serial port, e.g. COM5 or /dev/ttyACM0; any baud rate works.

Outputs. Each output is a voltage setpoint with a current limit: constant voltage until the limit, then constant current. Each has its own relay, and nothing changes on connect.

per output k = 1…8 voltage<k> setpoint, 0 … 150 V Vmeas<k>, Imeas<k> measured voltage and current Ilimit<k> current limit, 0 … 40 mA (setting) output<k> relay ON / OFF (setting)

Vectors: voltAll and IlimitAll write all 8 at once (all are checked first, nothing is set if one is out of range); VmeasAll and ImeasAll read all 8. Monitor VmeasAll to see all eight readings as curves.

ADC and filters: Vrate and Irate set the ADC SF (13–255); Vfilter and Ifilter set the IIR filter α.

Actions: all_off, reset, auto_calibrate (refused while an output is on).

Commands. The driver speaks the firmware's exact commands (VOLT n,v, OUTP n,ON, MEAS:CURR? n …). It reads the firmware's one-slot error register (SYST:ERR?) after every setting, so a refused value raises the firmware's message.

Fresh readings. Readings are round-robin over the 8 channels, every 8·24·SF/32768 s (76 ms at SF 13). After a change of a channel's setpoint, limit or relay, its next reading waits for fresh conversions. With an IIR filter it also waits for about 99 % of the step. The option settle = false turns this off.

Filters. The filters cannot be read back, so the driver sets them from its options on connect.

Emulator. SIM::cygnus emulates the firmware's parser with resistive loads (option load_ohm, default 10 kΩ).
