docs.title: Scripting and Python
docs.text:
An advanced topic

You don't need anything on these pages for everyday measurements. The Quick start and the tutorials do everything from the GUI. Come here when you notice that you are clicking the same thing for the tenth time, or the measurement you want can't be described as a grid of points.

docs.title: When the GUI is not enough
docs.text:
Some typical cases:

you want to … use run the same sweep at a list of temperatures, fields or gate voltages, one file each a queue script with a loop measure first, then decide where to measure next (find a peak, then zoom in) a queue script: run_sweep() returns the data put points closer together near something interesting, or walk a path that is not a straight line a custom sweep measure while something drifts by itself (a magnet ramp, a warm-up) a time trace: a custom sweep with no swept channel check a measurement while it runs, from a Jupyter notebook, or start it from your own program a Python client use an instrument easyMeasure has no driver for the Driver Wizard, or write a driver

docs.title: How much code?
docs.text:
easyMeasure has code at four levels. Each one is a small step up from the one before.

  1. Formulas. The scale of an alias, the formulas of a composite channel and the mapping of a sweep are single expressions such as (n + 0.15 + D/0.0452) / 1.2. You have used these in the tutorials.
  2. Point actions and user actions. A line or two of Python run at every point of a sweep (if abs(values['Ileak']) > 1e-9: end_sweep()) or at the click of a button (set_many({'Vbg': 0, 'Vtg': 0})). See tutorial 3.
  3. Queue scripts. A whole Python program that the backend runs from the queue, like a sweep. It can set and read channels, wait, and run sweeps one after another. This is the main subject of this chapter: Queue scripts and Custom sweeps.
  4. Python outside easyMeasure. A notebook or program that connects to the running backend: Python clients. And drivers, which are Python classes.

All of them use the same names: get('Rxx'), set('Vbg', 1.0), and so on. What you learn at one level works at the next.

docs.title: A sweep is a dictionary
docs.text:
Everything you set up in the sweep editor is stored as a plain dictionary. Sweep → Save… writes it to a JSON file, and every data file contains it. The Dirac-peak sweep from the Quick start looks like this (examples/graphene_dirac.json):

In the editorAs a dictionary 

{
  "name": "dirac_peak",
  "dimensions": [
    {
      "points": 161,
      "sweep": [
        {
          "channel": "Vbg",
          "start": -8,
          "stop": 8
        }
      ],
      "record": [
        "Rxx",
        "Ileak"
      ],
      "pre_delay": 0.02
    }
  ],
  "post": {
    "constants": [
      {
        "channel": "Vbg",
        "value": 0
      }
    ]
  },
  "metadata": {
    "sample": "BLG-01"
  }
}

Each box of the editor is a key: points is box 2, sweep box 3, record box 4. A script builds the same dictionary, or loads one saved from the editor and changes a few values. Every key is listed in the sweep definition reference.

Design in the GUI, repeat with a script

The easiest way to write a sweep for a script is not to write it at all. Set it up in the editor, check it with Sweep → Validate, save it (Sweep → Save…), and load it in the script with load_sweep(...).

docs.title: In this chapter
docs.text:
• Queue scripts: your first script, from the GUI's script editor; the functions a script can use; adaptive measurements and series of sweeps.
  • Custom sweeps: non-uniform points, paths through the (n, D) plane, hysteresis loops, time traces. With complete examples.
  • Python clients: control a running easyMeasure from a notebook or another program.
  • Writing a driver: support a new instrument in Python.

The Script API reference lists every function.

docs.title: Python clients
docs.text:
Everything the GUI does goes through backend commands, so a script or a notebook can do the same. There are three ways in:

client for connects BackendClient scripts and notebooks on the backend computer localhost socket, token from ~/.easymeasure/backend.json RemoteClient scripts on other computers HTTPS / WSS through the remote gateway Backend (in-process) tests, tools, embedding none: the backend runs in your process

docs.title: BackendClient
docs.text:
from easymeasure.client import BackendClient

c = BackendClient.connect(name="my notebook")      # finds the running backend
c.call("read_channel", name="Vg")
c.call("write_channel", name="Vg", value=0.2)      # ramps; call() waits for the end
c.call("queue_add", item={"kind": "sweep", "definition": sweep}, start=True)
c.close()

call(cmd, **args) blocks until the backend answers. The default timeout is 120 s; pass _timeout= for long ramps. A ramp of write_channel / set_many can be stopped from any client (or the Stop ramps button of the Manual panel) with c.call("stop_ramps"); the write then returns the value reached. ramp_state lists the ramps running now, and the event ramps announces every change. A refused command raises easymeasure.common.errors.RemoteError with the backend's message:

from easymeasure.common.errors import RemoteError
try:
    c.call("write_channel", name="Vg", value=5)
except RemoteError as e:
    print(e)            # Vg: value 5 above maximum 2

Any number of clients can be connected at once, together with any number of GUIs. Every client sees the same live state. Requests run concurrently, but each instrument serialises its own calls and the queue runs one item at a time. There is no locking between users: the last action wins.

docs.title: Starting a backend from a script
docs.text:
from easymeasure.client import BackendClient, start_backend_detached, wait_for_backend

if wait_for_backend(timeout=1) is None:
    start_backend_detached(["--setup", "examples/demo_setup.json"])
    wait_for_backend(timeout=30)
c = BackendClient.connect()

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
The backend pushes events. By default a client gets only the small status events:

event data queue the queue state (same as queue_state) sweep_start, sweep_end run number, path; header and progress (start) or status, error, footer (end). A continued run starts with progress done > 0 and continues (the run it continues); run_snapshot gives its data so far sweep_paused, sweep_resumed, sweep_warning run state, warning text item_end a queue item finished (sweep or script) user_action a user action started / ended ppt a slide was written (or went to the pending file) instrument_fault a safety fault (magnet quench): instrument, message, whether a run was aborted changed, settings the setup or settings changed

Ask for more with subscribe, or for everything with "*":

event data monitor monitored channel values sweep_point, sweep_phase, sweep_progress live sweep data, progress log log records 
c.on_event = lambda kind, data: print(kind, data)
c.subscribe(["monitor", "sweep_progress"])

The handler runs on the client's reader thread. Keep it short, and don't call c.call from inside it. Events nobody subscribed to are not even encoded by the backend.

docs.title: Waiting for a sweep
docs.text:
import threading
done = threading.Event()
result = {}
def on_event(kind, data):
    if kind == "sweep_end":
        result.update(data)
        done.set()
c.on_event = on_event
c.call("queue_add", item={"kind": "sweep", "definition": sweep}, start=True)
done.wait()
print(result["status"], result["path"])     # also result["error"], result["footer"]

docs.title: In a notebook
docs.text:
from easymeasure.client import BackendClient
from easymeasure.backend.storage import DataSet
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

c = BackendClient.connect(name="notebook")
c.call("queue_add", item={"kind": "sweep", "definition": sweep}, start=True)
# … later, also while it runs:
snap = c.call("run_snapshot")
path = c.call("current_run")["path"]
ds = DataSet.load(path)                 # partial while running
plt.pcolormesh(ds.data["I"].T); plt.show()

An idle client is never disconnected. examples/notebook_long_connection.ipynb shows a connection kept for days.

docs.title: RemoteClient
docs.text:
The same interface, through the remote gateway from another computer:

from easymeasure.client import RemoteClient

c = RemoteClient("https://lab-pc.example.org:8443", "alice", password,
                 fingerprint="87:68:0C:…")       # python -m easymeasure.remote cert
c.role, len(c.allowed)                           # 'operator', the permitted commands
c.call("read_channel", name="Vg")
c.subscribe(["monitor"])
c.on_event = lambda kind, data: print(kind, data)
c.close()
  • fingerprint pins the gateway's self-signed certificate.
  • cafile names a CA bundle.
  • With a real certificate (e.g. Let's Encrypt), neither is needed.
  • A command your role does not allow raises RemoteError ("permission denied: …").

docs.title: In-process Backend
docs.text:
from easymeasure.backend.service import Backend

be = Backend(home="C:/emtest", log_to_console=False)
be.load_setup(path="examples/demo_setup.json")
be.write_channel(name="Vg", value=0.1)
be.queue_add(item={"kind": "sweep", "definition": sweep}, start=True)
be.queue.wait_idle(600)
be.close()

The commands are methods with the same names and arguments. This is what the tests use. Only one backend should own a given set of instruments at a time.

docs.title: Custom sweeps
docs.text:
A plain sweep steps each channel in equal steps from start to stop. Many measurements need something else: more points where something interesting happens, a path that is not a straight line, a loop up and back down, or no stepping at all. This page shows how, first in the sweep editor where that is possible, then with a queue script for what the editor can't do.

All examples use the graphene setup of the tutorials (examples/graphene_setup.json). The .json files load in the sweep editor with Sweep → Load…; the .py files in the script editor with Open….

docs.title: Three ways to give the points
docs.text:
Each row of a dimension's Set swept channels table gets its values in one of three ways. The table has more columns than fit: scroll it to the right, or widen the window.

columns used the values example Start, Stop equal steps from start to stop −8 … 8 V in 161 points Mapping (plus Start, Stop) a formula, evaluated for every point start*(stop/start)**t: logarithmic steps Values the list you type, comma-separated 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 9

A mapping is a formula of these names:

name is i the point number: 0, 1, …, N−1 N the number of points t i/(N−1): runs from 0 to 1 start, stop the Start and Stop of the row x the plain linear value: start + (stop − start)·t

It can use sin, cos, exp, log, sqrt, sinh, sign, abs, pi and the other functions listed under expressions. Every value it gives is checked against the channel's limits before the sweep starts, like any other sweep: Sweep → Validate shows an error if the formula goes too far.

docs.title: More points near the Dirac peak
docs.text:
The resistance changes fast near the Dirac point and slowly far from it. Equal steps are either too coarse at the peak or wasteful elsewhere.

In the editor, with a mapping: Start −1, Stop 1, 161 points, and

0.3 + 7.7*sinh(3*x)/sinh(3)

As x runs from −1 to 1, this goes from −7.4 V to 8.0 V, with steps of 0.03 V at the peak (0.3 V) and 0.29 V at the ends: ten times denser where it matters, for the same number of points.

{
  "name": "dirac_dense",
  "dimensions": [
    {
      "points": 161,
      "sweep": [
        {
          "channel": "Vbg",
          "start": -1,
          "stop": 1,
          "mapping": "0.3 + 7.7*sinh(3*x)/sinh(3)"
        }
      ],
      "record": [
        "Rxx"
      ]
    }
  ],
  "post": {
    "constants": [
      {
        "channel": "Vbg",
        "value": 0
      }
    ]
  }
}

Other useful mappings:

mapping gives start + (stop - start)*t**2 dense near start sign(x)*x**2/stop (Start = −Stop) dense near zero, e.g. small fields start*(stop/start)**t logarithmic: frequencies, powers in W, times

With a script, when a formula is awkward, build the list with numpy. Here: 0.2 V steps everywhere, plus 0.02 V steps within 1 V of the peak.

# Sweep the back gate with points 0.2 V apart, but 0.02 V apart within 1 V of
# the Dirac point: a non-uniform sweep, built in Python and run as an ordinary sweep.
v_dirac = 0.3
coarse = np.arange(-8, 8.001, 0.2)
fine = np.arange(v_dirac - 1, v_dirac + 1.0001, 0.02)
values = np.unique(np.round(np.concatenate([coarse, fine]), 6))   # sorted, no duplicates

ds = run_sweep({
    "name": "dirac_dense",
    "dimensions": [{"points": len(values),
                    "sweep": [{"channel": "Vbg", "values": values.tolist()}],
                    "record": ["Rxx"]}],
    "post": {"constants": [{"channel": "Vbg", "value": 0}]},
})
log("%s: %d points, file %s" % (ds.status, len(values), ds.path))

"values": values.tolist() is the Values column of the editor, for any number of points. np.unique sorts the merged list and removes duplicates.

docs.title: A path through the (n, D) plane
docs.text:
Every channel in the same dimension is set at every point, each from its own row. With mappings, the rows can draw any curve. Here is a circle around the charge-neutrality point, using the composite channels nD.n and nD.D of tutorial 2:

  1. + sweep channel adds a second row to the same dimension. Row 1: nD.n, mapping 1.0*cos(2*pi*t). Row 2: nD.D, mapping 0.2*sin(2*pi*t). With 73 points, t goes once around the circle in 5° steps. Start and Stop are not used by these formulas.

nD.n and nD.D belong to the same composite, so they are set together at every point, and both gate voltages follow. The result, against nD.n:

The resistance is largest where the path crosses \(n = 0\), at \(D = \pm 0.2\) V/nm, where the gap is open. The two crossings give the same curve because the gap only depends on \(|D|\).

{
  "name": "circle_nD",
  "dimensions": [
    {
      "points": 73,
      "sweep": [
        {
          "channel": "nD.n",
          "start": 0,
          "stop": 0,
          "mapping": "1.0*cos(2*pi*t)"
        },
        {
          "channel": "nD.D",
          "start": 0,
          "stop": 0,
          "mapping": "0.2*sin(2*pi*t)"
        }
      ],
      "record": [
        "Rxx"
      ]
    }
  ],
  "post": {
    "constants": [
      {
        "channel": "Vbg",
        "value": 0
      },
      {
        "channel": "Vtg",
        "value": 0
      }
    ]
  }
}

With a script, the same circle at several radii, each in its own file. The values are computed with numpy and given as lists:

# A path that is not a straight line: circles around the charge-neutrality point in
# the (n, D) plane, at three radii.  n and D are swept together in one dimension,
# each from its own list of values, so every point is one (n, D) pair.
theta = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 73)            # 5° steps, back to the start
for radius in (0.5, 1.0, 1.5):
    n_values = radius * np.cos(theta)            # 1e12 cm^-2
    d_values = 0.2 * radius * np.sin(theta)      # V/nm: an ellipse, D is the smaller axis
    ds = run_sweep({
        "name": "circle_r%g" % radius,
        "dimensions": [{"points": len(theta),
                        "sweep": [{"channel": "nD.n", "values": n_values.tolist()},
                                  {"channel": "nD.D", "values": d_values.tolist()}],
                        "record": ["Rxx", "Vbg", "Vtg"]}],
        "metadata": {"radius": radius},
    })
    log("radius %g: %s, Rxx from %.0f to %.0f Ω" % (
        radius, ds.status, np.nanmin(ds.data["Rxx"]), np.nanmax(ds.data["Rxx"])))
set_many({"nD.n": 0, "nD.D": 0})

docs.title: Hysteresis loops
docs.text:
To sweep up and back down in one file, use a triangle wave. A gate sweep 0 → 5 → 0 → −5 → 0 V in 0.1 V steps (201 points), with Start 0, Stop 5 and the mapping

stop*(2/pi)*arcsin(sin(2*pi*t))

{
  "name": "gate_hysteresis",
  "dimensions": [
    {
      "points": 201,
      "sweep": [
        {
          "channel": "Vbg",
          "start": 0,
          "stop": 5,
          "mapping": "stop*(2/pi)*arcsin(sin(2*pi*t))"
        }
      ],
      "record": [
        "Rxx",
        "@elapsed"
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Plot Rxx against @elapsed to see the loop in time order, or against Vbg to compare the up and down branches.

In a script, the same with explicit pieces, each with its own step size if you like:

# A hysteresis loop: 0 → +5 V → −5 V → 0 in one sweep, from an explicit list.
up = np.linspace(0, 5, 51)
down = np.linspace(5, -5, 101)[1:]
back = np.linspace(-5, 0, 51)[1:]
values = np.concatenate([up, down, back])
ds = run_sweep({
    "name": "gate_hysteresis",
    "dimensions": [{"points": len(values),
                    "sweep": [{"channel": "Vbg", "values": values.tolist()}],
                    "record": ["Rxx", "@elapsed"]}],
})
log("hysteresis loop: %s" % ds.status)

Hysteresis in a map

In a 2-D sweep, the snake scan option of the inner dimension makes every second line run backwards. The even and odd lines of the map are then the two sweep directions.

docs.title: Time traces
docs.text:
A dimension with no swept channel just records, again and again. With a post-sample delay it is a time trace: watch a sample relax after a gate jump, or a drift overnight.

In the editor: + dimension, leave the Set swept channels table empty, choose what to record (add @elapsed, the time since the start of the sweep), set the number of points and the post-sample delay. 600 points every 0.5 s is 5 minutes:

{
  "name": "time_trace",
  "dimensions": [
    {
      "points": 600,
      "sweep": [],
      "record": [
        "Rxx",
        "B",
        "@elapsed"
      ],
      "post_delay": 0.5
    }
  ]
}

Measure while the magnet ramps. Stepping the field and waiting at every step, as in tutorial 1, is slow. Many groups instead ramp the magnet continuously and record as fast as possible, plotting against the field that was measured at each reading. That is a time trace that starts the ramp first and stops itself when the magnet has arrived:

# Measure while the magnet ramps continuously, instead of stepping the field: a sweep
# with no swept channel is a time trace.  It records every 0.1 s and ends itself
# when the magnet reports HOLDING.
set("Vbg", 1.1)                                  # n ≈ 0.5e12 cm^-2: Shubnikov-de Haas
set("B", 0)
wait_until(lambda: get("magnet.status") == "HOLDING", timeout=1200)
set("B", 3)                                      # starts the ramp; does not wait
ds = run_sweep({
    "name": "sdh_field_ramp",
    "dimensions": [{"points": 20000, "sweep": [],
                    "record": ["B", "Rxx", "@elapsed"], "post_delay": 0.1,
                    "hooks": {"post_record": {"enabled": True, "code":
                              "if get('magnet.status') == 'HOLDING': end_sweep()"}}}],
})
n = int(np.isfinite(ds.data["B"]).sum())
log("%s after %d readings, B up to %.2f T" % (ds.status, n, np.nanmax(ds.data["B"])))
set("B", 0)
set("Vbg", 0)
  • set("B", 3) only sets the magnet's target; the supply ramps by itself while the sweep runs.
  • The point action end_sweep() stops the trace once the supply reports HOLDING (see tutorial 3). 20000 points is just an upper limit; the file holds what was measured, the rest is nan.
  • In the plot, choose B as the X axis to see the Shubnikov–de Haas oscillations of Rxx.

docs.title: Deciding during the measurement
docs.text:
When the next points depend on what was just measured, use a script that runs one sweep, looks at the data and runs the next: see an adaptive measurement and safety checks first.

Within a single sweep, the point actions can skip a point (skip_point()), the rest of a line (skip_line()) or end the sweep (end_sweep()), based on the values just recorded.

docs.title: Instruments that take arrays
docs.text: Some channels take a whole array per point, such as the waveform of an arbitrary waveform generator. Their mapping returns the array: x*np.sin(np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 64)). See vector channels.

docs.title: Queue scripts
docs.text:
A queue script is a Python program that the backend runs from the run queue, just like a sweep. It waits its turn, it can be paused and aborted, and it appears in the queue history. Inside it you can set and read channels, wait for instruments and run sweeps, as many as you like, each into its own data file.

This page uses the graphene setup from the tutorials (Setup → Load setup… → examples/graphene_setup.json).

docs.title: Your first script
docs.text:
The task. You want to measure the Dirac peak carefully: 101 points in ±0.5 V around it, slowly. But you don't know exactly where it is, and it moves a little after every thermal cycle. By hand, you would run a quick coarse sweep, read off the peak, and then type the range into the editor. A script can do both steps in one go.

Open the Queue tab. At the bottom is the Script editor.

  1. Open… loads a .py file into the editor (and Save… saves it). Open examples/scripts/find_dirac_then_zoom.py, or type it in.
  2. The script. It is shown in full below.
  3. A name for the queue and the log. Opening a file uses the file name.
  4. Add script to queue. Then Start the queue (at the top of the tab), as for a sweep. Run now puts it at the front of the queue and starts it at once.
  5. Check looks at the script without running it: a syntax error is shown with its line, and a channel name in quotes that does not exist (get('Vbgg')) is a warning. Add script to queue and Run now check first, and refuse a script that does not compile.

The script:

# An adaptive measurement: a quick coarse sweep finds the Dirac point, then a slow
# fine sweep measures ±0.5 V around it.  run_sweep() returns the run's data, so
# the script can decide what to measure next.
coarse = run_sweep({
    "name": "dirac_coarse",
    "dimensions": [{"points": 81, "sweep": [{"channel": "Vbg", "start": -8, "stop": 8}],
                    "record": ["Rxx"]}],
})
vbg = coarse.setpoints[0]["Vbg"]
r = coarse.data["Rxx"]
v0 = float(vbg[np.nanargmax(r)])
log("coarse sweep: Dirac point near Vbg = %.2f V (Rxx = %.0f Ω)" % (v0, np.nanmax(r)))
state["dirac_point"] = v0                  # remembered for later scripts and actions

fine = run_sweep({
    "name": "dirac_fine",
    "dimensions": [{"points": 101,
                    "sweep": [{"channel": "Vbg", "start": v0 - 0.5, "stop": v0 + 0.5}],
                    "record": ["Rxx"], "pre_delay": 0.05}],
    "post": {"constants": [{"channel": "Vbg", "value": 0}]},
    "metadata": {"found_from": coarse.path},
})
log("fine sweep %s: peak Rxx = %.0f Ω" % (fine.status, np.nanmax(fine.data["Rxx"])))

Line by line:

  • run_sweep({...}) runs a sweep and waits until it has finished. The dictionary is the same as a sweep made in the editor (see A sweep is a dictionary): 81 points of Vbg from −8 to 8 V, recording Rxx. Like every sweep, it is checked against the limits of Vbg before it starts, and it is saved in its own data file.
  • run_sweep returns the measured data: coarse.setpoints[0]["Vbg"] holds the 81 gate voltages, and coarse.data["Rxx"] the 81 resistances, as numpy arrays.
  • np.nanargmax(r) finds the index of the largest resistance (nan points, if any, are skipped). v0 is the gate voltage of the peak.
  • log(...) writes a line to the log (the Log dock at the bottom of the window).
  • state["dirac_point"] = v0 keeps the result. state is a dictionary that stays in the backend until it is closed, so a later script or a user action can use state["dirac_point"].
  • The second run_sweep measures 101 points around v0, more slowly (pre_delay 0.05 s), sets Vbg back to 0 afterwards, and stores the file name of the coarse sweep in its metadata.

After it has run:

  1. The queue history shows the script. Its sweeps appear in Live data while they run, like any sweep: here the fine sweep around the peak.
  2. The log, with the lines from log(...) and the files of both sweeps. File → Browse recent runs… (or Open data file…) opens them again.

Pause and abort work everywhere

Pause and Abort in the Queue tab act on a script as on a sweep: in a running run_sweep() at the next point, and otherwise at the next line of the script. Even an endless while True: loop can be aborted. Use sleep(...) to wait, never time.sleep(...), so the wait can be aborted at once.

docs.title: What a script can use
docs.text:
Everything here is available without import:

name does get('Rxx') read any channel: an alias, a composite channel, a parameter, instrument.channel set('Vbg', 1.0) write any channel. An alias keeps its limits and ramp rate (waits until the ramp is done); set('bg.voltage', 0) writes the instrument's channel as it is set_many({'nD.n': 0, 'nD.D': 0.2}) set several at once; needed for the variables of one composite set('vna.preset'), set('gates_to_zero') run an action (of an instrument, or a user action) sleep(2) wait 2 s (abortable) wait_until(lambda: get('magnet.status') == 'HOLDING', timeout=600) check every 0.2 s until it is true, for at most timeout s. Returns False on timeout run_sweep(definition) run a sweep, wait for it, return its data (below) load_sweep(path) a sweep saved with Sweep → Save…, or the sweep of a data file, as a dictionary instrument('vna').raw_query('*IDN?') talk to an instrument directly log('text'), print(...) write to the log state a dictionary kept between scripts and user actions np, math, time numpy and the standard modules

The Script API reference has the full list. Any other module can be imported as usual (import json, from scipy.optimize import curve_fit).

docs.title: What run_sweep returns
docs.text:
run_sweep() returns a DataSet, the same object as DataSet.load(path) gives for a data file:

attribute is ds.status "finished", "terminated" (stopped by end_sweep()), "aborted" or "error" ds.data["Rxx"] the recorded values, a numpy array with one axis per dimension. Points not measured are nan ds.setpoints[0]["Vbg"] the set values of dimension 1 (setpoints[1]: dimension 2, …) ds.value_axes["S11"] the axes of a spectrum channel, e.g. the frequencies of a VNA trace ds.path the data file ds.header["definition"] the sweep that was run (its "metadata" key holds the metadata)

An aborted sweep does not raise an error: check ds.status if the script should stop then too.

docs.title: Start from a saved sweep
docs.text:
Rather than writing the dictionary by hand, design the sweep in the editor, check it with Sweep → Validate, and save it (Sweep → Save…). Then load it, change what should change, and run it:

# Repeat a sweep designed in the sweep editor (and saved there with "Save…") at
# several top-gate voltages.  The Dirac peak moves and grows: the top gate adds
# carriers and a displacement field.
base = load_sweep("examples/graphene_dirac.json")    # a full path works too
for vtg in (-2, -1, 0, 1, 2):
    set("Vtg", vtg)
    sweep = dict(base, name="dirac_at_Vtg_%+g" % vtg, metadata={"Vtg": vtg})
    ds = run_sweep(sweep)
    v = ds.setpoints[0]["Vbg"]
    peak = int(np.nanargmax(ds.data["Rxx"]))
    log("Vtg = %+g V: peak %.0f Ω at Vbg = %.2f V" % (vtg, ds.data["Rxx"][peak], v[peak]))
set("Vtg", 0)

dict(base, name=..., metadata=...) is a copy of base with two keys replaced, so each run gets its own name. Every run goes into its own file, with the top-gate voltage in its metadata.

load_sweep also takes a data file, so "measure again what I measured yesterday" is run_sweep(load_sweep("D:/data/2026-11-10/00012_dirac_peak.emj")).

Paths

A relative path such as examples/graphene_dirac.json is relative to the folder the backend was started in. A full path is always safe.

docs.title: A series of sweeps
docs.text:
A loop over conditions, with a wait for a slow instrument in between. This one runs a gate sweep at each of a list of fields. The fields need not be evenly spaced, and each gate sweep is its own file:

# A sequence: one gate sweep at each of a list of fields, each in its own file
# with the field in its metadata.  The fields need not be evenly spaced.
fields = [0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 9]
for b in fields:
    set("B", b)                                   # the magnet starts ramping
    wait_until(lambda: get("magnet.status") == "HOLDING", timeout=1200)
    sleep(1)                                      # let things settle
    ds = run_sweep({
        "name": "gate_at_%gT" % b,
        "dimensions": [{"points": 101, "snake": False,
                        "sweep": [{"channel": "Vbg", "start": -8, "stop": 8}],
                        "record": ["Rxx"]}],
        "metadata": {"B": b},
    })
    log("B = %g T: %s" % (b, ds.status))
    if ds.status != "finished":
        break                                     # aborted or failed: stop the series
set("B", 0)
set("Vbg", 0)
  • set("B", b) only sets the magnet's target. wait_until(...) waits until the supply reports HOLDING.
  • if ds.status != "finished": break ends the series when you abort one of the gate sweeps. Without it, aborting a sweep would just move on to the next field. To stop everything at once, use Abort all in the Queue tab.

The same structure works for temperatures (set("Tset", T), then wait until get("T") is close), for sample positions, and so on.

Compare this with tutorial 1, where the field is the outer dimension of a single 2-D sweep. A 2-D sweep is easier to plot as a map. A script is the better choice when the conditions are unevenly spaced, when something else has to happen in between (a gate sweep at some fields only, a warm-up, a recalibration) or when you want a separate file per condition.

docs.title: Safety checks first
docs.text:
Combine a quick test with the real measurement: find how far the gate may go, then use only 90 % of that.

# Safety first: find how far the back gate can go (stop at 1 nA of leakage), then
# measure the n–D map only within 90 % of that voltage.
test = run_sweep({
    "name": "leakage_test",
    "dimensions": [{"points": 201, "sweep": [{"channel": "Vbg", "start": 0, "stop": 10}],
                    "record": ["Ileak"],
                    "hooks": {"post_record": {"enabled": True,
                              "code": "if abs(values['Ileak']) > 1e-9: end_sweep()"}}}],
    "post": {"constants": [{"channel": "Vbg", "value": 0}]},
})
measured = np.isfinite(test.data["Ileak"])
v_max = float(test.setpoints[0]["Vbg"][measured][-1])
v_safe = 0.9 * v_max
log("leakage test %s: up to %.2f V, using %.2f V" % (test.status, v_max, v_safe))

# the largest |D| at n = 0 that keeps Vbg = (0.15 + D/0.0452) / 1.2 within v_safe
d_max = min(0.35, (1.2 * v_safe - 0.15) * 0.0452)
ds = run_sweep({
    "name": "n_D_map_safe",
    "dimensions": [
        {"points": 61, "sweep": [{"channel": "nD.n", "start": -1, "stop": 1}],
         "record": ["Rxx"], "snake": True},
        {"points": 15, "sweep": [{"channel": "nD.D", "start": -d_max, "stop": d_max}]}],
    "metadata": {"v_safe": v_safe},
})
log("map %s with |D| ≤ %.3f V/nm" % (ds.status, d_max))
set_many({"Vbg": 0, "Vtg": 0})

The first sweep is the leakage sweep of tutorial 3, with its point action written into the dictionary as "hooks". Its last measured point is the last finite (not nan) value. The map then sweeps the composite channels nD.n and nD.D of tutorial 2, with the D range computed from the safe gate voltage.

docs.title: Scripts and the rest of easyMeasure
docs.text:
• Queue a script after a sweep to have it run when the sweep is done, e.g. a script that ramps the field down at the end of the night.
  • Rerun a script from the queue history, or Copy to script editor to change it.
  • A script cannot be started from a user action or a point action, because they run outside the queue. Queue it instead.
  • Over remote access, scripts need the admin role: a script is Python with full access to the measurement computer.

Next: Custom sweeps.

docs.title: Writing a driver
docs.text:
For instruments the Driver Wizard cannot describe, such as binary protocols, vendor DLLs or unusual readouts, write a driver in Python. A driver is one file with a class deriving from Instrument.

Write the driver naively. The framework runs every call on a guarded worker thread with a deadline, retries and reconnects on errors, validates the returned data against the channel spec, and serialises access to shared ports.

docs.title: Where drivers live
docs.text:
directory easymeasure/drivers/ the built-in drivers <home>/drivers/ (~/.easymeasure/drivers/) drivers made with the wizard; your own can go here too the driver_paths setting any further directories

The driver name is the file name: my_supply.py is the driver my_supply. A driver that fails to import is reported in list_drivers()["errors"]; it is never fatal. After adding or changing a file, use rescan (c.call("rescan_drivers")).

docs.title: A complete driver
docs.text:
This is examples/driver_template.py, abridged:

from easymeasure.backend.instrument import ActionSpec, ChannelSpec, Instrument
from easymeasure.common.errors import ChannelError


class MyPowerSupply(Instrument):
    DESCRIPTION = "Example SCPI power supply"

    # access: 'r', 'w' or 'rw'; dtype: 'float' or 'str'
    # shape: () scalar, (-1,) vector of any length, (-1, -1) 2-D, (3,) fixed length …
    CHANNELS = [
        ChannelSpec("voltage", "rw", "float", (), "V", "output voltage"),
        ChannelSpec("current", "r", "float", (), "A", "measured current"),
        ChannelSpec("output", "rw", "str", (), "", "ON/OFF", config=True,
                    allowed=["ON", "OFF"]),
        ChannelSpec("range", "rw", "str", (), "", "current range", config=True,
                    allowed=["10 mA", "100 mA", "1 A"]),
        ChannelSpec("trace", "r", "float", (-1,), "A", "buffered current trace", timeout=30.0),
    ]
    ACTIONS = [ActionSpec("reset", "*RST"), ActionSpec("trigger", "*TRG")]
    DEFAULT_OPTIONS = {"timeout": 2.0, "baudrate": 9600, "call_timeout": 10.0, "retries": 2}
    INTERFACES = ("gpib", "usb", "tcpip", "tcp", "serial", "sim")
    IDN_MATCH = ("MYVENDOR,PS",)        # recognise it when ports are scanned
    SHARED_RESOURCE = False             # True for a bus several instruments share

    def connect(self):
        idn = self.resource.query("*IDN?")
        if "MYVENDOR" not in idn.upper():
            raise IOError("unexpected instrument %r" % idn)

    def _action_reset(self):
        self.resource.write("*RST")

    def _action_trigger(self):
        self.resource.write("*TRG")

    def _read_voltage(self):
        return self.resource.query("VOLT?")        # strings are converted to float

    def _write_voltage(self, value):
        if value < 0:
            raise ChannelError("negative voltages are not supported")   # not retried
        self.resource.write("VOLT %.6f" % value)   # value is already a float

    def _read_current(self):
        return self.resource.query("MEAS:CURR?")

    def _read_output(self):
        return "ON" if self.resource.query("OUTP?").strip() in ("1", "ON") else "OFF"

    def _write_output(self, value):
        self.resource.write("OUTP %s" % value)     # already "ON" or "OFF"

    def _read_trace(self):
        return self.resource.query("TRAC:DATA?")    # "1.0,2.0,3.0" → numpy array

docs.title: Channels
docs.text:
ChannelSpec(name, access, dtype, shape, unit, description, timeout=None, config=False, allowed=None):

argument meaning access "r", "w" or "rw" dtype "float" (scalars and arrays) or "str" shape () scalar; (-1,) vector of any length; (64,) fixed; (-1, -1) image; None anything unit, description shown in the front ends, stored in data files timeout per-channel deadline, for slow readings config a setting (range, mode …): listed apart, shown with ⚙, typical as a sweep constant allowed accepted values; writes are checked and normalised, front ends show a drop-down

Implement _read_<name>() and _write_<name>(value), or override read(channel) / write(channel, value) for all channels at once. Return values are converted and checked against the spec: strings like "1.5" or "1,2,3" become numbers and arrays, and a wrong shape is an error.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text: ActionSpec(name, description, timeout=None), implemented by _action_<name>(), or by overriding action(name). Actions are never retried automatically. An action is a write-only channel of the instrument (dmm.reset), so its name may not be the name of one of the driver's channels: such a driver fails to connect with a message saying which name.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: DEFAULT_OPTIONS are the defaults of the instrument's options. Users edit them per instrument, and they are passed to the port. Port options include timeout, baudrate, read_termination and write_termination. Framework options are listed under guard options. Read them as self.options[...].

docs.title: I/O
docs.text:
Inside driver methods, self.resource is the port, already inside a transaction:

method does write(cmd) send a command (text or bytes) read() read one reply (text) query(cmd, delay=0) write, then read read_raw(size=None) read bytes clear() clear the port

The same calls work on VISA, serial, raw TCP and the simulated buses. For non-message-based hardware such as a DAQ card or a vendor DLL, use the vendor's library directly in connect / _read_…, with the address NONE or DAQ::….

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• Raise ChannelError for a refused value (out of range, not supported). It is reported, and not retried.
  • Any other exception counts as an I/O problem. It is retried and, after reconnect_after failures, the instrument is reconnected.

docs.title: Channel lists that follow the instrument
docs.text:
Override get_channels() (and get_actions()) to return a list that depends on the state the driver knows, for example the mode it last set. The backend calls it again after every configuration write, action and reconnect, and the front ends follow. Keep it free of I/O:

def get_channels(self):
    src = "current" if self.mode == "Current" else "voltage"
    meas = "voltage" if src == "current" else "current"
    return [ChannelSpec(src, "rw", "float", (), "A" if src == "current" else "V"),
            ChannelSpec(meas, "r", "float", (), "V" if meas == "voltage" else "A"),
            ChannelSpec("mode", "rw", "str", (), "", config=True,
                        allowed=["Voltage", "Current"])]

docs.title: Shared ports
docs.text:
Set SHARED_RESOURCE = True (or the instrument option shared), and implement select to make this instrument the active one on the bus whenever it takes over:

def select(self, resource):
    resource.write("++addr %d" % self.options["gpib_addr"])

docs.title: Address suggestions and recognition
docs.text:
INTERFACES limits which addresses are accepted. IDN_MATCH strings mark scanned devices whose *IDN? contains them. A suggested_addresses classmethod can offer addresses without a scan, such as a built-in emulator:

@classmethod
def suggested_addresses(cls, driver_name):
    return [{"address": "SIM::" + driver_name, "description": "built-in emulator"}]

docs.title: Testing a driver without the instrument
docs.text:
The hardware drivers come with emulators (easymeasure/drivers/emulators/) that implement the instrument's command table from its programming manual. The tests check that every command a driver sends exists in that table. Model a new driver's tests on tests/test_drivers.py and tests/test_cygnus.py. The simplest check is:

be.add_instrument("ps", "my_supply", "SIM::ps")
assert be.read_channel(name="ps.voltage") == 0.0

See the driver reference pages for how the built-in drivers are organised, and Instrument for the full base class.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
The tutorials follow a new PhD student through the first measurements of a project. Each one is a real measurement, done entirely in the GUI, step by step with screenshots. Each introduces one or two new ideas.

All of them run on simulated instruments that come with easyMeasure: a dual-gated bilayer graphene Hall bar measured with a lock-in, a superconducting magnet, and a microwave resonator measured with a vector network analyzer. The simulations behave like the real thing (Dirac peak, Landau levels, a band gap that opens with displacement field, gate leakage, a resonance that shifts with power and field), so you can try everything before touching a real sample. With real instruments, only the driver and address change.

Start with the Quick start if you haven't yet: it sets up the instruments the first three tutorials use.

  • Tutorial 1: a Landau fan

    A 2-D map of gate voltage against magnetic field. Two dimensions, snake scans, waiting for a magnet that takes time to ramp, heat maps and curves with sliders.

  • Tutorial 2: rotated gate sweeps

    \(R_{xx} = V_{xx}/I\) from two lock-ins, and sweeps of carrier density and displacement field instead of two gate voltages: composite channels, and what happens to points the gates can't reach.

  • Tutorial 3: stop at a threshold

    Ramp a gate until the leakage current reaches 1 nA, then stop by itself. Point actions, and one-click buttons of your own (gates_to_zero).

  • Tutorial 4: a VNA power sweep

    The power and field dependence of a microwave resonance. Instruments that return a whole spectrum per reading, 2-D and 3-D data, and how to look at them.

After the tutorials, the User guide explains every part in full, and Scripting and Python shows what to do when the GUI is not enough: series of sweeps, measurements that decide where to measure next, and sweeps along any path you can write down.

docs.title: Tutorial 1: a Landau fan (2-D map)
docs.text:
You will learn: two-dimensional sweeps, snake scans, waiting for a slow instrument with a point action, and looking at 2-D data as a map and as curves.

This continues the Quick start. You have the graphene Hall bar with the instruments bg and lockin and the aliases Vbg, Ileak and Rxx. If you start fresh: Setup → Load setup… → examples/graphene_setup.json.

The physics. In a perpendicular magnetic field the electrons of graphene condense into Landau levels. \(R_{xx}\) drops whenever a whole number of levels is filled. For bilayer graphene this happens at filling factors \(\nu = nh/eB = 4, 8, 12, \dots\), so in a map of \(R_{xx}\) against gate voltage and field the minima lie on straight lines fanning out from the Dirac point: a Landau fan. You need a 2-D map: gate voltage (fast) × field (slow).

docs.title: 1. Add the magnet
docs.text:
In the lab this is the power supply of a superconducting magnet. Here it is sim_magnet, which, like a real one, takes time to ramp: 10 T per minute. Instruments → Add…:

Then select magnet, select its channel field, and click Make alias…. Name B, minimum −9, maximum 9 T:

No ramp rate this time: the magnet supply ramps by itself. Writing B only sets its target, and the field gets there at the supply's own rate.

docs.title: 2. Two dimensions
docs.text:
In the Sweep editor, start from your Dirac-peak sweep, or click New. A sweep can have any number of dimensions. Each one is a loop, and the first is the innermost. Use + dimension to add the second one.

Dimension 1 (inner, fast): the gate.

  1. The dimension list: Dim 1 is the innermost loop, Dim 2 runs around it.
  2. Sweep Vbg from −8 to 8 V in 101 points.
  3. snake scan: every other line runs backwards (−8 → 8, then 8 → −8, …). Otherwise the gate would ramp from +8 back to −8 V before every line, which takes 3 s at 5 V/s.
  4. Record Rxx.

Dimension 2 (outer, slow): the field.

  1. Sweep B from 0 to 9 T in 61 points (0.15 T steps), and record B (the field that was really reached).
  2. Tick the post-sweep action. A point action is a small piece of Python run at every point of this dimension, at a fixed place in the sequence. Post-sweep runs right after B was set.

  3. Its code waits until the magnet has arrived:

    wait_until(lambda: get('magnet.status') == 'HOLDING', timeout=600)

    get('magnet.status') reads the supply's status channel, which is RAMPING or HOLDING. wait_until checks it until it is true, for at most 600 s. Pause and abort still work while it waits.

    You don't need to type it: the + action box next to the code offers common snippets.

Each dimension is laid out in the order its steps happen at every point: set the swept channels → (post-sweep action) → delay → record. With several dimensions, the inner dimension's whole loop runs at the end of each outer point, and the editor shows where.

In the Post-sweep tab, set Vbg = 0 and B = 0, so everything returns to zero at the end. Then Sweep → Validate: 101 × 61 = 6161 points, every one checked against the limits of Vbg and B.

This sweep is examples/graphene_fan.json.

docs.title: 3. Run it and watch the field
docs.text:
Sweep → Add & start. While it runs, add B to the Monitor (choose B, click Monitor) to watch the magnet step and settle:

The whole map takes a few minutes in the simulation. In a real fridge you would use smaller field steps and slower gate sweeps, and it would take hours. You can close the GUI and come back later.

Ramping the field continuously

Here the field is stepped and the magnet settles at every step. The other common way is to sweep the field continuously and record as it goes, at a fixed gate voltage. That is a small script: see Custom sweeps → time traces.

docs.title: 4. Look at the map
docs.text:
For 2-D data the plot is a heat map: X = Vbg, Y = B, colour = \(R_{xx}\).

  • Drag the colour bar on the right to set the colour range. Its histogram shows where the values are.
  • ⚙ chooses the colormap and switches automatic levels on or off.
  • Zoom with the mouse wheel; right-click → View all.

The minima form straight lines from the Dirac point: the Landau fan. Their slopes give the filling factors.

As curves. Set the mode to Curve (1). Now you see one line, \(R_{xx}(V_{bg})\) at one field, and a slider (2) chooses which field. With follow latest the slider follows the line being measured. Stacked curves draws all lines at once, offset from each other.

More plots. Add plot shows another channel, or the same one in another mode. columns sets how many plots sit side by side.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• A dimension is a loop; dimension 1 is the innermost. A 2-D map needs two.
  • Snake scans avoid long ramps back to the start of each line.
  • A point action runs a line of code at a fixed place in every point. Post-sweep plus wait_until(...) waits for a slow instrument.
  • 2-D data are shown as a heat map, or as curves with a slider.

Next: Tutorial 2: rotated gate sweeps.

Reference

Sweeps and Point actions in the user guide have every option.

docs.title: Tutorial 2: rotated gate sweeps with composite channels
docs.text:
You will learn: composite channels. A composite read computes a channel from others (\(R_{xx} = V_{xx}/I\) from two lock-ins). A multivariate write lets you sweep physical quantities (density and displacement field) instead of instrument voltages. You will also see what happens to points that would need a gate voltage beyond its limit.

The physics. Your bilayer graphene has a top gate too. The two gates together set two physical quantities:

  • the carrier density \(n = (C_b V_{bg} + C_t V_{tg})/e + n_0\);
  • the displacement field \(D = (C_b V_{bg} - C_t V_{tg})/2\varepsilon_0\), which opens a band gap in bilayer graphene.

To see the gap open, you want to sweep \(n\) at fixed \(D\), then step \(D\). In the \((V_{bg}, V_{tg})\) plane these are lines at an angle, a rotated sweep: both gates move at every point. easyMeasure does this with a composite channel. You define \(n\) and \(D\) as channels of their own, give the formulas for the gate voltages, and then sweep \(n\) and \(D\) like any other channel.

For this device, \(C_b/e = 0.6\) and \(C_t/e = 0.9 \times 10^{12}\,\text{cm}^{-2}\,\text{V}^{-1}\), \(n_0 = -0.15 \times 10^{12}\,\text{cm}^{-2}\), and \(e/2\varepsilon_0 = 0.0452\) V/nm per \(10^{12}\,\text{cm}^{-2}\). Solving the two equations for the gate voltages (\(n\) in \(10^{12}\,\text{cm}^{-2}\), \(D\) in V/nm):

\[ V_{bg} = \frac{n + 0.15 + D/0.0452}{2 \times 0.6}, \qquad V_{tg} = \frac{n + 0.15 - D/0.0452}{2 \times 0.9} \]

docs.title: 1. The top gate
docs.text: Add a second sim_smu named tg (address NONE). Make an alias of tg.voltage named Vtg, with limits −10 … 10 V and ramp rate 5 V/s, exactly like Vbg (Quick start, step 4).

docs.title: 2. Measure the current too: Rxx = Vxx / I
docs.text:
So far, Rxx was the lock-in voltage × 10⁸, which assumes that exactly 10 nA flows. The current is set by the lock-in's 10 mV output and a 1 MΩ series resistor. That is fine while the sample has a few kΩ. But once the gap opens, the sample reaches hundreds of kΩ, the current drops, and \(V_{xx}/10\,\text{nA}\) underestimates \(R_{xx}\). The usual remedy is to measure the current with a second lock-in, locked to the first one's reference, and divide.

The second lock-in. Instruments → Add…: name ilockin, driver sim_lockin, address NONE. In the lab this is a second SR830 measuring with its current input. The simulation needs to know that it measures the current, driven by the first lock-in's output:

  1. Name ilockin.
  2. Driver sim_lockin.
  3. Options: "sample": "graphene", "measure": "current", "source": "lockin.amplitude".

Two aliases. Make an alias of lockin.X named Vxx (unit V), and one of ilockin.X named I (unit A).

Rxx as a composite read. On the Channels (aliased) tab, select the old alias Rxx and click Remove. Then, on the Channels (composite) tab, click Add…:

  1. Name Rxx, the same name as before, so every sweep that records Rxx keeps working.
  2. Type: Composite read, a read-only channel computed from others.
  3. Formula: Vxx / I. Any formula of channels works: 1/Rxx for a conductance, (V1 - V2)/I for a voltage measured as a difference, and so on.
  4. Unit: Ω.
  5. Check, then OK.

Reading Rxx now reads Vxx and I and divides. It can be recorded, monitored and plotted like any channel. In the gap, at \(D = 0.3\) V/nm, it reads about a third more than the old alias did, because only about 7.5 nA flow there.

docs.title: 3. The device's constants as parameters
docs.text:
The formulas for the gates contain four numbers that belong to this particular device: the two capacitances, the intrinsic doping and \(e/2\varepsilon_0\). Rather than typing them into formulas, give each a name as a parameter. When you cool down the next device, or calibrate the capacitances better from a Landau fan, you change the number in one place.

In Instruments & channels, on the Parameters tab, click Add…:

  1. Name Cb.
  2. Value or formula: 0.6. A number is a value; the line below says so.
  3. Unit 1e12 cm^-2/V (and a description, if you like).
  4. Check shows ✔ Cb = 0.6; OK checks again and saves it.

Add the others the same way:

Name Value Unit Description Cb 0.6 1e12 cm^-2/V back-gate capacitance / e Ct 0.9 1e12 cm^-2/V top-gate capacitance / e n0 -0.15 1e12 cm^-2 intrinsic doping kD 0.0452 V/nm per 1e12 cm^-2 e / 2ε₀

A parameter can also be a formula of other parameters: type Ct/Cb instead of a number. Parameters are constants: they can be changed here or in the Manual panel, but never by a sweep or a script. Every data file records their values. See Parameters.

docs.title: 4. The composite channel n, D
docs.text:
On the Channels (composite) tab, click Add… again:

  1. Name nD; Type: Multivariate write. You set variables, and the hardware follows.

  2. Variables: one row each, using Add variable.

    Name Min Max Unit Description n -4 4 1e12 cm^-2 carrier density D -0.45 0.45 V/nm displacement field

    Each variable gets its own limits, unit and, optionally, a ramp rate. Outside this editor, a variable is called after its composite: nD.n and nD.D. 3. Targets: one line per gate, channel = formula of the variables (and of parameters):

    Vbg = (n - n0 + D/kD) / (2*Cb)
Vtg = (n - n0 - D/kD) / (2*Ct)

    This is the pair of equations above, written with the parameters. Here, inside the composite, the variables go by their short names n and D.

  3. Out of range: what to do with a combination of n and D that would need a gate voltage beyond its ±10 V limit. Leave it at Skip the point (see below).

  4. Check asks the backend whether everything is right without saving anything: the names, the formulas, and that the targets exist and can be set. It answers ✔ defines nD.n, nD.D. OK checks again before it saves.

OK, and the composite appears in the table next to Rxx, with a row for each of its variables below it, ↳ nD.n and ↳ nD.D, by the names you use from now on:

nD.n and nD.D are now channels like Vbg: you can set them, sweep them and record them. Whenever one of them is set:

  • both gate voltages are computed;
  • everything is checked against all limits: the limits of nD.n and nD.D, and also the ±10 V of Vbg and Vtg;
  • both gates then ramp together, each within its own ramp rate.

docs.title: 5. Set n and D by hand
docs.text:
The Manual panel now has a group nD, with n and D (short for nD.n and nD.D) indented below it. Neither has been set yet, so neither has a value. Setting n alone would need a value of D to compute the gates, and there is none. The panel shows this:

  1. The group header of the composite nD, marked not set yet.
  2. n and D show NaN, and their sliders are greyed out.
  3. hold is ticked, and stays ticked until both have been set: whatever you type is held (blue), not sent.
  4. Set all to zero: n and D are set to 0 together, and both gates move there.

Click Set all to zero. Alternatively, type a value into n and one into D, then click Set all, which lights up once neither shows NaN.

Now the group works like any other channel: hold unticks itself, the sliders work, and you can change either variable alone; the other keeps its value.

To set both to other values at once, tick hold, type the values, and click Set all: the changes are collected and sent together.

docs.title: 6. Sweep n and D
docs.text:
In the Sweep editor, sweep the variables:

  1. Two dimensions.
  2. Dimension 1: nD.n from −4 to 4 in 101 points, snake scan. Dimension 2: nD.D from −0.45 to 0.45 in 31 points.
  3. Record Rxx.
  4. Sweep → Validate computes all 3131 combinations, converts each to gate voltages and checks them. Some of them are out of range: at large \(n\) and \(D\) of the same sign, \(V_{bg}\) would have to exceed 10 V. Validation says how many points will be skipped.

This sweep is examples/graphene_nD.json.

Out-of-range points. Usually the rectangle you want in \((n, D)\) doesn't fit in the square the gates allow. The composite's Out of range setting decides what happens to the corners:

Out of range in a sweep set by hand or from a script Skip the point (default) the point is skipped before anything is set: no gate moves, its data stay empty refused, with the reason Error the sweep does not start; validation names the first bad point refused Clamp to the limit the gate stops at its limit; the point is measured, but not at the \((n, D)\) it is labelled with the gate stops at its limit

For \(n\)–\(D\) maps, Skip is what you want: you get the whole region the gates can reach, and an empty corner where they can't. Error is for when every point must be measured. Clamp suits cases where running into the limit is harmless and the nearest reachable value is good enough.

nD.n is swept in dimension 1 and nD.D in dimension 2, but the gates never see one without the other. At every point, n and D are set together, so a new value of D doesn't move the gates with the old n from the end of the previous line.

docs.title: 7. The result
docs.text:
At \(n = 0\) the resistance grows steeply with \(|D|\): the band gap of bilayer graphene opening in a displacement field. The two empty corners are the skipped points, where \(V_{bg}\) would have exceeded 10 V. The same measurement plotted against \(V_{bg}\) and \(V_{tg}\) would show the same feature along a tilted line.

Sweeping two things in one dimension

You can also put both nD.n and nD.D in the same dimension, e.g. nD.n from −2 to 2 and nD.D from −0.3 to 0.3 together. That is a diagonal cut through the \((n, D)\) plane. Variables of one composite swept in the same dimension are set together at every point. With a formula for each, the path can be any curve, such as a circle around \(n = D = 0\): see Custom sweeps.

docs.title: Other kinds of composite channel
docs.text:
type what it does example Multivariate write variables of your choice drive hardware channels through formulas \(n, D\) → \(V_{bg}, V_{tg}\); detuning ε and energy U of a double dot Composite read a read-only formula of other channels \(R_{xx} = V_{xx}/I\); conductance 1/Rxx; a sum of two signals Simple mapping a one-to-one view of one channel, with formulas both ways (checked to be each other's inverse) a field in mT on a supply in A; a temperature in °C on a controller in K

Formulas can be piecewise: piecewise(x < 0, -x, 2*x), a if c else b, interp(x, [...], [...]). Composite channels can also build on each other. See Composite channels for everything.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• A composite read computes a channel from others, such as \(R_{xx} = V_{xx}/I\) from two lock-ins. It is read, recorded and plotted like any channel.
  • Parameters name the constants of a device (capacitances, doping), so formulas stay readable and a new calibration is one change.
  • A multivariate composite turns physical quantities (\(n\), \(D\)) into the voltages of several instruments. You sweep the physics; easyMeasure moves the hardware.
  • Every point is checked against the limits of the variables and of every gate. With Out of range: Skip, points the gates can't reach are left out of the map.
  • New variables show NaN until they are first set together: start with Set all to zero, then set either variable alone.

Next: Tutorial 3: stop at a threshold.

docs.title: Tutorial 3: stop a measurement at a threshold
docs.text:
You will learn: point actions that decide something at every point (here: stop the sweep when the leakage current gets too high), and one-click actions of your own.

The situation. How far can you push the back gate? Gate dielectrics leak more and more as the voltage rises, and eventually break down, which destroys the device. A careful way to find out is to ramp the gate up slowly while watching the leakage current, and stop the moment it exceeds a threshold, say 1 nA.

Alias limits (±10 V on Vbg) are a hard ceiling that nothing can cross. A threshold is different: easyMeasure watches a measured value and reacts to it.

docs.title: 1. The sweep
docs.text:
In the Sweep editor:

  • one dimension: Vbg from 0 to 10 V, 201 points;
  • record Ileak and Rxx;
  • in Post-sweep: Vbg = 0, so the gate goes back down at the end, however the measurement ended.

docs.title: 2. The point action
docs.text:
Tick post-record. This action runs at every point, right after the values were recorded:

  1. post-record: the action that runs right after recording.

  2. The code:

    if abs(values['Ileak']) > 1e-9:
    log('leakage %.2g A at Vbg = %.2f V: stopping' % (values['Ileak'], setpoints['Vbg']))
    end_sweep()
    • values holds what was just recorded: values['Ileak'] is this point's leakage current, in A.
    • setpoints holds what was set at this point: setpoints['Vbg'].
    • log(...) writes a line to the log.
    • end_sweep() ends the whole measurement normally. The data so far is saved, and the post-sweep phase runs, which here sets Vbg back to 0.
    • + action offers the common snippets, so you don't have to remember the names: Terminate the entire sweep, Skip this point, Skip this line, and actions of your instruments.
call like in a Python loop does end_sweep() exit stop the measurement; status terminated skip_line() break finish this line of a 2-D map early; the next line starts skip_point() continue skip the rest of this point; its data stays empty

This sweep is examples/graphene_leakage.json. Sweep → Add & start.

docs.title: 3. The result
docs.text:
The leakage current rises steeply above 8 V. At about 9.6 V it passes 1 nA and the sweep stops by itself:

  • its status is terminated (not aborted: it ended the way you asked);
  • the log says where and why;
  • Vbg ramps back to 0 V;
  • the points that were not measured are empty (NaN) in the file.

In a 2-D map, skip_line() instead of end_sweep() would finish just the current line, and the map would continue with the next one. A typical case is stopping each gate sweep at the leakage threshold while stepping the field.

docs.title: More things to do in point actions
docs.text: when code post-record if values['Rxx'] > 1e6: skip_line(): the device went insulating; next line pre-record set('dmm.trigger'): trigger a meter in triggered mode post-sweep wait_until(lambda: abs(get('T') - setpoints['Tset']) < 0.01, timeout=1800): wait for the temperature pre-sweep if 0.10 < setpoints['Vbg'] < 0.12: skip_point(): skip a known bad spot

docs.title: 4. One-click actions of your own
docs.text:
Some things you do again and again: bring both gates to zero, switch outputs off, ramp the magnet down. Make each one a button. On Instruments & channels, on the User Actions tab, click Add…:

  • Name: gates_to_zero (letters, digits and _: an action is a channel, and writing it runs it, so a script can also run it with set('gates_to_zero')), and a Description shown in the list.

  • Code: the same small Python as in point actions:

    set_many({'Vbg': 0, 'Vtg': 0})
print('both gates at 0 V')

    set_many sets several channels together, each with its limits and ramp rate. * ask before running: tick it for actions that should be confirmed first. * Check checks the code without running it: a syntax error, or a channel in quotes that does not exist. OK checks too.

Select it and click ▶ Run (or press Enter):

  1. Your actions, with the result of the last run.
  2. ▶ Run, and ■ Abort to stop a running action.

Your actions are also buttons at the top of the Manual panel, at hand while you work there:

  1. ▶ gates_to_zero runs the action. While an action runs its button turns orange (■), and clicking it again aborts it.
  2. Below the channels, under Parameters, the setup's parameters: type a value and press Enter to change one.

Actions run at once, not through the queue, so they also work while a measurement is paused. They are saved with your setup. Their code can use the setup's parameters by name, e.g. set('Vbg', V0).

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• A post-record point action sees each point's values and can stop the measurement (end_sweep), finish the line (skip_line) or skip the point (skip_point).
  • The post-sweep phase always runs, so the sample is brought back to a safe state.
  • User actions turn routine steps into buttons.

Next: Tutorial 4: a VNA power sweep.

docs.title: Tutorial 4: a VNA power sweep (high-dimensional data)
docs.text:
You will learn: instruments that return a whole spectrum per reading, how a 1-D sweep then gives 2-D data and a 2-D sweep gives 3-D data, and how to look at it.

The story. A new student in the group measures superconducting microwave resonators. The question: how do the resonance frequency and the quality factor depend on the microwave power? The vector network analyzer (VNA) measures the reflection \(S_{11}\) over a frequency window around the resonance. Each reading is a whole trace of 401 points. At low power the resonance is shallow, because two-level-system losses dominate. As the power rises, these saturate and the dip deepens. At high power the Kerr nonlinearity pulls the resonance down. Later, a magnetic field is added as a third parameter.

role real instrument simulated stand-in VNA Keysight PNA / Rohde & Schwarz ZNB / … (a driver from the Driver Wizard or written for it) sim_vna magnet supply any sim_magnet

Start with a fresh setup (Setup → Load setup… → examples/vna_setup.json has everything below).

docs.title: 1. The VNA
docs.text:
Instruments → Add…: name vna, driver sim_vna, address NONE.

Its channels:

channel is power source power, dBm: you will sweep this S11 one whole frequency sweep: the magnitude in dB, an array of points values S11_phase the same sweep's phase, degrees frequencies the frequency of each point ⚙ f_start, f_stop, points, if_bandwidth, output settings

Settings are changed with Set… under the channel list, or in a sweep's Pre-sweep constants (below), so every measurement records how the VNA was set.

Make aliases:

  • P for vna.power, with limits −80 … 0 dBm. This protects the sample and the amplifiers from too much power.
  • S11 and phase for the two traces.
  • B for magnet.field, with limits −1 … 1 T.

A look at the trace. Monitor S11. A 401-point trace is shown as a curve, refreshed every reading:

docs.title: 2. Power dependence: a 1-D sweep that gives 2-D data
docs.text:
1. Sweep P from −70 to 0 dBm in 36 points (2 dB steps).
  2. Record S11 and phase.

In Pre-sweep, set the constants vna.if_bandwidth = 1000 and vna.points = 401. In Post-sweep, set P = −30.

This sweep is examples/vna_power.json. Every recorded value is a trace of 401 points, so the result is two-dimensional: power × frequency. S11 is stored as an array of shape (36, 401).

The plot puts the frequency on X (the VNA tells easyMeasure the frequency of each point, so the axis is in Hz, not point numbers) and the swept power on Y. The resonance deepens from −70 to −40 dBm as the losses saturate, then bends to lower frequency at the highest powers. The low-power traces are noisier: less signal. In a real measurement you would use a smaller IF bandwidth or averaging there.

As spectra. Mode Stacked curves draws every trace, offset by power:

Curve shows one trace, with a slider for the power.

docs.title: 3. Add the field: 3-D data
docs.text:
Add a second dimension: B from 0 to 0.5 T in 11 points, recording B. Tick the post-sweep action and wait for the magnet, as in tutorial 1:

  1. Dimension 2 runs around dimension 1: a full power sweep at every field.
  2. B from 0 to 0.5 T.
  3. The post-sweep action: wait_until(lambda: get('magnet.status') == 'HOLDING', timeout=600).

This sweep is examples/vna_power_field.json. Now S11 has shape (36, 11, 401): power × field × frequency, three-dimensional.

A plot shows two of the axes, and every other axis gets a slider. Two plots of the same data, side by side:

  • Left: X = frequency, Y = P, and a slider (2) for B. This is the power dependence at one field. Move the slider to see it change with field.
  • Right: X = frequency, Y = B (3), and a slider (4) for P. The resonance moves down and broadens as the field rises (kinetic inductance and vortex losses).

Use Add plot for more views. Each plot's Y box (1, 3) picks the second axis, and (none) gives a curve with sliders for everything else. Any number of dimensions works the same way: add a temperature dimension and you have 4-D data and two sliders.

docs.title: 4. The data afterwards
docs.text:
The file holds the arrays with all their axes, including the frequency axis of the traces. In Python:

from easymeasure.backend.storage import DataSet
ds = DataSet.load("D:/data/2026-11-11/00002_power_and_field.emj")
S = ds.data["S11"]                          # (36, 11, 401): P × B × frequency
P = ds.setpoints[0]["P"]                    # 36 powers
B = ds.setpoints[1]["B"]                    # 11 fields (as set; ds.data["B"]: as measured)
f = ds.value_axes["S11"][0]["coords"]       # 401 frequencies, Hz

import numpy as np
f0 = f[np.argmin(S, axis=-1)]               # resonance frequency at every (P, B): (36, 11)

The HDF5 copy has the same, under /data/S11, /setpoints/0/P, /setpoints/1/B and /value_axes/S11/0 (the frequencies). See Data files.

docs.title: What you learned
docs.text:
• A channel can return a whole spectrum. Each reading then adds its own axis to the data, and the frequency axis comes from the instrument.
  • A 1-D sweep of a spectrum gives 2-D data; a 2-D sweep gives 3-D data. There is no limit.
  • Plots show any two axes; every other axis becomes a slider. Several plots can show different cuts of the same data.

docs.title: Where to go from here
docs.text:
• The User guide explains each part in full: instruments, sweeps, plots, data files, remote access.
  • Scripting and Python, when the GUI is not enough: loops over conditions, sweeps computed on the fly, controlling easyMeasure from a notebook.
  • Supported instruments, and the Driver Wizard for instruments without a driver.
